Lab Tests
CPK (Creatine Phosphokinase)
- Present in heart and skeletal muscle.
- Elevated levels: cardiac injury.
- Valuable in diagnosing a myocardial infarction (MI).
Ck-MB (Creatine Kinase MB Isoenzyme)
- Elevated after an MI.
- Peaks around 24 hours post-chest pain onset.
- Normalizes within about 3 days.
- Helps gauge heart muscle damage extent.
Creatinine clearance
- Reflects kidneys' waste filtration ability and indicates overall kidney health.
- Impaired in cases of glomerulonephritis and acute tubular necrosis.
- Testing Process:
- Involves 24-hour urine collection and serum creatinine level.
- Calculation offers insights into kidney function.
Glucose tolerance test
- Evaluates the body's response to glucose.
- Useful for diagnosing diabetes and gauging insulin sensitivity.
- Test Protocol:
- Patient ingests standard oral glucose load.
- Blood and urine samples were collected before and at intervals after glucose intake (30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, and
4 hours).

Allen's Test
- Purpose:
- To evaluate circulation within the hand. The nurse should perform Allen’s Test before arterial blood gas (ABG)
collection. The test identifies the presence of adequate circulation.
- Test Procedure:
- Patient forms a fist and the nurse compresses the ulnar and radial arteries, causing hand blanching.
- Patient opens the hand while the nurse releases pressure on one artery.
- Perfused Hand Confirmation:
- Successful test outcome is indicated by color returning to the hand.
Community Nursing
Community Nursing is the least important while studying. Spend the least amount of time surrounding Community Nursing.
Environmental health
- Nurses gather information to understand the effects that environmental hazards have on populations at risk (Migrant
workers/immigrants, poor/homeless, victims of abuse/violence, substance abusers, those with mental illness, older adults,
pregnant teens, individuals with communicable diseases).
- Nurse roles
- Encourage community involvement, conduct personal and population risk evaluations, execute risk communication
strategies, conduct epidemiological inquiries, and engage in policy formulation.
- Identify vulnerable groups.
Ethical principles to community health nursing
⎼ Distributive justice
- Sharing society's benefits and responsibilities, considering the needs and contributions of its members.
- Eligibility for healthcare services is determined by income and financial resources, particularly in the case of the
homeless population.
⎼ Nonmaleficence
- Ensures the absence of harm when implementing care standards.
- Formulating care plans that incorporate a mechanism for tracking and assessing outcomes.
⎼ Respect for autonomy
- Individuals select actions that fulfill their desires.
- Respecting a client’s right to self-determination (making a decision not to pursue radiation when diagnosed with
cancer).
Older adult population
- Home health nurses prioritize identifying household environmental hazards.
- Enhance sleep by having a light bedtime snack.
- Ensure safety with bars in baths and showers.
- Acknowledge reduced taste in older adults.
- Conduct private interviews if elder abuse is suspected.
Home visits
- Home visits let community health nurses assess homes and spot health risk obstacles.

Fundamentals of Nursing
Informed consent
- Not needed in emergencies.
- Capacity: Adult age, competence (understands and chooses), voluntary.
- Free choice, no force, fraud, duress, or coercion.
- No influence of drugs or alcohol on consent.
- Nurse's signature on the form confirms observed and authorized consent.
- If procedure refusal from the patient follows consent, nurse affirms treatment will not occur.
Reporting Act
- Abuse of children and the elderly, gunshot injuries and criminal actions, infectious illnesses (even Lyme Disease), ophthalmia
neonatorum, and phenylketonuria.
When to question provider orders
- Patient has questions, altered patient status, inconsistent with nurse’s familiarity/scope, lack doctor's co-signature, unclear to
the nurse.
Ethical principles for client care
- Autonomy: the privilege to make personal choices, even when they aren't ideal
- Beneficence: actions for others' benefit, without self-interest
- Fidelity: keeping promises
- Justice: equitable care and resource use
- Nonmaleficence: vow to prevent harm
- Veracity: commitment to truthfulness
Torts
Quasi-intentional Torts
Defamation
● Examples of defamation: A nurse spreads rumors about a patient's financial difficulties, causing harm to their reputation.
Breach of confidentiality
● Examples of breach of confidentiality: A nurse leaks a patient's psychiatric history to friends, unauthorized sharing of private data.
(Note: Nurses can send/share personal info if consent is obtained.)
● When a nursing manager observes employees accessing unrelated records, it's the manager's duty to instruct them to
close the records immediately.
Intentional
Assault
● Intending to harm or initiating physical contact without consent.
● Examples of assault: Raising a hand aggressively toward a patient, threatening to force treatment.
Battery
● Unlawful physical touch.
● Examples of battery: A nurse restrains a client and administers an injection against their wishes.
False Imprisonment
● Restraining or confining someone against their wishes.

text: ● Examples of false imprisonment: Locking a patient in their room, using restraints without consent, and confining a person
without medical justification.
■ No informed consent = false imprisonment
Unintentional
Negligence
● When a nurse fails to act reasonably in a situation.
● Can result in harm due to failure to fulfill responsibilities.
● Examples of negligence: A nurse neglects to secure a patient's bed rails, leading to a fall. A nurse fails to provide medication at
the right time, worsening the patient's condition.
Malpractice
● Showing a lack of skill or fidelity in professional duties.
● Examples of malpractice: Not intervening when a patient's condition deteriorates. Administering excessive medication doses due
to calculation errors, or giving IV bolus of Potassium (cannot be given IV bolus).
Nursing considerations regarding civil law violations:
1. Act when patient privacy or dignity is compromised.
2. Adequately shield the body during procedures.
3. Share medical records solely with a written patient agreement.
4. Safeguard client belongings; avoid searches without proper authorization.
Nursing Considerations in the Hospital
Advanced directives
Living will
- Official paper expressing a person's medical preferences for end-of-life scenarios when incapacitated. It often covers
life-prolonging interventions.
- The nurse should record whether the patient has an advanced directive and communicate with the family about the
provider's discussions.
- The nurse must assess the client's comprehension of life-sustaining actions, such as CPR, mechanical ventilation,
and artificial feeding.
- Designed to grant patients greater influence over end-of-life healthcare choices.
Documentation
- Documentation serves to ensure consistent care and improve communication among team members, ultimately enhancing
client safety.
Nursing considerations
- Begin every entry with the date and time.
- Enter information in permanent black ink without gaps.
- Avoid using correction methods like fluid, erasing, or scratching.
- Rectify mistakes promptly.
- Sign as stipulated, usually with name and title.
- Include assessment, interventions, and evaluations.
- Exclude personal opinions or client criticism from documentation.
Restraints
⎼ Physical restraints
- Must have a doctor's order (cannot write PRN prescriptions for restraints).
- In urgent cases, restraints can be used temporarily without a doctor's order.
- Restraints are necessary when a patient poses self-harm or harm to others, and alternatives are ineffective.

- Psychotropic medications are not intended for behavior management.
- Inappropriate use of chemical restraints can result in excessive sedation, agitation, combativeness, and potential

Telephone medication prescription
- Only when absolutely necessary.
- Reserved for critical need only.
- Include the client's name, medication name, dosage, administration time, frequency, and route.
- Double-check the prescription's accuracy by REPEATING IT to the provider.
- Employ aids for accurate spelling.
⎼ "Bravo" for 'B'

- Transcribe or input the prescription in the client's medical file.
- If feasible, involve a second nurse via extension or private speaker (maintaining confidentiality).

Antiembolic stockings
- Boost venous flow to avoid clotting.
- Avoid knee/lower leg pillow use.
- Prescription needed.
- Check stockings every 8 hrs for signs, smooth out wrinkles.
Sputum collection
- Wait 1-2 hours post-meal for sputum to reduce emesis risk.
- Apply chest physiotherapy to mobilize secretions.
- Sterile container, label, lab slip, and biohazard bag for lab delivery.
- Clean gloves, mask, and goggles if needed.
- Use a preservative container for a cytology specimen.
- Sterile container for routine cultures and AFB testing.
- For ineffective cough, collect the specimen by endotracheal suctioning.
- A strong productive cough means suctioning was successful!
- Elderly may need suctioning due to weakened cough reflex and muscle strength.
Prioritization
Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
1. Physical needs, physiological: water, food, shelter, oxygen
● The highest needs that must be attended to first.
● Airway, Breathing, Circulation (Always ABCs first!).
2. Psychological needs
● Supporting patients' needs and issues.
● Easing anxiety and pain.
● Example: Supervising a suicidal patient individually.
● Employ effective therapeutic communication.
● Pain relief is considered psychosocial.
3. Safety and Security
● Minimize excessive stimuli.
● Adapt environment for patient's needs.
● Example: Labeling rooms for confused patients, decluttering fall-risk areas.
● Childproof environment for safety.
4. Love and belonging
● Start with self-love before loving others.
5. Self-esteem
● Self-perception.
6. Self-actualization
● The aspiration to become a steadfast and determined individual.
Prioritize acute issues over chronic ones.
Begin with patients in restraints during shift change.
Urgent needs take precedence over non-urgent needs.
Address unstable findings before stable ones

Death and Dying
DABDA
Denial: Rejecting loss, often seen in hospital-hopping for alternate opinions.
Anger: Filled with emptiness and fury, recognizing reality.
Bargaining: Shift from denial to acceptance, seeking more time.
Depression: Inward-turning, giving up on loved ones, silent mourning.
Acceptance: Preparedness for loss, detachment from family is a normal response.
Postmortem Care
- Comply with federal and state laws for organ/tissue donation, autopsy permission, and death certificate documentation.
- Delegable postmortem care tasks: LPN or UAP.

- Prioritize family AFTER postmortem care completion.
- Respect religious preferences.
- Provider certifies death and notes interventions and therapies.
- Elevate the head with a pillow to prevent facial discoloration.
- If no organ donation or medical examiner's case, remove tubes.
- Return personal items to family, based on their preference.
- Place client supine with head elevated, hands on the sheet, eyes closed.
- Change linens, use gown, and place absorbent pads.
- Groom hair, secure hairpieces, and remove excess items.
- Adjust lighting and noise for comfort.
Infant care is similar: swaddle in a blanket, offer mementos, offer photos of the infant.
Pediatric patients' understanding of death
Birth to 1 year:
Death has no meaning.
1-4 years:
Regards death as a temporary separation.
5+ years:
Regards death as permanent and
irreversible.
Safety and Infection Control
Hand washing
- The most important procedure for the prevention of nosocomial infections.
Wounds
- Clean from the inside to the outside of the wound.
- Least contaminated (the incision) to the most (surrounding skin).
- Employ gentle friction.
- Avoid shedding products like cotton balls.
- For wound dehiscence or evisceration.
- Call for help, cover with moist sterile dressing.Place in low Fowler’s
position. Monitor for shock, and notify provider.
- Do not reinsert organs.
- In acute cases:
- Apply direct pressure to control bleeding.
- Cover wounds with sterile dressing.
- Establish recent Tetanus date.
- Clean wounds solely with normal saline solution.
Standard Precautions
- Exposure to blood, fluids, skin, and mucous membranes.
Medical Asepsis:
- "Clean Technique"
- Essential hand hygiene, protective clothing.
- Hand hygiene before/after client contact, glove removal.
- Use alcohol-based or soap and water.
- Wash when soiled, after fluids, before eating, and after restroom use.
- Encourage clients and visitors to practice hand hygiene.
Surgical Asepsis:
- "Sterile Technique"

- Check for latex allergies beforehand.
- The patient may also be allergic to avocados, bananas, kiwis, apricots, cherries, grapes, kiwis, passion fruit,
tomatoes, peaches, or chestnuts.
- Caution clients against sudden movements.

- Outer wrappings and 1-inch edges are not sterile.
- Discard objects touching the 1-inch border.
- Lower than the waist, and higher than chest are both contaminated.
- Do not turn back to the sterile area.
- Keep bottle caps face up on clean surfaces.
Sterile Gloving:
1. Set up sterile field first.
2. Open wrapper, handle outside only.
3. Pick up dominant glove by cuff.
4. Place fingers of dominant hand into the non-dominant glove.
5. Adjust fingers with sterile gloved hand.
6. If glove tears, remove both gloves.
Types of drainage
● Serous drainage: The portion of the blood (serum) that is watery and clear or slightly yellow in appearance (fluid in blisters).
● Sanguineous drainage: Contains serum and red blood cells.
○ It is thick and appears reddish.
○ Brighter drainage indicates active bleeding; darker drainage indicates older bleeding/drainage.
● Serosanguineous drainage: Contains both serum and blood.
○ It is watery and looks pale and pink due to a mixture of red and clear fluid.
● Purulent drainage: The result of infection.
○ It is thick and contains white blood cells, tissue debris, and bacteria.
○ It may have a foul odor, and its color (yellow, tan, green, brown) reflects the type of organism present (green for a
Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection).
● Purosanguineous: A mixed drainage of pus and blood (newly infected wound).
Systemic infection
- Fever, fatigue, general discomfort.
- WBC count above 11,000.
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 15-20, indicating inflammation.
Patient room placement
- The most important: Immunocompromised, then airborne, then droplet, then contact.
Transmission-Based Precautions
- Transferring clients within the facility ➣ Those with airborne or droplet infections wear a surgical mask.
- Ensure all draining wounds are adequately covered.

Hepatitis
- Acute inflammatory disease of the liver resulting in cell damage from liver cell degeneration/necrosis.
- Statins (atorvastatin) can increase the risk of liver dysfunction and myopathy.
Symptoms:
- Jaundice (icterus)
- Clay-colored stools, tea-colored urine
- Anorexia and right upper quadrant pain
- Elevated AST and ALT (liver enzymes)
Patient teaching
- Bed rest for severe symptoms, avoid alcohol and hepatic toxic prescriptions (Aspirin, Tylenol, sedatives)
Lyme's disease
- Nurse must ensure the health department has been notified.
- Multi-system infection transmitted to humans from ticks (vector-borne).
Symptoms: Rash evolving from papules to lesions with clear centers. Appears at bite site within 2-30 days. Possible bullseye
rash. Flu-like symptoms within 1 to several months. Arthralgias: inflamed joints, possibly lasting years.
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)
- Syndrome from HIV with immune system deficits. Leads to infections, enteric pathogens, and malignancies.

- Monitor for HIV in the blood.
- AIDS has a CD4 cell count below 200.
- Watch for opportunistic infections (pneumonia, stomatitis, esophagitis).
- CBC shows leukopenia, lymphopenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
It's essential that clients on HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy) adhere to their prescribed doses without skipping.
Missing doses can lead to medication resistance and limit treatment choices.

Activate the facility's alarm system, then report the fire's specifics and location.
Contain the fire by shutting doors/windows, cutting off oxygen and electrical sources; ventilate life support clients with a bag-valve
mask.
Extinguish the fire if feasible using the right fire extinguisher.

Nursing Considerations
BP cuffs
- Too small = falsely high readings.
- Too big = too low.
- Should be 2/3 of the width of the limb where blood pressure is being monitored.
Latex allergies
- The patient may also be allergic to avocados, bananas, kiwis, apricots, cherries, grapes, kiwis, passion fruit, tomatoes,
peaches, or chestnuts.
- Signs of a reaction: facial swelling, rhinitis, urticaria, and respiratory distress.
Iodine allergy
- The patient may also be allergic to shellfish.
Mouth care
- On an unconscious patient, ensure the patient is in a side-lying semi-Fowler’s position (risk for aspiration).
Passive ROM
- Contraindicated during the inflammatory phase of rheumatologic diseases as well as joints that are dislocated or fractured.
- During these exercises, never push a movement beyond the point at which the client complains of discomfort or when you
feel resistance.

slides.title: Crutches Canes
text: Crutches Canes
● Have the client bend the elbows at 20-30 degrees.
● The length of the crutch should be measured by placing two
fingers between the axillary bars and 6-8 inches out from
heel.
○ Do not alter after fitting.
● When ambulating with a patient who is using crutches, stand
on their affected side and use a gait belt.
● When going up the stairs, good leg goes up first, bad leg
follows.
● Remember, good go to heaven and bad go to hell.
● Hold the crutches in one hand and grasp the arm of the chair
with the other hand for balance while sitting and rising from a
chair.
● Stand with a straight back.
DO NOT place any weight on the axillae.
● Stand on the affected side and hold onto gait belt.
● Teach the patient to place the cane on their unaffected side so
the cane and the weaker leg work together.
● Maintain two points of support on the ground at all times.
● Properly sized cane will extend from the greater trochanter to
the floor allowing for 20-30 degrees flexion.
1. Support body weight on both legs.
2. Move the cane forward 15-25 cm (6-10 in).
3. Move the weaker leg forward toward the cane.
4. Advance the stronger leg past the cane.
CANE →C.O.A.L →CANE OPPOSITE AFFECTED LEG
Crutches
4-point gait
- Weight-bearing on BOTH extremities.
- Alternate legs and opposite crutch, ensuring three points of support.
3-point gait
- Weight-bearing on ONE extremity.
- Affected leg doesn't touch the ground.
2-point gait
- Partial weight bearing on both feet.
- Mirror normal arm and leg motion during walking.
- When going upstairs, lead with unaffected leg, followed by crutches and injured leg.
- When advancing upstairs, the patient leads with the unaffected leg, and then the crutches and injured leg together.
Walker
- Move the walker forward and then step into it.
Wheelchair
- When assisting the patient, place the chair on the unaffected side of the body.

● Compromised airway
● Shock
● Unstable wounds
● Chest trauma

Leadership
Quality of Care
Quality of care audits
- Audits gather essential quantitative data.
Quality of care = evidence-based practice data
Structure Audits: Evaluate the influence of elements that exist separate from or outside of the client-staff interaction.
- Equipment and staffing levels.
Process Audits: Review how care was provided and assume a relationship exists between nurses and the quality of care provided.
Outcome Audits: Determine what results, if any, occurred as a result of the nursing care provided.
- Some outcomes are influenced by aspects of care.
- The quality of medical care, the level of commitment of managerial staff, and the characteristics of the facility’s
policies and procedures.
- Nursing-sensitive outcomes are those that are directly affected by the quality of nursing care.
- Client fall rates and incidence of hospital-acquired infections.
Disciplinary and Intervening
Nursing actions
- If a staff member observes odd behavior in a coworker, report this immediately, this is cause for CONCERN.
One of the most important functions of a nurse is the duty to INTERVENE when the safety or well-being of a client
or another person is at risk.
If the nurse witnesses an incorrect action by another RN, LPN, UAP, etc., the first step should be to ask if they need assistance.
Finding out what that personnel knows about the task and providing education.
Interprofessional Team and Effective Collaboration
Nurse's role in effective collaboration:
- Involve the client in care plan development.
- Initiate consultations on health issues.
- Provide referrals to post-discharge resources.
- Collaboration equals a win-win for the client and team.

slides.title: - Involve client, family, and interprofessional team.
text: - Involve client, family, and interprofessional team.
- Support resource referrals for clients.
- Value each team member's unique skills in collaboration.
Legal Responsibilities
Incident reports
- Document facts without judgment or opinion.
- DO NOT place incident reports in a patient's chart.
- If a patient wants to leave AMA, it is the provider's responsibility to advise the patient of any risks involved when they refuse
care.
- Incident reports contribute to changes that help improve healthcare quality.
If leaving AMA, the nurse legally has responsibility for notifying the client of risks involving leaving. The client must sign an
AMA form to provide legal protection for the hospital.
- NEVER prevent the client from leaving the hospital, physically or threatening.
Informed consent
- Form signed by a competent adult.
- Emancipated minors consent themselves.
- Interpreter use:
- Family members can NOT be used as an interpreter (adult or child).
- The nurse must ALWAYS speak directly to the client, not the interpreter.
- Examples of informed consent needed: PICC placement, G-Tube placement
Provider: Obtains informed consent Nurse: Witnesses informed consent
Client Advocacy
Nurses must:
- Clients informed of rights for decisions.
- No directing or controlling the choice of the patient.
- Nurse advocates for clients:
- End-of-life choices.
- Health care access.
- Privacy safeguard.
- Informed consent.
- Address subpar care.
- Challenge harmful prescriptions.
- Nurses accountable for actions, even under provider's orders.
Medical Surgical Nursing
Cardiovascular
Electrocardiogram
- Records heart's electrical activity.
- Detects heart issues, irregularities, and electrolyte imbalances.
Cardiac catheterization
- Catheter inserted into heart vessels.
- Measures pressure and cardiac output.

text: - Complications include myocardial infarction, therefore chest pain should be reported immediately.
Holter monitor
- Records heart activity for 24 hours.
- Diary of activities kept.
Troponin
- Any value >0 indicates damage to cardiac tissue and should be reported.
Nontunneled percutaneous central venous catheter (CVC)
- 18-25 cm length, one to five lumens.
- Short-term use.
- Inserted in subclavian/jugular vein.
- Tip in the distal third of the superior vena cava.
- For blood, antibiotics, and nutrition.
- Check recent chest x-ray before use.
Peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC)
- Sterile technique → sterile gloves and mask.
- Up to 12 months.
- Basilic or cephalic vein insertion.
- Tip in lower one-third of SVC.
- For blood, chemo, antibiotics, nutrition.
Nursing considerations: Clean the site with chlorhexidine for 30 seconds and allow it to air dry prior to insertion.
- Post placement: Confirm placement of the PICC with an x-ray. Assess the site for redness, swelling, drainage, tenderness,
and condition of the dressing. Clean the insertion port with alcohol for 15 seconds and allow it to dry completely prior to
accessing it.
- Assess for phlebitis (a common complication of PICCs): Redness (initial sign), pain/burning at site and vein,
discomfort when tip is touched, warmth, swelling, hard vein, red streak or cordlike appearance, slow infusion, temp rise
by 1°F, infection after 7-10 days.
Pacemakers
- Report uncontrollable hiccupping immediately, as it can indicate a dislodgement.
- Prevent rigorous arm and shoulder movements for 6 weeks after pacemaker insertion.
- Report hiccuping to provider.
Angina
Stable Angina
- 5 to 10 min chest pain.
- Rest or nitro relief.
- Nitroglycerin, isosorbide lower oxygen demand.
- Isosorbide is avoided in glaucoma.
- NOT associated with nausea, epigastric distress, dyspnea, anxiety, or diaphoresis.
Unstable angina
- Not relieved by rest or nitro.
- Can progress to MI.
- ST elevation.
Hypertensive crisis
- Nitroprusside treats (vasodilator).
- Rapidly lowers BP, and reduces preload/afterload.
- Caution: hypotension risk.
- Administer slowly, monitor heart, and keep supine.
- Nitroprusside overdose: Can cause delirium, and mental changes.
- Monitor thiocyanate level (<10 mg/dL).
Hypertension
- Headaches in a patient with hypertension are considered a priority due to the risk of stroke.

Heart Failure
Left-Sided
(L=Lungs)
Congestion occurs mainly in the lungs due to inadequate
ejection of the blood into the systemic circulation.
Primarily pulmonary symptoms such as orthopnea, cough,
and crackles.
Right-Sided
Congestion occurs systemically due to inadequate pumping of
the blood from the systemic circulation into the lungs.
Symptoms include peripheral edema, ascites, jugular vein
distention, and hepatomegaly.
Heart Arrhythmias
Normal Sinus Rhythm
● Both atrial and ventricular rhythms are essentially regular (a slight variation in rhythm is normal).
● There is one P wave before each QRS complex, and all the P waves are of a consistent morphology or shape.
● The PR interval and the QRS complex are both constant.
Myocardial Infarction
- Cardiac muscle is destroyed by the interruption or insufficient blood supply to one of the major coronary arteries for a
prolonged time.
- “Heaviness in my chest” “Feels like an elephant is sitting on my chest”
- ST elevation
- Patients will always have cardiac rehab after an MI.
- This is a priority post-MI for nurses to consider before/during discharge.
Asystole
A lack of QRS depolarizations (a straight line)
Treatment: Epinephrine, Atropine (in that order)
Atrial Flutter
Rapid P-wave depolarizations in a saw-tooth (flutter)

slides.title: Treatment: Catheter ablation
text: Treatment: Catheter ablation
Atrial Fibrillation
Chaotic P-wave depolarization (lacks any discernible pattern).
Chaotic is ALWAYS used to describe fibrillation.
Patient are typically on anticoagulants due to being at increased risk of emboli/stroke.
Treatment: Cardioversion
Ventricular Fibrillation
Chaotic QRS depolarization.
No cardiac output → no brain perfusion → brain death occurs in approximately 8 minutes.
● Remember, the FIRST step in management of care for an unresponsive, pulseless patient is to place a backboard
under the patient’s back while the patient is supine. If no backboard is placed, the patient will be pushed into
the bed during CPR, thus creating ineffective compressions. After, immediately start compressions.
Treatment: Shock (for vfib you defib)
Ventricular Tachycardia
Wide, bizarre QRSs.
Tachy is always a discernible repeating pattern.
There IS cardiac output.
Bizarre is ALWAYS used to describe tachycardia.

slides.title: Treatment: Lidocaine
text: Treatment: Lidocaine
Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVC)
Periodic wide, bizarre QRSs.
Generally low to moderate priority, never a HIGH priority.
PVCs after an MI are common and are a low priority.
Be concerned if:
○ More than 6 per minute
○ 6 in a row
○ PVC falls on T-wave of the previous beat (R on T)
■ May precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
○ If any of these occur, notify the cardiologist immediately.
Treatment: Lidocaine, Amiodorone
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
Regular narrow-complex (QRS) tachycardia.
The heart rate is typically 150-220/min with no visible P wave.
Treatment: Vagal maneuvers and IV adenosine. Hemodynamically unstable clients with SVT may require
synchronized cardioversion.
● Synchronized cardioversion is a cardiac procedure used to convert tachyarrhythmias with a pulse to stable
cardiac rhythms.
● Adenosine: Push in <8 seconds and do not worry about asystole unless >30 seconds.
● Nurses preparing to perform cardioversion must verify that the defibrillator's "sync" feature is engaged to
prevent delivery of an asynchronous shock, which may cause life-threatening arrhythmias.

slides.title: Lethal arrhythmias
text: Lethal arrhythmias
● Asystole
● V-fib
Potentially life-threatening arrhythmia
● V-tach
○ Pulseless v-tach is the same as asystole and v-fib and would depend on time.
Endocrine
Pancreas
- Secretes two hormones: insulin and glucagon that are necessary for carbohydrate metabolism.
- Failure of the pancreas to produce an adequate amount of insulin can lead to diabetes mellitus (glucose intolerance).
Diabetes Insipidus
● Lacks antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
● No water reabsorption = diuresis.
● DI linked to damaged hypothalamus.
● Treat with fluids, vasopressin.
● Large amounts of urine are excreted as a result of a deficiency of ADH from the
posterior pituitary gland.
● Treatment of DI consists of massive fluid replacement, administration of synthetic
vasopressin, careful attention to laboratory values, and replacement of essential nutrients as
indicated.
○ Desmopressin is the medication of choice for DI.
■ Monitor for overhydration (sleepiness, edema, weight gain, pounding
headache).
Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)
● Overproduction of ADH and is linked to damaged hypothalamus.
● Client has low sodium and chloride.
● Treat with furosemide and 0.9% sodium chloride.
● Treatment consists of fluid restriction, administration of oral conivaptan, and treatment of
hyponatremia, with 3% hypertonic saline solution for severe cases.
● If SIADH is present, the client can have disorientation, headache, vomiting, muscle
weakness, decreased LOC, irritability, loss of thirst, and weight gain.
○ If severe or untreated, this condition can cause seizures and a coma.

slides.title: Thyroid gland
text: Thyroid gland
● Levothyroxine speeds up metabolism. Weight loss is an expected effect.
Hypothyroidism
● Low thyroid hormone, slows metabolism.
Complications: myxoedema, hypermetabolic coma.
Symptoms: Slow metabolism, hypoventilation, hypothermia, hypotension.
● Life-long Synthroid use.
Hyperthyroidism
● Excess thyroid hormone, often Graves disease.
“Thyroid storm”
○ Apply ice packs to lower fever. If persists, obtain a prescription for a cooling blanket
for hyperthermia.
● Patient will present with goiter and abnormal protrusion of the eyes, called exophthalmos
Symptoms: Tremors, tachycardia, and palpitations
Addison's disease
- Adrenocortical insufficiency that is caused by damage or dysfunction of the adrenal
cortex. The production of mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids is decreased,
resulting in decreased aldosterone and cortisol.
Symptoms:
- Weakness, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, hypotension, tachycardia, low blood sugar and sodium, high potassium/calcium,
craving for salt, hyperpigmentation of skin.
- Patient will need replacement therapy for life.
- Addisonian crisis has a rapid onset and is a medical emergency.
Cushing's Syndrome
- Cushing’s (hypercortisolism): caused by an oversecretion of the hormones the adrenal cortex produces.
- Can be the result of a tumor in the pituitary gland, resulting in the release of the hormone ACTH (adrenocorticotropic
hormone).
- Results from long-term use of glucocorticoids to treat other conditions (asthma or rheumatoid arthritis).
- Patient has a high risk for fluid volume excess.
- Always monitor fluid and electrolytes.
Symptoms:
- Moon face, buffalo hump, neck fat, high blood sugar/sodium, low potassium and calcium, bruising and petechiae,
hypertension from sodium and water retention, muscle wasting, thin/fragile skin.
Diabetes Mellitus
Symptoms: Polyuria, polyphagia, and polydipsia
Assess for the presence of ketones in the urine, which indicates the body is using fat as the major source of energy.
Type 1 Diabetes:
● Autoimmune dysfunction destroys insulin-producing cells.
● Triggers: immune cells, antibodies, genetics, viruses.
● Managed with exercise, a low-fat diet, regular meals.
Type 2 Diabetes:
● Cells resist insulin, insulin production drops.
● Linked to obesity, sedentary lifestyle, heredity.
● Metabolic syndrome may precede type 2 diabetes.
Insulin
● Regular insulin is the only one that can be given IV.

slides.title: ○ Clear in color.
text: ○ Clear in color.
● NPH and Lente insulin are cloudy.
● Inject at a 90° angle (45°angle if the client is thin). Aspiration for blood is not necessary.
● Insulin can be left at room temperature for up to 4 weeks.
● Current vials of insulin being used should not be refrigerated due to the possibility of local irritation insight.
● Always rotate sites to prevent lipodystrophy, never massage the site after injection.
● Treatment for insulin-induced hypoglycemia is Glucagon.
Interactions
● Salicylates with insulin can cause hypoglycemia.
Mixing insulin
Regular insulin should be withdrawn first followed by the intermediate-acting insulin.
REMEMBER Nancy Regan, RN
1. Inject air into NPH insulin.
2. Inject air into regular, short-acting insulin.
3. Keep the needle and the regular insulin and draw up regular.
4. Finally, draw up NPH.
Rapid-acting insulin: Insulin lispro, insulin aspart, insulin glulisine, inhaled human insulin
● Administer before meals to control the postprandial rise in blood glucose. Onset is rapid (10 to 30 min), depending on which
insulin is administered.
● Administer in conjunction with intermediate- or long-acting insulin to provide glycemic control between meals and at night.
Short-acting insulin: Regular insulin
● Administer 30 to 60 min before meals to control postprandial hyperglycemia.
Intermediate-acting insulin: NPH insulin
● Administered for glycemic control between meals and at night. Not administered before meals to control postprandial rise in
blood glucose.
● Contains protamine (a protein), which causes a delay in the insulin absorption or onset and extends the duration of action of the
insulin.
● Administered subcutaneous only and as the only insulin to mix with short-acting insulin.
Long-acting insulin: Insulin glargine, insulin detemir
● Administer once daily, anytime during the day but always at the same time each day.
● Administer glargine insulin and insulin detemir subcutaneously only. Never administer IV.
Never mix Glargine with other insulins.
Ultra long-acting insulin: U-300 insulin glargine, insulin degludec
● Duration is longer than 24 hr. Both medications are available only as a prefilled pen.
Onset Peak Duration
Rapid-Acting: Lispro 15-30 min 0.5-2.5 hr 3-6 hr
Short-Acting: Regular 0.5-1 hr 1-5 hr 6-10 hr

Long-acting: Glargine 70 min None 24 hr
HBA1C
- Used to monitor diabetes treatment and measures the amount of glucose in the blood over the course of 100 to 120 days.
- Want 7% or below.
- Anything above is a cause for concern or change in the care plan.
No diabetes mellitus = HbA1c 5.9% or less
Good diabetes control = HbA1c less than 7%
Fair diabetes control HbA1c 8% to 9%
HbA1c at or above 9% indicates inadequate or poor diabetes control.
Hypoglycemia
Symptoms: Diaphoresis, headache, weakness, irritability, and slurred speech
- Treatment
- Orange juice or glucose tablet if they are able to swallow.
- IV D50 if unable to swallow/unconscious.
Hyperglycemia
- Blood glucose levels above 120.
Symptoms: Hot, dry skin, thirst, and fruity breath.
- Encourage oral fluid intake of sugar-free fluids to prevent dehydration.
- Administer insulin as prescribed.
- Test urine for ketones and report if outside of the expected reference range.
- High ketones in the urine associated with hyperglycemia (exceeding 300 mg/dL) is a medical emergency.
Diabetic Foot Care – Client Education
- Wash with soap and water and inspect feet daily.
- Always ensure water is not hot with a thermometer or an arm.
- Gently dry between the toes by patting, not rubbing.
- For sweat, use cornstarch foot powder.
- Referral for a podiatrist.
- Separate overlapping toes using cotton.
- Choose proper shoes, never wear open-toe/heels.
- Wear clean, absorbent socks, no mending.
Avoid
- Hot water bottles, commercial remedies, going barefoot.
- Prolonged sitting/standing/crossing legs.
- Soaking feet.
COMPLICATIONS OF DM
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
- An acute, life-threatening, rapid onset condition characterized by uncontrolled hyperglycemia (greater than 300 mg/dL),
metabolic acidosis, and an accumulation of ketones in the blood and urine.
Symptoms: Fast, deep labored breathing, acetone, fruity breath, Kussmaul's respirations.
- Treatment
- Fluid replacement, electrolyte replacement, insulin therapy (usually a drip).
Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State
- Acute, life-threatening condition with profound hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL) and hyperosmolarity, causing dehydration and
absence of ketosis.
- Gradual onset over days.

slides.title: - Result of sustained osmotic diuresis.
text: - Result of sustained osmotic diuresis.
- Common in adults aged 50-70, with higher mortality due to delayed medical attention, and age-related changes (decreased
thirst perception).
- Other factors contributing: infection, stress, medical conditions (MI, sepsis), and medications (glucocorticoids, diuretics).
Electrolytes
Calcium Bone/teeth formation, blood pressure, blood clotting,
nerve transmission
Decreased levels:
- Chvostek’s Sign – Cheek → you touch their cheek →
spasm, which is a sign of neuromuscular irritability
- Trousseau's Sign – Spasm of the hand when you put
a BP cuff on
- Tetany
Food Sources: Dairy, broccoli, kale, fortified grains, spinach
Hypocalcemia: Tetany/cramps, paresthesia,
dysrhythmias, Trousseau's sign, Chvostek sign, seizures
Hypercalcemia: Muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, N/V,
lethargy/coma, dysrhythmias, kidney stones
Potassium Decreased levels: Assess the heart, prepare to administer K+,
call provider.
- Decreased deep tendon reflexes, decreased blood
pressure, orthostatic hypotension, paralytic ileus can
develop, ST depression, prolonged PR interval.
- “No P = No K.” If the client is not urinating, do
NOT administer Potassium.
Increased levels: Hold all K+, assess the heart, and prepare to
give kayexalate.
- First vital sign you check with HYPERkalemia is
pulse due to the risk of dysrhythmias.
Food Sources: Oranges, dried fruits, tomatoes, avocados,
dried peas, meats, broccoli, bananas, dairy products, meats,
whole grains, potatoes, sardines, turnips, collard greens.
↓Low K+ = ↓ST depression
↑ High K+ =↑ ST elevation
Hypokalemia: Muscle weakness, fatigue, decreased
DTR, N/V, irritability, confusion, decreased bowel
motility, abdominal distention, paralytic ileus, paresthesia,
dysrhythmias, orthostatic hypotension, flat/inverted T
waves, ST depression, prominent U wave.
Hyperkalemia: Muscle twitching and paresthesia (early
symptoms), ascending muscle weakness (late symptoms),
increased DTR, increased bowel motility, diarrhea,
ventricular dysrhythmias, hypotension and bradycardia,
elevated/peaked T wave.
Spironolactone is a Potassium-sparing diuretic and
clients should be assessed for hyperkalemia.
For Hyperkalemia: Sodium Polystyrene (Kayexalate):
Helps K+ exit the body (through stool)
Kayexalate (K+ exit)
Sodium Maintains osmotic pressure and acid-base balance.
Decreased levels: Assess for fluid overload (edema, increased
weight).
Increased levels: Assess for dehydration (poor skin turgor,
dark urine, hot flushed skin, weak thready pulse, increased
urine specific gravity).
Foods high in sodium: Canned foods, table salt, prepared
seasoning, and processed foods.
HypoNatremia = Volume overload
Hyponatremia: Weakness, lethargy, confusion, seizures,
headache, anorexia, N/V, muscle cramps/twitching,
hypotension, tachycardia, weight gain, edema, low
specific gravity, elevated Hgb.
Hypernatremia: Fever, swollen/dry tongue, sticky
mucus membrane, hallucinations, lethargy, restlessness
irritability, seizures, tachycardia, HTN, hyperreflexia,
twitching, pulmonary edema.

slides.title: HyperNatremia = Dehydration
text: HyperNatremia = Dehydration
Vitamin D Assists in the absorption of calcium and phosphorus and aids in
bone mineralization.
- Sunlight enables the body to synthesize vitamin D in
the skin.
Food sources: Fatty fish, eggs, and fortified products
(ready-to-eat cereals, milk, orange juice).
Deficiency results in bone demineralization, and extreme
deficiency can cause rickets and osteomalacia.
Excess consumption can cause hypercalcemia.
Vitamin K Assists in blood clotting and bone maintenance.
Food sources: Carrots, eggs, and dark green vegetables
(spinach, broccoli, asparagus).
Deficiency results in increased bleeding time.
Used as an antidote for excess anticoagulants (warfarin).
HYPOKALEMIA ST depression
Shallow, flat, or inverted T wave
Prominent U wave
HYPERKALEMIA Tall peaked T wave
Flat P wave
Widened QRS complexes
Prolonged PR interval
HYPOCALCEMIA Prolonged ST segment
Prolonged QT interval
HYPERCALCEMIA Shortened ST segment
Widened T wave
Heart block
HYPOMAGNESEMIA Tall T waves
Depressed ST segment
HYPERMAGNESEMIA Prolonged PR interval
Widened QRS complexes
Gastrointestinal
Gastric bleeding
- Insert a nasogastric (NG) tube for gastric lavage (irrigate with normal saline or water to stop active gastric bleed) as indicated.
- Obtain an x-ray to confirm the placement of the NG tube prior to fluid installation to prevent aspiration. Monitor
NG tube for absence/presence of blood. Assess the amount of bleeding and prevent gastric dilation.
- Inserting a LARGE-BORE NG tube is the first nursing action.
- For gastric lavage, turn the patient on the LEFT side, 200-300mL NOT more.
- Test hematocrit and hemoglobin.
The auscultatory method of checking placement is NOT considered reliable. Initial placement of the NG tube should be
checked by x-ray. Subsequent placement should be checked by aspirating stomach or intestinal contents and measuring pH.
Gastric pH: 1.4-4 Intestinal pH: ~6 Respiratory pH: ≥7

slides.title: If residual exceeds 100 mL for intermittent feedings or 2 hours worth of a continuous feed, hold or stop the feeding. Do
text: If residual exceeds 100 mL for intermittent feedings or 2 hours worth of a continuous feed, hold or stop the feeding. Do NOT
refeed aspirate. Notify the provider.
Diarrhea
- Occurs with the use of magnesium-containing antacids and can lead to transient lactase deficiency.
Patient teaching: Avoid milk when having diarrhea.
Constipation
- Potential side effects of antacids that contain aluminum.
- Never give Lactulose to clients with bowel obstruction.
L Laxative, loose stools
A Ammonia decreases (lose ammonia through loose stools)
C Cognition returns (improvement in mental status)
Fecal impaction
- Seepage of liquid stools will be a Hallmark sign.
Biliary obstruction
- Stool will be seen as light, gray, or clay-colored.
H-pylori testing
- Gastric samples are collected via endoscopy.
Upper GI diagnostic tests
- Patient must be NPO, receive a laxative prep, and push fluids after the procedure.
- The patient must remain NPO until the gag reflex returns.
Colonoscopy
- Pre-procedure includes laxative prep as well as a clear liquid diet that avoids red-colored juices and jello.
- Given every 10 years.
Sigmoidoscopy
- Pre-procedure involves an enema.
Gallbladder series
Patient teaching: Avoid fatty foods prior to the procedure.
Ileostomy
- A surgical opening into the ileum to drain stool.
- When the entire colon must be removed due to disease (Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis).
Patient teaching: Fluid will drain continuously.
Stomatitis
- Inflammation of the oral cavity as a result of trauma or disease.
Symptoms: Excessive salivation and halitosis.
Patient teaching: Bland diet and cold drinks.
Esophageal hernia (Hiatal hernia)
- Herniation of a portion of the stomach through the esophageal opening in the diaphragm.
- Risk factors: Obesity, ascites, muscle weakness, and tumors.
Symptoms: May be asymptomatic or complain of heartburn and reflux, the patient may also complain of chest pain while
lying down.
Treatment: Sleep with the head of the bed elevated. Remain upright for 30 minutes after all meals.
GERD
- Reflux pushes stomach contents to the esophagus, causing regurgitation, heartburn, and irritation.
- Reflux risk: higher aspiration chance.
- Assessment: Dyspepsia (indigestion) post-meal, along with regurgitation. Pain radiating to neck, jaw, or back.
Atypical chest pain, resembling a heart attack. Pyrosis (burning sensation in esophagus). Odynophagia (painful swallowing).
Increased flatus and eructation (burping). Relief from pain by drinking water, sitting upright, or using antacids. Chronic
GERD may lead to dysphagia.

slides.title: Patient teaching: Small, frequent meals, increase fluid intake, and avoid alcohol, caffeine (coffee), spicy foods, choco
text: Patient teaching: Small, frequent meals, increase fluid intake, and avoid alcohol, caffeine (coffee), spicy foods, chocolate, and
citrus.
Peptic ulcer disease
- Patients commonly experience an aching, burning feeling and gnawing in their epigastric region.
- The patient will feel more intense pain on an empty stomach.
- Meals help to relieve pain.
- Complication includes bleeding. Aspirin should be avoided because it contains salicylates which are irritating to the gastric
mucosa.
Patient teaching: Avoid caffeine, alcohol, smoking, stress, and salicylates.
Treatment: Triple therapy including two antibiotics and a proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole) or an H2 antagonist
(ranitidine).
Gastric ulcers
- Pain when eating.
Treatment is Misoprostol
- Prior to administration, perform a pregnancy test in female patients.
Duodenal ulcers
- Pain is relieved by eating.
- Sucralfate (Carafate) coats a duodenal ulcer.
- Can cause constipation.
Cholecystitis
- Inflammation of the gallbladder caused by stones (cholelithiasis).
Symptoms: Pain in the right upper quadrant, sometimes occurs after eating a meal consisting of fried or fatty foods. Pain can
radiate to the back.
- Acute phase: Patient should be NPO and slowly advance to clear fluids and then a low-fat, bland diet as tolerated.
Pancreatitis
- The process of autodigestion when the pancreatic enzymes are activated while still in the pancreas, not when they reach the
intestines where this is supposed to occur.
Patient teaching:
- Avoid alcohol
- Patient will be NPO and slowly advance from clear liquid to a low-fat, small, frequent meal regimen
- Low-fat, high protein, and high-carbohydrate diet
- Want patients to eat broiled chicken with rice (high-protein and high-carbs).
Appendicitis
- Periumbilical pain followed by elevated temperature, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting.
- Pain is localized at Mcburney's point, between the umbilicus and the right iliac crest.
- Rovsing’s sign: Occurs when palpation of the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower
quadrant.
- Post-op: Scheduled analgesics for 24 hours post-op.
Diverticulitis
- Inflammation of the diverticula and surrounding intestine.
- Acute onset of abdominal pain often in the left lower quadrant.
Patient teaching:
- Instruct client for regular bowel function: Avoid laxatives and enemas. Stay well-hydrated. Clear liquid diet during
symptoms. Progress to low-fiber, then high-fiber diet. Skip seeds, nuts, and popcorn to prevent blockage. Skip
irritating foods/drinks like alcohol. Limit fat to 30% daily calories.
Irritable bowel syndrome
- Causes changes in bowel function (chronic diarrhea, constipation, bloating, and/or abdominal pain).
Patient teaching: Instruct the client to limit the intake of irritating agents (gas-forming foods, caffeine, alcohol). Encourage a
diet high in fiber and fluids. Instruct client to keep a food diary to record intake and bowel patterns (to adjust diet to prevent
exacerbations).

slides.title: Crohn's disease
text: Crohn's disease
- Cannot be cured by surgical intervention.
- Affects all layers of the bowel wall, from the mouth to the anus, most often the terminal ileum.
Symptoms: Malaise, fever, rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, fistulas, ulcers.
- High risk for developing colon cancer.
Ulcerative colitis
- Can be cured by surgical intervention.
Symptoms: Rectal bleeding, rare to see masses or fistulas.
Do not confuse inflammatory bowel disease with irritable bowel syndrome, which is much less severe. Inflammatory bowel
disease is an autoimmune disorder and it includes Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis.
Bleeding is common with ulcerative colitis. This helps differentiate it from Crohn’s disease, in which bleeding is rare.
Dumping syndrome
- Following a gastrectomy, this occurs due to the Rapid emptying of large amounts of food into the small bowel.
Patient teaching: Instead of with meals, encourage drinking liquids between meals.
Colostomy
- In the descending colon, will consist of formed and soft stools.
- Irrigation
- 1000 CCs of tap water that is 100 to 105 degrees.
- Bottom of the irrigation bag should be placed at the client's shoulder level.
Abdominal surgery
- Peristalsis is temporarily halted and usually does not return for 1-2 days post-op.
Important meds
- Omeprazole (Prilosec)
- Proton pump inhibitor that inhibits gastric acid production.
- Cimetidine (Tagamet)
- Histamine antagonist that blocks the secretion of hydrochloric acid.
- Metoclopramide (Reglan)
- Increases gastric motility and gastric emptying.
- Side effects: EPS (tardive dyskinesia).
- Reglan regulates bowels (helps with nausea and vomiting and delayed gastric emptying).
Fluid Imbalances
Hypovolemia Hypervolemia
● Hypovolemia, or isotonic dehydration.
● Inadequate water and electrolytes, reducing blood volume.
● Severe dehydration can trigger seizures.
● Can lead to hypovolemic shock.
○ Decreased LOC
● Older adults prone to dehydration due to physiological
changes.
● Decreased total body mass and thirst detection.
● Skin turgor assessment may not be reliable in older adults due
to natural loss of skin elasticity.
● Hypervolemia, or fluid volume excess.
● Excess water and electrolytes in correct proportions.
● Excessive sodium intake causes water retention.
● Can lead to pulmonary edema and heart failure.
● Compensatory mechanisms: increased natriuretic peptides, more
sodium and water excretion by kidneys, decreased aldosterone
release.

slides.title: Expected Findings
text: Expected Findings
● Hypothermia (due to hypovolemia) or hyperthermia (caused
by dehydration), tachycardia, thready pulse, hypotension,
decreased central venous pressure, tachypnea, hypoxia
● Neuromusculoskeletal: Dizziness, syncope, confusion,
weakness, fatigue, seizures (rapid/severe dehydration)
● GI: Thirst, dry mucous membranes, dry tongue, nausea,
vomiting, anorexia, acute weight loss
● Renal: Oliguria (decreased production of urine)
● Other: Diminished capillary refill, cool clammy skin,
diaphoresis, sunken eyeballs, absence of tears, decreased skin
turgor, flattened neck veins (late sign), oliguria (late sign),
decreased central venous pressure (late sign)
Expected Findings
● Tachycardia, bounding pulse, hypertension, tachypnea,
increased central venous pressure
● Neuromusculoskeletal: Confusion, muscle weakness, altered
level of consciousness, paresthesias, visual changes; seizures (if
severe, sudden hyponatremia/water excess).
● GI: Increased motility, ascites
● Respiratory: Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles
● Other: Pitting edema, distended neck veins, weight gain, skin
pallor and cool to touch
Hematologic, Immune System, and Cancer
HIV
- CD4 cell count lower than 200.
- Transmitted through blood, semen, vaginal secretions, urine, feces, saliva, and tears.
- Can be transmitted through pregnancy and through vaginal birth.
- If HIV clients are neutropenic, use dedicated equipment for that client.
ELISA: Test for antibodies to HIV in serum or plasma.
- Most widely used serologic test for AIDS.
Western blot: Done if the Elisa is inconclusive, this one is highly predictive of HIV infection.
Blood
- Type and screen is the lab test.
- Transfusions
- Most common transfusion reaction is fever.
- Only solution that can be given with blood during a transfusion is normal saline (must be transfused within 4 hrs).
- Nurse must stay during the first 15 minutes.
- If a reaction is suspected, stop transfusion, keep IV access, and replace transfusion with normal saline.
- If hives are the only reaction during a transfusion, proceed at a lower rate.
- Assess for circulatory overload, which can occur at any time during the transfusion.
Symptoms: Crackles, dyspnea, cough, anxiety, jugular vein distention, and tachycardia. Manifestations can
progress to pulmonary edema.
- Slow or stop the transfusion depending on the severity of manifestations. Position the client upright with
feet lower than the level of the heart.
- Administer oxygen, diuretics, and morphine, as prescribed.
Blood products
- Packed RBCs: Increases the number of RBCs.
- Replacement therapy for acute blood loss to surgical procedures or trauma.
- Always prime IV tubing for PRBCs with 0.9% Normal Saline.
- Will cause volume expansion in clients who have dehydration, extensive burn injury, and shock.
- Watch for fluid overload: Difficult breathing, cough, crackles, anxiety, JVD, and tachycardia.

slides.title: - May lead to pulmonary edema.
text: - May lead to pulmonary edema.
- Platelets: Replaces coagulation factors.
- Apheresed granulocytes: Replaces neutrophils/granulocytes.
- Albumin: Expands circulating blood volume by exerting oncotic pressure.
- Always verify with a second nurse to ensure blood compatibility and assess the client’s lungs prior to infusion of PRBCs.
Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
- Caused by incompatible blood type/Rh factor and can occur even with a small volume (10 mL) of mismatched blood.
- Range from mild to severe, potentially leading to DIC or circulatory collapse.
Symptoms: Chills, fever, pain, tachycardia, flushing, hypotension, chest pain, tachypnea, nausea, anxiety, hemoglobinuria, and
sense of doom.
- Stop transfusion. Disconnect IV access. Avoid further blood product infusion. Administer 0.9% Sodium Chloride with new
tubing. Monitor vital signs and fluid status. Send blood bag and tubing to the lab for testing.
Anemia
Symptoms: Fatigue and activity intolerance, pallor, tachypnea, irritability, generalized weakness.
Iron deficiency anemia
- Provide the patient with frequent rest periods.
- Iron Replacements should be diluted and given through a straw to prevent staining of the teeth.
- If given via IM injection, use z-track method to ensure it will not stain skin.
- If given orally, give with orange juice to enhance absorption cell anemia (Vitamin C).
- Foods high in iron: Spinach, beef, liver, prunes, pork, broccoli, whole bread, and whole cereal.
Pernicious anemia
- These patients are susceptible to gastric carcinomas.
- B12 injections for life.
- Schilling test: Assesses vitamin B12 absorption, with/without intrinsic factor. Used to distinguish malabsorption from
pernicious anemia.
Sickle Cell Anemia
- Clots fast, causes pain.
- Avoid acute episodes by avoiding tight clothing, strenuous exercise, cold temperatures (vasoconstriction), smoking.
- Encourage adequate hydration to prevent crisis.
- Acute chest syndrome is a group of symptoms that occurs when sickled cells clump together in the lungs.
- Substernal retractions should be reported immediately to the provider.
Meperidine is NOT used for the treatment of pain in sickle cell anemia. Children with sickle cell disease are particularly at risk
for seizures.
Hemophilia
- Patient should be instructed to avoid contact sports.
Multiple myeloma
- Most common assessment finding is pathological fractures.
DIC
- The patient begins to hemorrhage after initial hypercoagulability and uses up all the clotting factors in the blood
(simultaneous bleeding and clotting).
- Occurs in massive crush injuries, burns, and allergic responses.
- The body's clotting ability is exhausted because it is trying to repair so many areas with coagulation.
- Treatment: Heparin
- Prolongs the time needed for blood to clot, but it does not thin the blood.
Thrombocytopenia
- Decreased number of platelets, which are necessary for clot formation.
Patient teaching: Decrease risk of bleeding: do not blow nose, instead, wipe nostrils.
Symptoms:

slides.title: - Petechiae and bruising.
text: - Petechiae and bruising.
- When these are present, obtain platelet count!
Epistaxis (nose bleed)
- Have the client sit up and lean slightly forward to avoid vascular pressure on the nose and avoid aspiration of blood.
- Pinch the side of the nose with thumb and forefinger.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
- Chronic, progressive, systemic inflammatory disease that can cause major organs and systems to fail.
- Erythema of the face (butterfly rash). No cure for Lupus.
- Monitor BUN and creatinine levels for signs of renal impairment.
- Treatment: Hydroxychloroquine (decreases inflammation and fatigue, but takes months to work).
- WATCH FOR retinal damage and vision problems.
- Eye appointments every 6-12 months.
Cancer
Breast cancer
- Hard or irregular axillary nodes, skin dimpling, nipple retraction, elevation, and discharge.
- Self-exams should be performed monthly.
- Mammography begins yearly at age 35.
- Mastectomy
Post-op nursing considerations: Initiate early arm and hand exercises (rubber ball squeezing, elbow flexion/extension,
hand-wall climbing) for lymphedema prevention and restoring full range of motion.
- Closed-suction drain
- Empty closed-suction drainage collection devices as needed to maintain compression.
- Report increases in drainage (possible hemorrhage).
- Reset the vacuum by compressing the container.
Cervical cancer
- Pap smear is the screening tool.
Uterine cancer
- When cancer has spread beyond the uterus, brachytherapy and external radiation therapy can be good treatment options.
- Brachytherapy
- Brachytherapy involves inserting an applicator into the vagina and placing a radioactive isotope in it for a
few minutes, 2 to 10 times weekly, requiring bed rest.
- Educate the patient to report symptoms like vaginal bleeding, urethral burning, hematuria, fatigue, diarrhea,
fever, or abdominal pain.
- Dosimeter film badge should be worn by the nurse to record personal amounts of radiation exposure.
- Visitors maintain 6 feet distance to patient and limit to 30-minute visits.
Testicular cancer
- Largest risk factor is undescended testicles.
- Normal testes: Should feel like small hard-boiled eggs, not firm and hard. Feel with thumb and forefinger.
Hodgkin's lymphoma
- Painless progressive enlargement of one or more lymph nodes, as well as the presence of reed-Sternberg cells.
Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
- Multiple lymph nodes and lymphoid tissues are involved.
Implanted Port
- A surgically implanted port is placed in a chest wall pocket, and a catheter goes into the subclavian vein with its tip in the
SVC.
- Long-term vascular access, often for chemotherapy.

slides.title: - Only properly trained personnel in masks and aseptic conditions should access ports.
text: - Only properly trained personnel in masks and aseptic conditions should access ports.
- Use a non-coring (Huber) needle for access.
Chemotherapeutic drugs
- Produce bone marrow depression, resulting in a reduced red blood cell count, white blood cell count, and platelet count.
- May cause anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.
Cancer – Radiation treatment
- Adverse effects of radiation:
1. Provide a well-balanced diet that does not contain red meat. Radiation can cause dysgeusia (altered taste), making foods
such as red meat unpalatable.
2. Help the client manage fatigue by scheduling activities with rest periods in between and using energy-saving measures
(sitting during showers and ADLs).
3. Monitor CBC (possibly decreased platelets and WBCs)
4. Monitor for radiation injury to skin and mucous membranes and implement a skin care regimen.
- Skin: blanching, erythema, desquamation, sloughing, hemorrhage.
- Mouth: mucositis, xerostomia (dry mouth).
- Neck: difficulty swallowing.
- Abdomen: gastroenteritis.
Patient teaching:
- For mucositis: avoid spicy, salty, and acidic foods.
- Opt for cold foods over hot ones.
- Gently cleanse irradiated skin with mild soap and dry using gentle patting, not washcloth.
- Keep radiation tattoos, and avoid creams/perfumes.
- Wear loose, soft clothing.
- Avoid sun/heat on treated skin and protect skin due to reduced sensation.
Cancer – radiation implant
- Clients who receive seed implants might go home with the implants. The client’s excretions are radioactive until the isotope
has been completely eliminated from the body.
- Ensure no one touches the client’s excretions.
Nursing considerations:
- Forceps and lead containers should be kept in the patient’s room, never touch with bare hands.
- Wear a lead apron when providing care and always have the front of the apron facing the source.
- Decrease time at the bedside and keep radiation exposure to a minimum.
- Place the client in a private room. Keep the door closed as much as possible.
- Place a sign on the door warning of the radiation source and wear a dosimeter film badge that records the
personal amount of radiation exposure.
- Limit visitors to 30-minute visits and maintain a distance of 6 feet from the source.
- Individuals who are pregnant, trying to conceive, or under the age of 16 years
should not enter the client’s room.
Methotrexate
- For rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and cancers.
1. Weakens immune system 2. Low platelet count 3. Fetal death
Integumentary System
Burns
- ALWAYS FIRST stop the burning process.
- If minor burns, place the child in a horizontal position and roll in a blanket to extinguish the fire. Remove clothes,
apply tepid water, and flush chemical burns with water.

slides.title: - Then maintain airway and ventilation (ABCs).
text: - Then maintain airway and ventilation (ABCs).
Sepsis is the most common cause of death following burn injury.
- Use surgical aseptic technique with dressing changes.
- Maintain a protective environment. Restrict plants and flowers. Restrict consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables.
Limit visitors; do not allow sick individuals, small children, or other patients to visit. Use client-dedicated equipment
(blood pressure cuffs, thermometers). Administer tetanus toxoid.
- Administer antibiotics to treat infection.
- Watch for allergic reactions to antibiotics such as difficulty breathing, hypotension, hives/rash, or itching.
Hypovolemic shock is possible with inadequate fluid replacement. Excessive or rapid replacement can lead to heart failure.
- Monitor inadequate perfusion, confusion, hypotension, or decreased urine output.
- Monitor excessive hydration (bounding pulse, lung crackles, persistent edema, venous distention).
- Administer half of the total 24-hour IV fluid volume within the first 8 hr from the time the burn occurred and the
remaining volume over the next 16 hr.
- Infuse isotonic crystalloid solutions (0.9% sodium chloride or lactated Ringer’s).
- After the first 24 hours of burn: Infuse colloid solutions (albumin or synthetic plasma expanders).
- Monitor urine hourly for color, specific gravity, and protein, and to ensure output of at least 30 mL/hr (0.5
mL/kg/hr).
After a chemical burn
Wash with water or normal saline.
After a thermal burn
The most important goal is to maintain fluid and electrolyte
balance, as well as the acid-base balance to prevent
complications such as shock, dice, respiratory and cardiac failure,
and acute tubular necrosis.
Burns destroy the epidermis, allowing tissue fluid to escape and leaving the patient vulnerable to infection.
Rule of Nines
- Assesses the % of burns and is used to help guide treatment decisions, including
fluid resuscitation.
Treatment
- Silver nitrate solution 0.5% for treatment, including a wet dressing 1-2x
daily.
- Silver sulfadiazine 1% cream can be placed with a light dressing
- Mafenide acetate.
- Placed on the wound using an open exposure method, applied
up to four times a day.
- This medication is known to be painful on application,
premedicate the patient before application.
Pressure ulcers
● Breaks in the skin caused by friction or interference with the blood supply to the tissues.
● Always have more than one healthcare worker assist in turning the patient or sliding up in bed due to the
increased risk of friction.
Prevention
● Turning the patient every two hours while on bedrest and elevating bony prominences off the bed to prevent
ulcers from occurring.

slides.title: Stage 1
text: Stage 1
Nonblanchable erythema of intact skin.
Stage 1
Treat aggressively.
Stage 2
Partial thickness skin loss with exposed dermis: Involves the
epidermis and the dermis. The wound bed is viable with a
reddish-pinkish bed without slough, eschar, granulation tissue, or
adipose tissue.
Stage 2
It can appear as an intact or ruptured
blister.
Stage 3
Full-thickness skin loss: Visible adipose tissue with possible
granulation tissue and epibole (wound edges appear rolled under); some
slough, and eschar present.
● No exposed muscle, tendons, ligaments, cartilage, or bones.
Stage 3
Possible undermining or tunneling.
Stage 4
Full-thickness skin and tissue loss: Skin and tissue loss with
cartilage, bone, fascia, muscle, ligaments, or tendon exposed in the
wound or easily palpable.
Stage 4
Tunneling is common.
Unstageable
Obscured, full-thickness skin, and tissue loss:
No determination of stage because eschar or slough obscures the
wound bed.
Unstageable
The actual depth of injury is unknown
unless slough and eschar are removed, at
which time the wound is restaged.
Contact dermatitis
- Caused by exposure to a physical or chemical allergen.
- Rash is well-demarcated and localized.
- Treatment: Diphenhydramine
- Monitor the client for anorexia, dry mouth, and drowsiness.
Symptoms: Itching, raised papules.
Impetigo
- Contagious superficial skin infection caused by S. Aureus.
- Characterized by a small, red macule that turns into a vesicle that becomes pustular with honey-colored crusts.
- Can lead to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Herpes zoster
- Highly contagious infection that's transmitted by direct contact with vesicular fluid or airborne droplets.
- Patient will be in isolation until the vesicles are crusted over.
- The virus can be transmitted through direct contact, causing chickenpox. Avoid exposing infants, pregnant women who have
not had chickenpox, and clients who are immunocompromised.
- Moisten dressings with cool water or 5% aluminum acetate (Burrow’s solution) and apply to the affected skin for 30-60
minutes, 4-6 times a day.
- Use lotions (calamine lotion) or recommend colloidal oatmeal baths to help relieve itching.
Scabies
- Look for gray or brown burrows, curved or linear ridges on the skin, and follicular papules.
- Patients often report intense nighttime itching.
- Rash commonly appears between fingers, in popliteal folds, and in the inguinal region.

slides.title: - Mites appear as black dots at the end of grayish-brown burrows, leaving thin pencil-like marks on the skin.
text: - Mites appear as black dots at the end of grayish-brown burrows, leaving thin pencil-like marks on the skin.
Peripheral Vascular Disorders
Disorders of the peripheral vascular system
- Narrowing, obstruction, or damage to the arteries or veins resulting in ischemia, a lack of blood flow to the tissues or organs
involved or venous stasis.
Arterial revascularization surgery
- The priority action is to maintain adequate circulation in the repaired artery. The location of the pedal or dorsalis pulse should
be marked, and its pulsatile strength compared with the contralateral leg on a scheduled basis using a Doppler.
- Graft occlusion is a significant issue after arterial revascularization, usually happening within the initial 24 hours post-surgery.
- Inform the healthcare provider about signs of graft occlusion such as diminished pedal pulses, heightened pain, and altered
limb color or temperature.
- Notify the provider if the patient develops chest pain.
Arterial disease
- Pain is provoked by exercise and activity, relieved by rest, and worsened with elevation.
- Intermittent claudication refers to leg pain that occurs after exercise and is relieved after rest.
- Arterial disorders typically mean patients should place their legs in a dependent position.
Buerger’s disease
- Recurring inflammation of the small and medium arteries and veins of the lower extremities.
- Usually the result of occlusion of the vessels by a thrombus formation.
- Occurs largely in younger males who smoke.
- First clinical symptoms: A bluish color to an extremity or a feeling of coldness in the affected limb.
- Smoking cessation is the largest goal of Buerger's disease and Raynaud's disease.
Raynaud's disease
- Intermittent construction of cutaneous blood vessels precipitated by exposure to cold, emotional stress, caffeine ingestion, and
tobacco use.
- Smoking cessation is the largest goal of Buerger's disease and Raynaud's disease.
- Usually in women from the ages of 16 to 40.
Patient teaching: Wear protective cotton gloves.
Leg measurements to detect swelling
- Should be done with a patient in dorsal recumbent position.
- Positive Homan’s sign will show the presence of thrombophlebitis, which occurs when there is pain in the calf of the leg
when the foot is dorsiflexed.
Aneurysm
- Localized or diffuse dilation or outpouchings of the vessel wall.
- Patients may complain of back pain or neurologic pain.
- Patients who complain of sudden onset angina may indicate a rupture or dissection.
Symptoms: Pulsating mass in the center of the abdomen, chest wall, or in the periumbilical region.
Varicose veins
- Abnormally lengthened, dilated, superficial veins, usually saphenous, result from incompetent valves, especially in the lower
extremities.
- Goal is to promote venous return by encouraging frequent walks, discouraging prolonged sitting, and discouraging sitting
with crossed legs.
- Treatment: Vein ligation and stripping
Post-op nursing considerations:
- Elevation of the extremities, compression stockings, and anticoagulant therapy.
- Ensure that compression stockings are removed twice a day for a half hour each to ensure skin integrity.
Arterial ulcers
- Caused by peripheral vascular disease.

slides.title: - Arterial stasis ulcers: Usually on the tips of toes and indicates arterial insufficiency.
text: - Arterial stasis ulcers: Usually on the tips of toes and indicates arterial insufficiency.
- Progressive disorder that leads to further risk of impaired tissue integrity.
Venous ulcers
- Caused by chronic venous insufficiency from a clot, varicose vein, valve defects, prolonged immobility, and heart failure.
Bruit
- Caused by turbulent blood flow through stenotic blood vessels.
- Always check clients with dialysis shunt for the presence of bruits and thrills indicating patency.
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
- Prevent by moving and exercising the legs frequently.
- Do not massage the affected limb.
- Elevate the client’s affected extremity when in bed.
- When DVT is already formed, ensure the patient stays on bed rest.
Arteriosclerosis
- Loss of elasticity, thickening, and hardening of arterial walls.
- Usually precedes angina pectoris and myocardial infarction.
- Most common type is atherosclerosis caused by plaque.
Musculoskeletal System
Gout
- Deposits of uric acid crystals in the synovial joints.
- Diagnosis is based on serum uric acid levels, which should be below 8 mg/dL.
- Avoid alcohol, organ meats, shellfish, or anchovies.
- Increase fluid intake.
- Treatment: Allopurinol.
Purine metabolism
- Problems with this metabolism result in an increase in uric acid levels in the blood.
- Treatment: Allopurinol is the preferred treatment to treat gout.
- Colchicine helps to reduce the pain and swelling during an acute gout attack, important to administer with foods and increase
fluids while on this medication.
Rheumatoid arthritis
- Chronic, progressive disease that destroys synovial bone joints and connective tissue.
- Will have elevated ESR and Platelets.
- Normal platelets: 150,000-400,000.
- ESR: 70 to 150 mm/hr is severe inflammation.
Symptoms: Joint swelling, low-grade fever, fatigue, weakness, and paresthesias.
- Can also cause bilateral and symmetrical stiffness in the joints that are worse in the morning.
Complications
- Triad of manifestations: dry eye, mouth, and vagina.
- Ischemia
- Pleurisy, pneumonitis, diffuse interstitial fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension.
- Pericarditis and myocarditis
- Treatment: Humira IM
- Increase iron and protein intake.
Osteoarthritis
- Non-inflammatory degenerative joint disease marked by progressive pain that is relieved by rest.
- Typically involves the weight-bearing joints and is characterized by a loss of cartilage on the articular surfaces of the joints,
also spur development.
- Pain will be worse during activity and the patient is usually overweight.
Osteoporosis
- Most common metabolic bone disorder, causing decreased bone mass and increased risk of fractures.

slides.title: - Causes: Calcium and estrogen deficiency
text: - Causes: Calcium and estrogen deficiency
Symptoms: Gradual loss in height after menopause.
- Encourage: Fish, vitamin D foods, green leafy vegetables, egg yolks, fortified milk, and cereal.
- Discharge instructions: perform weight-bearing exercises.
Hip arthroplasty
- Primary goal after surgery is to prevent hip adduction and hyperflexion (dislocation).
Patient teaching
- Prevent the patient from bending at the hips beyond 90 degrees.
- Use elevated seating and a raised toilet seat. Use straight chairs with arms.
- Externally rotate the toes.
- Use abduction pillows between the legs to reduce the risk of a dislocation.
- Avoid turning to the operative side.
- Avoid crossing legs while sitting.
Knee arthroplasty
- A continuous passive motion (CPM) machine can be prescribed to promote motion in the knee, promote circulation, and
prevent scar tissue formation. CPM is usually placed and initiated immediately after surgery. CPM provides passive range of
motion from full extension to the prescribed amount of flexion.
- Turn it off during meals.
- If tracing is noticed on the cords, immediately remove them from the client’s room.
Malignant hyperthermia
- Acute life-threatening medical emergency.
- Hypermetabolic condition alter calcium activity in muscle cells, causing muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and CNS damage.
- Triggering agents include inhalation anesthetics and succinylcholine.
- It's a complication of general anesthesia.
- Early signs: increased CO2, decreased oxygen saturation, and tachycardia.
- Followed by dysrhythmias, muscle rigidity, hypotension, tachypnea, skin mottling, cyanosis, and myoglobinuria.
- Extremely high temperature (up to 44°C or 111.2°F) may occur as a late manifestation.
Nursing considerations:
- Stop the surgery and administer IV dantrolene, a muscle relaxant.
- Administer 100% oxygen.
- Obtain specimens for ABGs to monitor for metabolic acidosis and blood tests to check for hyperkalemia.
- Infuse iced IV 0.9% sodium chloride.
- Apply a cooling blanket; ice to axillae, groin, neck, and head; and iced lavage.
- Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to monitor output and for hematuria.
- Monitor cardiac rhythm and treat dysrhythmias and transfer client to intensive care.
Lumbar laminectomy
- The patient should only be moved by way of log rolling.
Compartment syndrome
- Secondary edema that causes an increase in the pressure in closed spaces of the tissue compartment formed by an elastic fascia.
- This is an EMERGENCY.
- As the pressure increases, obstruction of the venous circulation and arterial occlusion occur, leading to ischemia.
Symptoms:
- Progressive pain that is distal to the injury, unrelieved by analgesics.
- Edema, paralysis, pallor, decreased or absent peripheral pulses, delayed capillary refill, colder lamp temperature.
Fat embolism
- A serious complication that occurs after a bone fracture, especially the long bones.
- Pulmonary circulation is typically where the fat emboli become obstructed, which leads to dyspnea, chest pain, coughing,
tachycardia, and restlessness.
- Petechiae over the chest and axilla are present with fat emboli.
Multiple myeloma

slides.title: - Bone fractures are a common complication.
text: - Bone fractures are a common complication.
Paget's disease
- Common bone disease that affects middle-aged and elderly people is marked by inflammation of bones, softening and
thickening of bones, excessive bone destruction, and unorganized bone repair, resulting in the bowing of long bones.
Phantom limb pain
- Occurs when an amputee complains of severe pain in the removed body part.
Nursing considerations:
- Stump care to promote healing.
- Exercise to maintain the tone of the unaffected muscle.
- Physiological support.
- Never assume that they do not have pain in the removed limb, treat all pain aggressively.
- To reduce swelling, the residual limb should be elevated on a pillow for 24 hours.
- Cast care
- Support drain cast on pillows, do not cover (allow it to air-dry).
- Frequently assess pulse, color, movement, and sensation distal to the cast.
- Monitor neurovascular status of the extremity 1-2 hours after the application of the cast skin traction.
- Used for relief of painful muscle spasms.
Buck’s traction
- A short-term immobilization device used for femur or hip fractures to reduce muscle spasms and immobilize the injured limb
until surgery.
Bryant's traction
- Vertical suspension where the pelvis is elevated from the bay.
- Used for congenital hip dislocation and fractured femurs in infants and children who weigh less than 35 lb.
- The butt will be just slightly off the bed.
Skeletal traction
- Appliance of direct traction to the bone using pins and wires.
- A surgical immobilization device applied to long bones (femur, tibia) and cervical spine, not utilized for hip fractures.
- UAPs should never touch skeletal traction devices (bags or weights).
Cold treatment
Promotes vasoconstriction.
Decrease swelling, muscle spasms, and pain.
Heat treatment
Increases vasodilation.
Decrease muscle spasms, joint stiffness, and pain.
