text: Neurosensory System
Migraines
- Elevate the head of the patient’s bed to 30 degrees and ensure to maintain a cool, dark, quiet environment.
- Tyramine foods can trigger migraines.
- Complementary therapies
- Yoga, meditation, tai chi, exercise, biofeedback, and massage promote relaxation and alleviate muscle tension.
- Biofeedback requires concentration to control physiological responses.
- Acupuncture and acupressure therapy.
Stroke
- Disruption in cerebral blood flow due to ischemia, hemorrhage, brain attack, or embolism.
- Stroke types: Hemorrhagic (brain bleed) and ischemic (thrombotic or embolic).
- Ischemic strokes (thrombotic/embolic) can be reversed with alteplase (tPA).
- Administer alteplase within 3-4.5 hr of initial symptoms (unless contraindicated). Alteplase dissolves clots and restores blood
flow.
- Monitor for bleeding, thrombocytopenia, anemia.
- CT can is immediate for an expected stroke
- Clients may have self-image issues following a stroke. Assist in setting short-term goals and display empathy.
- When patient is discharged with weakness following a stroke, ensure a medical alert system is in place at the patient’s
home in case of a fall.
The left cerebral hemisphere The right cerebral hemisphere
Responsible for language, mathematics skills, and analytic
thinking.
Logic

proprioception.
Creative
Symptoms of Left Hemisphere Stroke
● Cautious and slow behavior
● Expressive and receptive aphasia (inability to speak and
understand language)
● Alexia (reading difficulty)
● Agnosia (unable to recognize familiar objects)
● Agraphia (writing difficulty)
● Right extremity hemiplegia (paralysis) or
● hemiparesis (weakness)
● Depression, anger, and quick to become frustrated
Symptoms of Right Hemisphere Stroke
● Poor judgment and impulse control
● Altered perception of deficits (overestimation of abilities)
● Unilateral neglect syndrome (when the patient is unaware of the
left side of the body.
● No depth perception
● Left hemiplegia or hemiparesis
Aphasia
- Complete or partial loss of language skills caused by damage to the cortical areas of the brain's left hemisphere.
Expressive aphasia
- Provides the patient with a communication board or an alternative way of communication.
- Knowing what you want to say but can’t get it out.
Global aphasia
- Most severe, when someone is listening to words/communication but cannot understand.
Hemianopia
- Characterized by defective vision or blindness in half of the visual field.
- A symptom of stroke.
Cerebral edema
- Treatment medications are corticosteroids.

slides.title: - Maintain seizure precautions.
text: - Maintain seizure precautions.
- Follow fluid restrictions to prevent worsening of the condition.
- Cerebral edema is a risk with hypertonic solutions.
Glasgow coma scale
- Used to assess levels of consciousness and clients with neurological problems.
The scoring system is based on a scale of 3 to 15 points.
The lowest possible score is 3 points (deep coma or death).
The highest possible score is 15 points (fully awake).
● A score lower than 8 indicates that coma is present.
Less than 8 = intubate
Motor Response Points
● Obeys a simple response = 6
● Localizes painful stimuli = 5
● Normal flexion (withdrawal) = 4
● Abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) = 3
● Extensor response (decerebrate posturing) = 2
● No motor response to pain = 1
Verbal Response Points
● Oriented = 5
● Confused conversation = 4
● Inappropriate words = 3
● Responds with incomprehensible sounds = 2
● No verbal response = 1
Eye-Opening Points
● Spontaneous = 4
● In response to sound = 3
● In response to pain = 2
● No response, even to painful stimuli = 1

Meniere's disease
- Balance disorder that causes vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus.
Patient teaching:
- Encourage the patient to adhere to a low-sodium diet, as well as avoid alcohol, caffeine, and tobacco.
Increased ICP
- Most significant sign is a decrease in LOC.
- Monitored by placing a screw, catheter, or sensor through a burr hole into the ventricle, or the subarachnoid, epidural, or
subdural space. The expected reference range is 10-15 mm Hg.
Symptoms:
- Widening pulse pressure, lethargy, decreased pulse, increased blood pressure, elevated temperature.
- Sunsetting eyes.
Nursing considerations:
- Elevate HOB to 30 degrees.
ICP elevation can result from:
● Hypercarbia causing cerebral vasodilation.
● Endotracheal or oral tracheal suctioning
● Coughing.
● Extreme neck or hip flexion/extension.
● Keeping the head of the bed below 30 degrees.
● Raising intra-abdominal pressure (due to restrictive clothing, Valsalva maneuver).
Manage ICP by:
● Raise the head by at least 30 degrees for reduced ICP and improved venous drainage.
● Prevent extreme head movements, maintaining a neutral midline position.
● Ensure a clear airway and offer mechanical ventilation if needed.
● Administer oxygen as required to maintain PaO2 above 60 mm Hg.
● Provide stool softeners and discourage the Valsalva maneuver for elevated ICP.
● Create a quiet environment with limited visitors and minimal noise.
● Intubated patients may undergo controlled hyperventilation briefly after 24 hr post-injury to lower ICP.
○ Avoid this during the first 24 hr to prevent cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia.
Retinal detachment
- Patient will see floating spots and a veil-like curtain as well as flashes of light.
- NOT blindness, NOT painful.
- After retinal detachment surgery, the patient will need a patch on both eyes and keep the eyes bandaged for 24 hours.
Macular Degeneration
- Loss of central vision.
Cataracts
- A normally transparent lens becomes cloudy and opaque, leading to progressive blurring/gradual loss of vision.
- After surgery, teach the patient to avoid increasing intraocular pressure by coughing or rapid head movement.
- Halo around lights and absent red reflex.
Glaucoma
- Impairment of optic nerve function or structure.
- IOP elevation due to fluid imbalance affects optic nerve and vision.

slides.title: - Normal IOP range: 10 to 21 mm/Hg.
text: - Normal IOP range: 10 to 21 mm/Hg.
- Leading cause of blindness.
Open-angle
● Gradual peripheral vision loss, causing tunnel vision
● Headache and mild eye pain
● Reduced peripheral vision
● Accommodation decline
● Halos around lights
● Increased IOP
Angle-closure
● Sudden IOP increase due to rapid iris-sclera angle closure
● Immediate treatment needed
● Rapid onset of elevated IOP (30 mm Hg+)
● Blurred or decreased vision
● Halos around lights
● Nonreactive pupils
● Severe pain and nausea
● Sensitivity to light
EEG
- Avoid stimulants prior to the procedure such as coffee or tea.
- Ensure the client’s hair is clean and without hair product.
Seizures
st nursing priority: Protect patient’s head from injury and move anything in the environment that may enter the patient.
- Avoid restraining the patient and stay with them until the seizure is completed.
Nursing considerations:
- Place the patient on their left side to prevent aspiration.
- Dilantin may be used to treat seizures, teach patient that it can cause gum hyperplasia and red-colored urine.
- Nothing in the mouth.
Seizure Precautions
- Padded side rails with the side rails up, call light within reach.
- Do not attempt to open the jaw or insert an airway during a seizure.
- Turn the client to the side to prevent aspiration.
- Always ensure patient has venous access.
- Loosen restrictive clothing.
Romberg's test
- “The falling test”
- Assesses the patient's ability to maintain balance and assess vestibular function.
- Usually performed in addition to the Weber and Rinne tests, which evaluate hearing.
- Rinne and Weber tests utilize tuning forks to determine whether hearing loss is present.
- Weber: Place a vibrating tuning fork on top of the client’s head. Ask whether the client can hear the
sound best in the right ear, the left ear, or both ears equally.
- Expected finding: The client hears sound equal in both ears (negative Weber test).
Babinski's reflex
- When the sole of the foot is stroked from the heel to the ball, the toes should curl downward (negative).
- If the toes flare up word this indicates a positive test and is abnormal after the age of 2 years.
- If positive, indicates head trauma.
Parkinson's disease
- Progressive, degenerative disorder caused by dopamine depletion and results in a decline in muscular functioning.
Symptoms: Tremor at rest, rigidity, slow movements, shuffling gait, mask-like face, emotional lability, drooling, and
sweating.
Nursing considerations:
- Maintain a safe environment
- Levodopa-carbidopa
Multiple Sclerosis
- Progressive CNS disorder caused by demyelination in the brain and spinal cord.

slides.title: - Diagnosed by MRI to see plaque on the brain and spine.
text: - Diagnosed by MRI to see plaque on the brain and spine.
Symptoms:
- First indication is visual problems.
Nursing considerations:
- Provide a safe environment and maximize the patient's independence.
Treatment: Interferon Beta 1A and Beta b
Myasthenia gravis
- Autoimmune disorder causing muscle weakness and fatigue that worsens with activity and improves with rest, leading to
persistent fatigue.
- Myasthenic crisis: Too little Acetylcholine → weak, patient is hypertensive.
- Cholinergic crisis: Too much Acetylcholine → hypermotility, hypersecretions, hypotension.
- Give anticholinergic (atropine)
- Diagnostic test: Tensilon test
Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
- Progressive, fatal, motor neuron disease causing progressive muscular atrophy.
Nursing considerations:
- Monitor respiratory function and the patient's ability to swallow.
- Referral to a speech-language pathologist is a priority.
- Cause of death is usually pneumonia.
Bell's Palsy
- Paralysis of one side of the face, usually due to inflammation of the 7th cranial nerve.
Patient teaching:
- Usually lasting only two to eight weeks, the patient should prevent corneal drying by
using artificial tears.
Guillain-Barre syndrome
- Autoimmune disorder characterized by Progressive ascending paralysis that most often ceases
within 4 weeks, with complete recovery around 3 to 6 months.
- Causes motor weakness symmetrically. Weakness starts in the feet and moves upwards.
Nursing considerations:
- Maintain an airway, because the airway is compromised when the disease reaches the diaphragm.
Huntington's disease
- Inherited disorder causing progressive atrophy of the basal ganglia and portions of the cerebral cortex.
Symptoms:
- Extreme emotional lability, dementia, and uncontrolled limb movements.
Spinal cord injuries (SCI)
- C3 or above are usually fatal because the muscles used for breathing are now paralyzed.
- Thoracic and lumbar injuries affect the legs, bladder, and bowel.
Nursing considerations:
- Watch for autonomic dysreflexia: bradycardia, facial flushing, severe headache, and
hypertension.
- Position change every 2 hours (1 hour in a wheelchair) is vital to prevent pressure sores.
- SCI patients can't move or feel pain from prolonged pressure.
- Use pressure-relief devices in bed and wheelchair consistently.
Head injury
- Hyperthermia around 105°F can occur.
- Test cerebrospinal fluid for glucose to confirm CSF leakage.
- Deafness and vertigo suggest cranial nerve #8 involvement.
- Stabilize the cervical spine until X-ray clearance.
- Prevent cervical injury; neck immobility is crucial.

slides.title: - The primary concern is potential spinal cord damage in case of a cervical injury. The top nursing priority is
text: - The primary concern is potential spinal cord damage in case of a cervical injury. The top nursing priority is
maintaining neck immobilization until cervical spine injury is ruled out.
- Report CSF presence from the nose or ears to the provider.
Meningitis
- Droplet precaution
- Lumbar puncture is the diagnostic test.
- Patient will lay on their side with their knees curled
up toward the chest or sitting down and curled
forward into a C shape.
- Following the procedure, the patient will be on bed
rest for 6 to 8 hours.
Dementia
Nursing considerations:
- Assess cognitive status, memory, judgment, and
personality changes.
- Initiate bowel and bladder program based on a set
schedule.
- Assist client to the bathroom frequently as a
measure to increase client safety.
- Help with memory loss by placing a calendar in the
client’s home.
- Offer finger foods when the client gets agitated.
Alzheimer's disease
Medication
Memantine slows brain-cell death by blocking calcium entry into nerve cells. Approved for moderate to severe AD stages.
Nursing considerations:
○ Cholinesterase inhibitor can be used concurrently with Memantine.
■ Rivastigmine, Donepezil, and Galantamine
○ Monitor for common adverse effects, including headache, dizziness, confusion, and constipation.
Risk factors: Genetics, ionizing radiation and electromagnetic fields exposure, previous head injury
Early stages
● Forgetfulness, particularly in short-term and recent memory.
● Provide nursing care by ensuring a recognizable environment and consistent schedule.
● Offer respite care to the family → the client may be able to stay at home if that is the family’s desire.
Middle stages
● Personality shifts can manifest–mood swings and irritability.
● Speech and language difficulties, such as expressive aphasia, may develop.
● Expressive aphasia involves knowing what to say but struggling to communicate.
● Nursing care involves engaging in activities demanding reduced concentration.
● Assess remote memory, asking questions like "Which high school did you attend?"
Final stages
● Complete memory loss, reduced mobility, and loss of bowel and bladder control.
● Common cause of death is complications related to immobility, like sepsis or pneumonia.

Renal
Intravenous pyelogram (IVP)
- Allergy to shellfish contraindicates the use of this contrast medium.
Cystoscopy
- Visualization of the urethra and bladder.
Urinalysis
- Detects various conditions like diabetes mellitus, dehydration, UTI, kidney trauma, and glomerulonephritis.
- Reflects glomeruli damage leading to protein and red blood cell leakage.
- Collecting a urinalysis
Clean-catch midstream for culture & sensitivity (C&S)

- After a thorough cleansing of the urethral meatus, clients catch the urine sample midstream, not the beginning of the
stream.
Catheter urine specimen for C&S
- A sterile specimen is obtained from a straight or indwelling catheter using surgical asepsis (sterile technique).
Timed urine specimens
- Always discard the first voiding.
- Collect all other urine. Refrigerate, label, and transport the specimen.
Straight or indwelling catheter insertion
- Equipment
- Usual size and type of catheter
Children: 8 to 10 Fr
Females: 14 to 16 Fr
Males: 16 to 18 Fr
- For patients with latex allergies: Use silicon or Teflon products.
- Catheterization kit with a sterile drainage bag for indwelling catheter insertion.
- Provide privacy and explain the procedure.
Urinary issues
- Less than 30 mL/hr for more than 2 hours is a cause for concern.
Creatinine clearance test
- The best indicator of the kidney's filtration function.
- Measures the amount of creatinine filtered by the glomeruli over 24 hours.
Serum creatinine level
- The best indicator of the status of glomerular filtration.
- The only condition that raises serum creatinine levels is kidney disease.
24-hour urine collection
- Empty the bladder completely and discard the urine.
- Save all the urine for the next 24 hours.
Chronic Kidney Disease
- Progressive destruction of the kidney tissue resulting in worsening function of the kidney that is typically irreversible.
Symptoms:
- Ammonia in the skin and alimentary tract resulting from bacterial interaction with urea leading to inflammation of
mucosal membranes.

slides.title: - Results in retention of phosphate, and decreased calcium, all leading to muscle spasms, tetany, increased
text: - Results in retention of phosphate, and decreased calcium, all leading to muscle spasms, tetany, increased
parathormone release, and eventually demineralization of bones.
- Results in increased creatinine.
- Results in waste product retention, which leads to depressed bone marrow function, decreased red blood cells,
renal tissue hypoxia, decreased erythropoietin production, and eventually further depression of bone marrow
functioning.
Patient teaching:
- Increase fluids to flush the kidneys, and check urine for protein, blood, and specific gravity.
- Meticulous perineal care is important.
- Eat 1g/kg of protein per day.
- Complications
- Metabolic acidosis, electrolyte imbalance, fluid overload, dysrhythmias, hypertension, uremia, and secondary
infection.
Acute renal failure (acute kidney injury)
- Specific gravity of the scanty output will be low because the kidney is unable to concentrate water.
- Can be caused by pyelonephritis and glomerulonephritis.
- Patients at high risk include untreated streptococcal infection, bowel incontinence, and renal reflux.
- Rapid onset of oliguria accompanied by a rising BUN level and serum creatinine.
- Typically this is reversible.
Symptoms: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, azotemia(elevated BUN and creatinine always means end-stage kidney disease),
weight gain, altered mental status.
Patient teaching:
- Low protein, sodium, and potassium.
- Low sodium, high calcium, iron, Vitamin B, C, D.
- High carbohydrates.
Glomerulonephritis
- Inflammation of glomerulus that leads to leakage of RBCs and protein into the urine.
- Acute glomerulonephritis often follows an infection.
- 20 to 30 years: chronic glomerulonephritis develops.
- Causes: Post strep infection
Symptoms:
- Hypertension, decreased GFR, edema, tea-colored urine from hematuria, elevated BUN, proteinuria.
Treatment:
- Monitor BP and fluid status, watch for hyperkalemia, and limit sodium.
- Implement potassium, phosphate, sodium, and magnesium restrictions.
- Due to the high rate of protein breakdown, teach the patient to consume a high-protein diet.
Acute glomerulonephritis
- Inflammatory disease of both kidneys that interferes with glomerular filtration.
- Most commonly caused by repeated streptococcal infections during childhood.
Symptoms: Hematuria and proteinuria.
Treatment: If azotemia is present, protein will be restricted.
Nephrotic syndrome
- Changes to glomerulus that lead to massive leakage of protein in the urine.
Symptoms: Massive proteinuria, foamy, frothy dark urine, hypoalbuminemia (low protein in blood), edema.
- Serum albumin is an indicator of nutritional status.
Treatment: Diuretics and IV albumin and a low sodium diet.
Dehydration
- Reduced urine output, will lead to elevated specific gravity, indicating concentration of particles from water loss.
- Report urine output less than 30 mL/hr.
Urinary tract infections

slides.title: - Pyridium (OTC: Azo) is typically used to treat.
text: - Pyridium (OTC: Azo) is typically used to treat.
Patient teaching:
- It is NORMAL to turn the urine orange.
- Discourage the use of bubble baths.
- Encourage urination before and after sexual intercourse.
Kidney infection
- Hallmark sign is flank pain and vomiting.
Pyelonephritis
- Acute or chronic inflammation due to bacterial infection of the parenchyma and pelvis of the kidney.
Symptoms: Kidney pain, impaired sodium reabsorption, and protein loss.
Urolithiasis
- Presents and formation of stones in the renal calculi or pelvis that pass through the lower regions of the urinary tract.
Symptoms: Severe flank pain (renal colic), pallor, sweating, syncope, shock, and possible vomiting.
Patient teaching:
- Strain all urine and check for the presence of stones.
- Encourage decreased calcium and increased fluids (3- 4L/day).
- Increase ambulation to help pass the stones.
- Adhere to a low-purine diet.
Dialysis
- Effectiveness is measured in a decrease in serum creatinine and BUN as well as the reduction in fluid retention.
- Patients typically will have problems with fluid and electrolyte imbalances.
- Hemodialysis
- Hemodialysis is needed when glomerular filtration rate is showing less than 20 mL/min.
- Complications include dialysis disequilibrium syndrome, hypotension, anemia, arrhythmias, and transfusion
reactions.
- Advanced age raises the risk of dialysis disequilibrium and hypotension due to quick fluid and electrolyte
changes.
- Evaluate AV fistula or AV graft for palpable thrill and bruit, as well as ample circulation and distal pulses.
- To determine fistula's patency for dialysis, check AV fistula bruit.
- Peritoneal dialysis
- Complications include peritonitis, hypoalbuminemia, and bowel or bladder perforation.
- Peritonitis: Cloudy or opaque effluent.
- During the procedure, maintain surgical asepsis.
- Monitor for infection: discolored, purulent, or cloudy drainage, fever, swelling, and redness.
Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
- The most common surgical procedure for BPH.
- Removal of prosthetic tissue by instrumentation through the urethra.
Post-operative nursing considerations:
- Know that venous bleeding is common for several days after the procedure.
- Includes placement of an indwelling three-way catheter.
- If the catheter gets blocked (bladder spasms, reduced irrigation outflow), pause the CBI (continuous bladder
irrigation) and flush with 50 mL of irrigation solution using a large piston syringe. Inform the surgeon if clot
removal is unsuccessful.
- Always clean the perineal area after bowel movement.
Autonomic dysreflexia
- Caused by a lesion in the thoracic or cervical cord.
Symptoms: Hypertension, sweating, and headaches.
- May occur with blockage in the urine catheter or fecal impaction.
Stress incontinence
- Encourage kegel exercises.

text: Inhaled agents for asthma
- With inhaled agents, administer bronchodilators BEFORE anti-inflammatory medication.
- Bronchodilators (Albuterol, Ipratropium, Theophylline)
- Suck on hard candies to help moisten dry mouth while taking Ipratropium.
- Anti-inflammatory medications (Corticosteroids such as Fluticasone and Prednisone or Leukotriene antagonists
such as Montelukast).
Acute Pulmonary Edema
- Results from heart failure due to excessive quantity of fluid in the pulmonary interstitial spaces.
Symptoms: Moist rales, and pink, frothy sputum.
- Measured by the depth of the indentation of the thumb.
- Survival is rare. This is a life-threatening emergency. Immediate, aggressive treatment is used.
Nursing considerations:
- High-Fowler’s, administer oxygen, positive airway pressure, intubation, or place the patient on a ventilator.
- IV morphine (decreases anxiety, venous return, and respiratory distress).
- Rapid-acting loop diuretic (furosemide).
- Client teaching to improve tolerance to activity, such as alternating periods of activity with periods of rest.
- Consult with the patient’s provider before beginning an exercise regimen and remain physically
active.
Pulmonary embolism
Symptoms: Dyspnea, sharp, stabbing pain on inhalation.
- Risk factors: Oral contraceptives and estrogen therapy → estrogen and progesterone increase the risk for blood clots.
- Note: History of thrombophlebitis, impaired liver function, and hypertension are contraindications of oral
contraceptives.
Pneumothorax
Symptoms: Tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia/cyanosis, and dyspnea.
- When air or gas gets into the pleural space it causes lung collapse.
- Confirmation of hemothorax: Thoracentesis.
- Confirmation of hemothorax or pneumothorax: Chest x-ray.
- Pneumothorax: Due to trapped air, you will hear hyperresonance on percussion.
- Tension pneumothorax: Tracheal deviation to the unaffected side.
- Hemothorax (blood): Dull percussion.
- Flail chest: Paradoxical chest wall movement.
Nursing considerations: Insertion of a chest tube in the pleural space will drain blood, fluid, or air.
- Negative pressure will re-establish.
- Lung expansion will occur.
- Restore normal intrapleural pressure.
Venturi Masks
- 4-10L/min
- The most precise O2 delivery.
- Best for patients with COPD or other chronic lung diseases.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
- Irreversible
Symptoms:
- Low oxygen levels (normal is 95% to 100%).
- Barrel chest or increased chest diameter (with emphysema).
- Right-sided heart failure causing dependent edema.
- Late stage: Clubbing of fingers and toes.
Patient teaching:
- Promote smoking cessation.

slides.title: - Avoid exposure to secondhand smoke.
text: - Avoid exposure to secondhand smoke.
- Promote adequate nutrition.
- Increased work of breathing increases caloric demands.
- Proper nutrition to prevent infection.
- Encourage fluids to promote hydration.
- Dyspnea decreases energy available for eating, so soft, high-calorie foods should be encouraged (three
large meals a day).
Aerosol mask/face tent
- Good for patients with burns or facial trauma.
Home oxygen education
- Avoid synthetic or wool fabrics (encourage wearing cotton).
- Educate to apply a water-soluble lubricant to soothe irritation
of the mucous membranes, NOT vaseline.
- No smoking around the oxygen tank.
- Ensure oxygen tank stays away from safety hazards (curtains,
drapes).
Incentive spirometer use
- Keep the mouth closed and ensure a tight mouth seal around the mouthpiece. Inhale and hold breath for 3-5 seconds.
Tracheostomy care
- The maximum suction time should only be 15 seconds.
- After suctioning, re-oxygenate the patient.
- Suctioning means the airway is deprived of oxygen and air exchange because of applied negative air pressure from
external.
- There is a significant risk of hypoxia and ischemia if the suction is done for a longer duration.
- Allow the patient 20 to 30 seconds to rest between suction passes.
- Sterile technique is needed for trach suctioning (sterile gloves).
Chest tubes
- Tidaling (respirations causing movement of the fluid level) is normal and expected in the water seal chamber.
- Spontaneous respirations: Fluid level rises with inhale, falls with exhale.
- Positive-pressure ventilation: Fluid level rises with exhale, falls with inhale. No tidaling means lung re-expansion or
obstruction.
- No tidaling: Lung re-expansion or an obstruction within the system.
- Continuous bubbling indicates an air leak.
- Intermittent bubbling is common when tubes remove air from the pleural space, often occurring during exhalation,
sneezing, or coughing.
- The absence of bubbling indicates complete air removal.
- Following open heart surgery, tubes are in the mediastinal space, bubbling and tidaling are not expected; pulsations in the
fluid level might be seen.
Before insertion During insertion After insertion
Supine or Semi-Fowler’s position. The chest tube drainage system should be
below the client’s chest level with the
tubing on the bed. The tubing from the
bed to the system is straight to promote
drainage via gravity.
Assess oxygen, breath sounds, vital signs,
color, and respiratory effort as indicated
by the status of the client at least every 4
hr.
Check water seal and encourage deep
breathing/coughing every 2 hr.
Add fluid as needed, if evaporated.

slides.title: Keep the drainage system below the
text: Keep the drainage system below the
client’s chest level, even during
ambulation.
Must-Know Clinical Signs
Babinski reflex
- Dorsiflexion of the big toe after stimulation of the lateral sole.
- Associated with corticospinal tract lesions.
Brudzinski's sign
- Flexion of the hip and knee induced by flexion of the neck.
- Associated with meningeal irritation.
Chadwick's sign
- Sign of vaginal and cervical mucosa.
- Associated with pregnancy.
Chovstek’s sign
- Facial muscle spasms induced by tapping on the facial nerve branches.
Cheyne-Stokes respirations
- Rhythmic cycles of deep and shallow respirations often with apneic periods.
- Associated with the central nervous system.
Cullen's sign
- Bluish discoloration around the umbilicus.
- Indicative of acute pancreatitis.
Harlequin’s sign
- In the newborn infant, reddening of the lower half of the laterally recumbent body and blanching of the upper half.
- Due to temporary vasomotor disturbances.
Hegar’s sign
- Softening of the fundus of the uterus.
- Associated with first trimester of pregnancy.
Homan's sign
- Pain behind the knee induced by dorsiflexion of the
foot.
- Associated with peripheral vascular disease, especially
venous thrombosis in the calf.
Kernig’s sign
- Inability to extend the leg when sitting or lying with
the thigh flexed on the abdomen.
- Associated with meningeal irritation.
Kussmaul's breathing
- Paroxysmal air hunger, associated with acidosis,
especially diabetic ketoacidosis.
- Characterized by deep sighing respiratory patterns.
Mcburney's sign
- Tenderness at Mcburney's point, two-thirds of the distance from the umbilicus to the anterior
superior iliac spine.
- Associated with appendicitis.
Rovsing's sign
- Pain in the right lower quadrant when the lower left quadrant is pressed.
- Associated with appendicitis.

slides.title: Patient Positioning
text: Patient Positioning
“centesis” think “big needle” (thoracentesis) “scope” think “visualize” (bronchoscopy)
Bed and Patient Positions
Prone
● Contraindicated for tracheostomies, cervical injuries, or breathing difficulties.
● Good for Covid-19.
● Flat on their abdomen/chest with their head to one side.
○ A pillow may be placed under the leg. This promotes relaxation by permitting some knee flexion and dorsiflexion of the
ankles.
● This position promotes drainage from the mouth after oral or throat surgery but inhibits chest expansion.
● Used for short-term use only.
● Following a lower extremity amputation, helps prevent hip flexion contractures.
Semi-Fowler’s
● Supine, HOB 15, 30, or 45 degrees.
● Clients who have difficulty swallowing: prevents aspiration or regurgitation of enteral feedings.
○ Note: If patients develop diarrhea during enteral feeding, slow the rate of feeding.
● Clients with dyspnea or are receiving mechanical ventilation: promotes lung expansion.
Fowler’s
● Supine, HOB 45 to 60 degrees.
● Nasogastric tube insertion and suctioning: allows for ample chest expansion and ventilation.
● Improves dependent drainage after abdominal surgeries.
High-Fowler’s
● Supine, HOB 60 to 90 degrees.
● Promotes lung expansion by lowering the diaphragm which relieves severe dyspnea.
● Good to prevent aspiration during meals.
Supine or dorsal recumbent
● Lies on their back with head and shoulders elevated on a pillow. Forearms on pillows or at their sides. A foot support prevents
foot drop from occurring.
○ Vertebrae must be in straight alignment without excessive flexion/extension of the head/neck.
● Dorsal recumbent: For examination of the abdomen, breast, and anterior chest.
Lateral or side-lying
● Lies on their side with most of the weight on the dependent hip/shoulder and the arms in flexion in front of the body. Place a
pillow under the head/neck, upper arms, legs, and thighs to maintain alignment.
○ Used for patients who have sensory or motor deficits on one side of the body.
● This is a good sleeping position, but the client needs to turn regularly to prevent the development of pressure ulcers in the
pressurized areas.
○ A 30-degree lateral position is a priority for clients at risk for pressure ulcers.
Sims’ or semi-prone

slides.title: ● Lies on their side halfway between lateral and prone positions, with the weight on their humerus and clavicle. The upp
text: ● Lies on their side halfway between lateral and prone positions, with the weight on their humerus and clavicle. The upper arm is
in front of them and their lower arm is behind them. Both legs are in flexion. The upper leg is flexed at a greater angle than the
lower leg at the hip as well as at the knee.
○ It differs from the side-lying position in the distribution of the client’s weight.
● Promotes oral drainage and is a comfortable sleeping position.
● Good for pregnant women because of the comfort it provides when lying down.
● Position of choice for an enema insertion.
Orthopneic
● Sits upright in the bed/at the bedside with a pillow on the side table. The client rests their arms on the table.
● Beneficial for COPD clients and allows for chest expansion.
Trendelenburg
● HOB lower than the foot of the bed. The entire bed is tilted.
● Facilitates venous return and postural drainage.
● Modified Trendelenburg
○ Legs above the level of their heart while the client remains flat.
○ Helps facilitate venous return and prevents/treats hypovolemia.
Reverse Trendelenburg
● FOB lower than HOB. The entire bed is tilted.
● Prevents esophageal reflux and promotes gastric emptying.
Knee to chest position
- Recommended for rectal examinations and patients with heart conditions that cause cyanosis.
Thoracentesis
- Patient is in a sitting position bending over the bedside table.
- Ensure that the patient has voided before the procedure.
Paracentesis
- Patient is in an upright position with the feet supported.
- Watch 4 complications such as hypotension and hypovolemic shock.

slides.title: - In hypovolemic shock, REPLACE VOLUME FIRST.
text: - In hypovolemic shock, REPLACE VOLUME FIRST.
- Ensure that the patient has voided before the procedure.
Liver biopsy
- Patient is on their left side.
- After the procedure, place the patient on the right side to put pressure on the insertion site and to prevent hemorrhage.
Lumbar puncture
- Obtains CSF for examination, relieving pressure, or to introduce medication.
- Patient is in a lateral knee to chest position or a fetal position.
Pre-operative
- Once a nurse administers preoperative medications, ALWAYS raise the side bed rails for patient safety.
Colonoscopy
- Patient is sedated and positioned on their left side.
STIs
Chlamydia
- May lead to PID (Pelvic Inflammatory Disease).
- Incubation Period: Typically 5-10+ days before symptoms manifest.
Symptoms: Vaginal discharge, burning, bleeding, or pain.
Treatment: Oral antibiotics usually azithromycin and doxycycline.
- Note: Penicillin is not suitable for treating chlamydia.
Syphilis
- Transmitted through contact with syphilitic lesions on skin or mucous membranes.
- First sign: open chancre sores on genitalia.
- Screening Procedures: Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL): An older, still-performed syphilis test or Rapid Plasma
Reagin (RPR): A newer syphilis test, replacing VDRL in many places.
Treatment: Procaine Penicillin G: Given via IM or IV; effective narrow-spectrum medication.
Gonorrhea
- Males: Painful urination, pelvic pain, fever, epididymitis.
- Females: Often asymptomatic, but possible vaginal discharge, urinary frequency and pain.
Complications: Can lead to PID, which may cause sterility.
- Special Considerations: Infection risk to newborn's eyes during delivery. Prophylactic antibiotics or 1% silver nitrate for
newborns. Treat all sexual partners to prevent reinfection.
Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)
- Painful/draining vesicles.
- Virus affects the fetus. A C-section is required.
- Special considerations: Maintain appropriate precautions during vaginal exams and maintain isolation precautions during
hospitalization.
Maternity
The ATI Comprehensive Predictor is notoriously high in maternity-related
questions.
Folic acid
- An expecting mother should take folic acid at least two
months before conception and throughout early
pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects.

slides.title: Anemia
text: Anemia
- Iron deficiency anemia is the most common during pregnancy.
- Vitamin C increases the absorption of iron.
- Constipation and teeth discoloration: side effect of iron supplements (discoloration occurs in liquid form). To avert
gastrointestinal manifestations, take with food. Encourage veggies, fresh fruits, and a high-fiber diet.
Ovulation
- Approximately 14 days after the start of the menstrual period.
- The fertilized ovum will stay in the fallopian tube for 4 days before implants in the uterine wall.
- There are seven days between conception and implantation.
Point of viability
- Infants' ability to survive outside the uterus.
- No specific gestational week, but 22 to 25 weeks: threshold of viability.
Weight gain during pregnancy
- 3-4 lb during the first trimester. 1lb per week for a total of 25 to 35 lb.
- Fetal weight increases the most during the third trimester.
Supine hypotensive syndrome
- Occurs when a pregnant mother lies on her back.
- Lie the patient on their left side to promote fetal perfusion.
Monitoring fetal development
- The heartbeat can be heard by Doppler late in the first trimester.
- Listen at the midline, right above the symphysis pubis, by holding the Doppler firmly on the abdomen.
- Measure fundal height starting in the second trimester.
- From weeks 18 to 30, the fundal height in centimeters is approximately the same as the number of weeks gestation.
- Fetal health assessment: Begin assessing for fetal movement between 16 and 20 weeks of gestation.
Vaccines during pregnancy
Rubella vaccine is contraindicated because rubella infection can develop.
- Received postpartum due to the effects on the fetus while pregnant.
Influenza vaccine is encouraged during pregnancy.

slides.title: Signs of Pregnancy
text: Signs of Pregnancy
1. Presumptive signs: Always considered subjective, the patient will tell you.
- Menses more than 10 days late (amenorrhea), morning nausea, skin pigmentation changes, fatigue, urinary frequency, breast
changes, uterine enlargement.
- Quickening (The first time fetal movement is felt by the mother. Around 16 to 20 weeks for a multipara and about 18 weeks
for a primipara).
2. Probable signs: Indicate suspected pregnancy and mainly involve physical uterine changes.
- Can be caused by non-pregnancy factors such as pelvic congestion or tumors.
- Abdominal enlargement, HCG in urine, Goodell's sign, fetal outline felt by examiner, Braxton Hicks.
Hegar's sign: When the uterus becomes globular in shape, softens, and flexes over the cervix, considered a probable sign of
pregnancy.
Goodell's sign: Cervical softening due to increased vascularity, congestion, and edema, considered a probable sign of
pregnancy.
Chadwick's sign: Bluish discoloration of the cervix, considered a probable sign of pregnancy.
- Ballottement
- Techniques that involve the palpating of the uterus in such a way that the rebound of the floating fetus is felt by the
examining finger.
3. Positive signs: Visualization of the fetus on ultrasound, fetal heart sounds, fetal movement palpated by a professional.
Pregnancy Complications
Pre-existing diseases
- Hypertension and diabetes place the mother and an increased risk of developing complications during pregnancy.
- Women who have had more than four pregnancies are also at risk for higher complications.
Gestational diabetes
- Abnormal glucose tolerance due to decreased effectiveness of insulin during the second and third trimesters.
- High BMI is a risk factor.
- If left untreated, it can lead to polyhydramnios (excessive amniotic fluid) or macrosomia(large fetus), as well as preeclampsia,
neonatal hypoglycemia, and respiratory distress.
Gestational hypertension
- Development of hypertension in a normotensive client without proteinuria.
- Blood pressure returns to normal by postpartum day 10.
- Methylergonovine is contraindicated in patients with hypertension.
- Experiencing postpartum hemorrhage: Methylergonovine is prescribed.
Preeclampsia
- Pregnancy-induced hypertension that includes proteinuria and edema of the face, hands, and ankles.
Serious symptoms include blurred vision.
- Mild: 30 mmHg rise in baseline systolic blood pressure or 15 mmHg rise in baseline diastolic blood pressure.
- Can progress to eclampsia when seizures occur.
- Risks: African American and young primiparous.
- Treatment: Magnesium sulfate, given to lower blood pressure and works as an anticonvulsant.
Remember: Magnesium Mellows the Muscle
Placenta previa
- The placenta completely or partially covers the cervical opening, or the placenta can be implanted low in the uterus without
covering any part of the opening.
Symptoms: Painless, bright red bleeding that occurs late in pregnancy.
Abruptio placentae
- Bleeding that is accompanied by abdominal and lower back pain.

slides.title: - Blood will be dark in color. Mothers are more likely to have an infection or hemorrhage.
text: - Blood will be dark in color. Mothers are more likely to have an infection or hemorrhage.
Incompetent cervix
- Cervix dilates prematurely because it is unable to support the weight of the growing fetus.
- If left untreated, an incompetent cervix may result in spontaneous abortion.
- Vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping or back pain will be seen.
- NEVER perform a vaginal exam in the presence of unexplained vaginal bleeding. Patients with vaginal
bleeding should always have IV access.
- Treatment: Placement of a purse string suture (cerclage) in the cervix to close it.
Breech position
- Major complication of a breech fetus includes a prolapsed umbilical cord.
- The nurse applies manual pressure to the presenting part and the mother will
be placed in a knee to chest position.
Vertex presentation: Check fetal heart tones below umbilicus, right or left lower quadrant.
Breech presentation: Check fetal heart tones above umbilicus, right or left upper quadrant.
Hyperemesis gravidarum
- Excessive and persistent vomiting during pregnancy that results in dehydration and electrolyte
imbalances.
Additional pregnancy complications
● Bleeding from the vagina at any time or uncontrollable leakage of fluid.
● Unusual abdominal cramps or pain.
● Persistent nausea or vomiting especially in the second and third trimester.
● Persistent headache or blurred vision.
● Swelling of the ankles, hands, and face.
● Painful or burning urination with chills or fever.
Unstable clients should be placed closest to the nurse’s station.
Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
Early
decelerations
Fetal head is pressed against the mother’s pelvis and returns to baseline by the end of the contraction.
○ NOT associated with fetal compromise and require NO intervention.
○ Causes: Compression of the fetal head resulting from uterine contraction, fundal pressure, or a vaginal
exam.
Late
decelerations
Non-reassuring patterns that imply uteroplacental insufficiency or poor placental exchange.
○ Similar to early decelerations, but begin after the contraction begins and return to baseline after the
contraction ends.
Interventions for late decelerations: Immediately improving placental blood flow and fetal oxygenation.
1. Place in a side-lying position.
2. If infusing, D/C oxytocin.
3. Apply a nonrebreather mask, give oxygen 8 to 10 L/min.
4. Elevate the client’s legs.
5. Notify the client’s provider.
Reposition the mother and then notify provider. ALWAYS patient before notifying.
Variable
decelerations
Caused by conditions that restrict flow through the umbilical cord.
○ These do NOT have the uniform appearance of early and late decelerations.

slides.title: ○ These fall and rise abruptly with the onset and relief of cord compression.
text: ○ These fall and rise abruptly with the onset and relief of cord compression.
○ These are also non-periodic, occurring at times unrelated to contractions.
Interventions for variable decelerations:
1. Change position (side to side or knee-chest).
2. D/C oxytocin infusion, if infusing.
3. Provide 8-10 L/min oxygen via a nonrebreather mask.
4. Help with amnioinfusion, if ordered.
To decrease compression on the umbilical cord: intrauterine instillation of warm saline.
PATTERN CAUSE
Variable decelerations Cord compression
Early decelerations Head compression
Accelerations Okay
Late decelerations Placental insufficiency
Magnesium sulfate
- A tocolytic that relaxes smooth muscles which suppresses contractions by inhibiting uterine activity.
- Remember: Magnesium Mellows the Muscle
- Women must also be given oxytocin in order to strengthen uterine contractions.
- Excessive magnesium → causes loss of deep tendon reflexes → followed by respiratory depression.
Patient teaching: There can be initial feelings of flushing, heat, sedation, diaphoresis, and burning at the IV site with
the magnesium sulfate bolus.
- Contraindicated: Dilation of the cervix greater than 6 cm, acute fetal distress, active vaginal bleeding,
chorioamnionitis, or greater than 34 weeks of gestation. Do not use concurrently with nifedipine. Do not give to
clients who have myasthenia gravis.
- D/C tocolytic treatment if the client shows signs of pulmonary edema: Chest pain, breathlessness, respiratory
distress, audible wheezing, crackling sounds in the lungs, or a cough with blood-tinged sputum.
Treatment for toxicity
- Calcium gluconate (this is the priority when magnesium sulfate toxicity occurs AFTER discontinuing mag
sulfate)
- Symptoms of toxicity: No patellar deep tendon reflexes, urine output <30 mL/hr, breathing <12/min, reduced
consciousness, heart rhythm abnormalities.
Labor and Delivery
Hyperemesis gravidarum
- Excessive nausea and vomiting extending beyond 16 weeks of gestation.
- Can cause weight loss, dehydration, nutrient deficiencies, electrolyte imbalances..
- Manifests as increased pulse rate, lowered blood pressure, poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, and ketonuria.
- Puts fetus at risk for intrauterine growth restriction, small for gestational age, or preterm birth if it persists.
Treatment:
- Hydration: Administer IV Lactated Ringer’s.
- Administer pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as tolerated.
- Initial treatment: Start with pyridoxine alone or combined with doxylamine due to their safety/effectiveness.
- Caution when using antiemetic drugs (ondansetron, metoclopramide) for severe nausea and vomiting.
- Administer corticosteroids to manage refractory hyperemesis gravidarum.

slides.title: Designated station
text: Designated station
- Location of the presenting part in relation to the level of the ischial spines.
- Indicates the degree of advancement of the presenting part through the pelvis.
- Expressed in centimeters above and below the level of the ischial spine (zero).
Progressive, true labor
● Dilation of the cervix, will have uterine contractions.
● Contractions move from the back to the front of the
abdomen. Not relieved by walking.
False labor
● Contractions decrease with activity.
● Intermittent, felt typically in the abdomen, and are irregular.
Effacement
- Progressive thinning and shortening of
the cervix.
- Progression is referred to by the
percentage indicating effacement at
Dilation
- Opening of the cervical os during labor.
- 1-10 centimeters. 10 is “complete
dilation.”
Cervical Ripening
- Cervical ripening can lower the dosage
of or eliminate the need for oxytocin to
induce labor, and promote a more
successful and shorter induction.
- Utilize low-dose oxytocin infusion for cervical priming.
- Administer misoprostol to facilitate cervical softening and thinning.
- Monitor fetal heart rate (FHR) and uterine activity following cervical-ripening agent administration.
Oxytocin (Pitocin)
- Produces uterine contractions, which can cause fetal anoxia.
- Watch fetal heart rate closely.
- Discontinue if fetal tachycardia arises (above 160 bpm).
Induction of labor
- Initiates uterine contractions for birth stimulation prior to natural onset, using chemical or mechanical methods.
- Administer IV oxytocin for induction.
- Monitor maternal vital signs (blood pressure, pulse, respirations) every 30 to 60 minutes and after dose adjustments during
oxytocin administration.
- Increase oxytocin until the desired contraction pattern is obtained and then maintain the dose if there is:
- Cervical dilation rate: 1 cm/hr
- Contraction duration: 80 to 90 sec
- Time from the uterus contracting until it relaxes.
- Contractions every 2 to 3 min
- Frequency: Timed from the beginning of one contraction to the beginning of the next contraction.
- Contraction strength: 40 to 90 mmHg (IUPC) or strong when palpated.
- Uterine tone at rest: 10 to 15 mmHg (IUPC).
- Reassuring FHR range: 110 to 160/min.
- D/C Oxytocin if uterine tachysystole occurs with contraction duration <80 seconds.
Relaxation period
- The end of one contraction to the beginning of the next.
Normal labor

slides.title: - Will consist of regular contractions, cervical dilation, effacement, descent, and then the delivery of the fetus divid
text: - Will consist of regular contractions, cervical dilation, effacement, descent, and then the delivery of the fetus divided into four
stages.
- Regular contractions will increase in frequency and duration radiating from the lower back to the lower abdomen.
- During labor, if bleeding is present, refrain from any vaginal exams.
- Could be a sign of placenta previa or abruptio placentae.
- Contractions lasting 80 seconds are a CAUSE FOR CONCERN.
Stages of labor
st
stage 2
nd
stage 3
rd
stage 4
