stage
From onset of regular uterine
contractions to full
effacement/ dilation of cervix.
This is longer than the 2nd
and 3rd stages combined.
Nursing Consideration:
Perform Leopold maneuvers.
Perform a vaginal examination
as indicated (if no evidence of
progress) to allow the
examiner to assess whether the
client is in true labor and
whether membranes have
ruptured.
Once membranes have
ruptured, always apply a
fetal heart rate monitor!
From fully dilated to the birth
of the baby.
Begins with complete
dilation/effacement.
Lasts from the birth of the
fetus until the placenta is
delivered.
Nursing Consideration:
Give 1 and 5 min Apgar scores
to the neonate.
Administer oxytocics as
prescribed to stimulate the
uterus to contract and to
prevent hemorrhage.
Begins with the delivery of the
placenta and includes at least
the first 2 hr after birth.
Nursing Consideration:
Assess maternal BP and pulse
every 15 min for the first 2 hr.
Take the mother’s temperature
at the beginning of the
recovery period, then assess
every 4 hr.
Assess fundus/lochia every 15
min for the 1st hour and then
follow hospital protocol.
Massage the uterine fundus
and/or administer oxytocics to
ensure uterine tone and to
prevent maternal hemorrhage.
To prevent bladder
distension, encourage
voiding.
Never place a pregnant client flat on her back because of supine hypotension/vena cava syndrome.
Nitrazine test
- Determines whether or not the membranes have ruptured. Will show the presence of amniotic fluid.
Amniotic fluid is alkaline: Nitrazine paper is deep blue, indicating pH of 6.5 to 7.5.
Urine is slightly acidic: Nitrazine paper remains yellow.
Rupture of membranes
- Immediate action of the nurse is to check fetal heart rate patterns.
Nursing considerations: Watch for infection and bleeding. Watch for prolapse of the umbilical cord if the head has not
engaged.
Betamethasone (Glucocorticoid)
- IM administration in two doses, 24 hr apart.
- Requires 24 hr for effectiveness.
- Enhances fetal lung maturity and surfactant production.

slides.title: - Used for fetuses between 24-34 weeks gestation.
text: - Used for fetuses between 24-34 weeks gestation.
Nursing considerations:
- Give 12 mg IM betamethasone in two doses 24 hr apart. Ideally, administer at least 24 hr (but not more than 7 days)
before delivery via deep IM injection in ventrogluteal or vastus lateralis muscle.
- Watch for maternal hyperglycemia.
- Check preterm infant's lung sounds.
Patient teaching: Report findings of pulmonary edema (chest pain, shortness of breath, and crackles).
Feelings during pregnancy
- Feelings of ambivalence, always ask how they’re feeling and have the client describe their emotions.
Preterm labor
- Risk factors include multiple gestations, abortions, younger than 15 years of age, older than 35 years of age, poor nutrition,
alcohol and drug use, and smoking.
- Terbutaline: inhibits uterine contractions and activity and relaxes smooth muscles.
- Always encourage hydration in preterm labor!
- Dehydration prompts the pituitary gland to release antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin.
- Preventing dehydration stops oxytocin release, which stimulates uterine contractions.
Precipitous delivery
- Where there is no physician, the nurse will apply gentle pressure to the perineum and deliver the head between contractions.
Amniotic fluid
- Amniotic fluid should be watery, clear, and have a slightly yellow tinge.
- Odor should not be foul.
- If meconium stained, this is associated with fetal compromise.
- Risk of infection.
Non-pharmacological pain management
- Hypnosis promotes increased control of pain perception during contractions.
Pregnant patients with tachycardia, think of hemorrhage first.
Postpartum Assessment
The fundus should be palpated in the midline of the abdomen.
- If full bladder, the fundus will be deviated to the left or right.
- A boggy fundus signals uterine atony.
- Massage the fundus until it becomes firm and clots are expressed.
- Give Oxytocin to promote contractions and reduce blood loss.
- On the day of delivery, the fundus should be at the level of the umbilicus, and eventually fall below the umbilicus by one
finger breadth per day.
If above the umbilicus, document as +1
If below the umbilicus, document as -1
Voiding postpartum
- Evaluate ability to void (painful voiding due to edema in first 24-48 hr) and help void within 6-8 hr post-delivery; consider
catheterization if needed.
- Monitor urine output pattern; diuresis (over 3,000 mL/day) normal in first 2-3 days.
- Check for signs of bladder distention: Fundal height, displacement to the side, bulging, excessive lochia.
- Assess tenderness in the bladder area.
- Frequent voiding of <150 mL suggests urinary retention.
- Prompt patient to void if bladder displacement is suspected; prevent atony.
Maternal bradycardia

slides.title: - Common for the first 6 to 10 days postpartum.
text: - Common for the first 6 to 10 days postpartum.
Elevated temperature
- Normal, related to the excretion and dehydration from labor.
- Not a concern until it exceeds 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit for 2 days.
Postpartum hemorrhage
- Classified as: >500 mL blood loss after vaginal birth, >1,000 mL after Cesarean.
- Complications: Hypovolemic shock and anemia.
- Can be caused by uterine atony, prolonged labor or oxytocin-induced labor, subinvolution of the uterus, or retained placental
fragments.
- Assessment: Blood clots larger than a quarter, or perineal pad saturation in 15 minutes or less. Formation of hematomas.
Boggy uterus (uterine atony). Persistent lochia rubra beyond day 3 (retained placental fragments). Change in LOC.
Symptoms of shock.
Involution (Firm)
- Fundus near umbilicus after delivery and descends approximately 1 cm/day.
- Breastfeeding enhances.
- Full bladder impedes involution.
Subinvolution
- Failure of the uterus to revert to pre-pregnancy state through gradual reduction in size and placement.
- Massage, void frequently, and administer Oxytocin.
Naloxone
- Given to counteract respiratory depression in the newborn.
Prolactin
- Stimulates the secretion of milk from the mammary glands.
Umbilical cord
- Contains two arteries and one vein.
Lochia
- Note color, amount (scant to moderate), presence of clots, and odor (fleshy).
- Color:
Rubra: Lasts 1-3 days.
- Bright red. May contain small clots. Transient flow increases during breastfeeding and upon rising.
Serosa: Lasts from day 4-10.
- Brownish red or pink.
Alba: Lasts from day 11 up to and beyond 5 weeks postpartum.
- Yellowish, white creamy color.
Rhogam
- Given to unsensitized Rh-negative mothers after delivery of an Rh-positive infant to prevent the development of sensitization.
- Also recommended at 26 to 28 weeks gestation. Given to suppress the mother's antibody formation.
- Is ineffective against Rh-positive antibodies that are already in maternal circulation.
- Rh-negative clients with Rh-positive newborns require Rh immune globulin IM within 72 hr.
Direct Coombs test
- Demonstrates if the patient’s RBCs have been attacked by antibodies against them, usually seen with Rh-negative mothers.
- Done on the umbilical cord to indicate Rh incompatibility.
Indirect Coombs test
- Detect circulatory antibodies against RBCs
- During the prenatal period to show previous exposure to Rh-positive antigens.
- Indirect Coombs’ test identifies clients sensitized to Rh-positive blood. For clients who are Rh-negative and not sensitized, the
indirect Coombs’ test is repeated between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation.
Rubella

slides.title: - The fetus of a pregnant woman that requires rubella may develop congenital rubella syndrome that includes blindness,
text: - The fetus of a pregnant woman that requires rubella may develop congenital rubella syndrome that includes blindness,
deafness, heart defects, mental retardation, cleft lip and palate.
Vitamin K
- Increases prothrombin time in newborns.
HIV and AIDs
- There's a risk of sending HIV to the newborn, even with aggressive treatment to the mother.
Patient discharge teaching
- Prior to discharge, the nurse should include infant cord and male circumcision care to the mother and family.
- Circumcision: Apply petroleum jelly with diaper changes. Assess for urinary retention.
- Prevent cord infection by keeping it dry and diaper folded underneath. Cord infection (a complication of inadequate
cord care) can result if the cord is not kept dry and clean.
- Watch for moist, red, foul-smelling, or draining cord. Notify provider if signs of infection appear.
- Sponge baths until the cord falls off (around 10-14 days). Baths and submersion can follow.
Postpartum urination
- Frequent voiding of <150 mL of urine is a sign of urinary retention.
- Hand hygiene before/after voiding.
- Cleanse perineal area with warm water or antiseptic after voiding with a hand-squeeze bottle provided by the hospital.
- Replace perineal pad by removing the front part first, peeling it towards the back. Always remove clean to dirty.
Newborn Assessment
⫸ Maintaining a patent airway is the primary objective in the care of a newborn ⫷
● First, the pharynx is cleared with a bulb syringe, followed by the nasal passages.
● First indication of respiratory distress is nasal flaring.
● Normal respirations for a newborn are 30-60 breaths per minute.
>70 is cause for CONCERN.
● Sunken eyes and sunken fontanel suggests dehydration.
Fetal bradycardia
- FHR <110/min for 10 minutes or more.
- Causes: maternal hypotension, hypoglycemia, or hypothermia.
Lack of eye muscle control is present (normal!) in all newborns, strabismus will be present.
- Macula: The region of sharpest vision, is absent at birth. Develops by 4 months and matures by 8 months.
Axillary thermometer: Used to monitor temperature. Avoid rectal temperatures due to the chance of injury to the delicate rectal
mucosa. An initial rectal temperature may be obtained to determine abnormalities.
APGAR score
- Lowest when the mother has had general anesthesia.
- Used to determine major body systems responses to birth.
- Heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and color at 1 minute, and again at 5 minutes after birth.
- The higher the score, the better the condition is, with a maximum total of 10.
- While it is not an emergent finding, check gluteal and popliteal folds of the hips to identify hip dysplasia.
- Remember to auscultate a newborn’s apical pulse for 60 seconds.
APGAR: Scoring given to newborn to determine extrauterine life adaptability
Minimal/no difficulty:
Moderate difficulty:
Severe distress:
Fontanels

slides.title: - Bulging can indicate increased intracranial pressure.
text: - Bulging can indicate increased intracranial pressure.
Anterior closes by 12-18 months
Posterior closes by 2 months
Lanugo
- Fine hair on the skin that tends to disappear during the first week.
Cold stress
- Jitteriness of the hands.
Mongolian spots
- Bluish discoloration of the skin, common in African American babies.
- Can look like abuse (bruising).
Vernix caseosa
- Substance that covers the skin of the newborn, and protects the baby from infection.
Strabismus
- Normal within the first month of life, newborns do not have binocularity and cannot focus.
Head circumference
- Should be equal to or larger than the chest.
- The nurse will measure above the eyebrows to the occipital prominence.
- Average is 13 to 14 in.
Caput succedaneum
- Soft swollen area on the newborn’s scalp that extends over suture lines (normal!).
Hydration
- Indicated in 6-8 wet diapers a day.
- No tears = dehydration
- Breastfed baby:
- 6 to 10 small, loose, golden yellow stools per day.
- Formula-fed baby:
- Dark green, pastry stools.
Meconium stool
- Expected within 24 to 48 hours.
- Infant cannot be discharged until meconium stool is observed and recorded.
- Traditional stools usually appear by the third day.
Weight loss
- 5% loss is normal in healthy newborns.
- Brown fat is located in superficial areas, considered a unique source of heat for the newborn.
Newborn genetic screening
- Capillary heel stick at 24 hours after birth.
- Accurate if newborn fed formula/breast milk for 24 hr. If discharged before 24 hr, retest in 1 to 2 weeks.
Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)
- Baby must be lying supine in their bed, with no pillow or blanket.
- Pillows, blankets, etc. are all at risk for suffocation.
Hypoglycemia
Symptoms: Jitteriness or lethargy.
- In the hospital setting, blood glucose will be taken with a heel stick.
ECMO (Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation)
- Used in meconium aspiration syndrome to oxygenate the blood while the lungs heal.
Cocaine-addicted newborn
- Constant crying, jitteriness, poor feeding, emesis, respiratory distress, and seizures.
Neonatal abstinence syndrome
- Constant high-pitched cry suggests CNS issues in neonatal abstinence syndrome.

slides.title: Symptoms: Hypertonicity, convulsions, increased muscle tone.
text: Symptoms: Hypertonicity, convulsions, increased muscle tone.
- Reduce environmental stimuli (decrease lights, lower noise level).
Phototherapy
- Newborns should have their eyes protected, and only wear a diaper.
- Turn the newborn every hour.
Vitamin K
- Aquamephyton: Given to newborns to promote blood clotting and prevent hemorrhage.
Ophthalmia neonatorum
- Acute conjunctivitis in the newborn is often caused by gonorrhea and chlamydia.
- 0.5% erythromycin solution is placed in the newborn's eyes to prevent the contraction of the disease.
Phenylketonuria (PKU)
- The newborn should be tested within 48 to 72 hours after birth.
- The newborn should be drinking breast milk or formula for 2 to 3 days before the test.
- If positive, they will avoid aspartame, because it is converted to phenylalanine in the body.
- A synthetic food providing enough protein for growth and tissue repair must be substituted for phenylalanine.
Down’s Syndrome
- Decrease muscle tension and strength (hypotonia).
- Hallmark sign at birth.
- Newborns will also have a deep, straight line across the palm called a SIMIAN crease.
- The newborn will also have slanting eyes and low-set ears.
Do NOT give anything by mouth to an infant with a respiratory rate >60 breaths/minute or to children with severe
respiratory distress.
Diagnostic Tests
Doppler
- Auscultation of fetal heart rate is usually done at 10 to 12 weeks of gestation.
- Can also help to rule out fetal abnormalities.
Pelvic sonogram
Nursing considerations: Ensure that the patient has a full bladder.
Fetoscope
- Used to auscultate fetal heart rate at 18 to 20 weeks of gestation.
- Heart rate is best heard at the center of the pubic hairline.
- Normal fetal heart rate during this time is between 120 and 160 beats per minute.
Ultrasound
- Will confirm gestational sac by week 6 and can provide imaging of fetal heart motion by week 7.
- The patient should drink 1-2 L of water prior to the procedure and avoid urinating until the procedure has been completed.
Daily fetal movement count
- Assesses feel activity and reported by the pregnant mother.
- Normal: Three movements per hour.
Amniocentesis
- Used to detect the presence of biochemical or chromosomal abnormalities such as fetal lung maturity and genetic studies.
- Usually performed between 14 and 16 weeks of gestation.
- Ensure that the client has voided before the procedure.
- Monitor for contractions after amniocentesis (complication).
Nonstress test
- Evaluate the response of the fetal heart rate to fetal movement.
- The monitor records fetal heart rate when the mother senses fetal movement, used to assess fetal oxygen.
- In a healthy fetus, the fetal heart rate will accelerate with each movement.

slides.title: Patient teaching:
text: Patient teaching:
- Before procedure: Eat, empty bladder, and sit in a reclining chair, or in a semi-Fowler’s or left-lateral position.
- May drink orange juice or rock her abdomen to stimulate fetal movement.
- Will have a Doppler wrapped around her abdomen during the test.
- Disadvantages: High rate of false nonreactive results with the fetal movement response due to fetal immaturity, sleep
cycles of the fetus, nicotine use disorder, or maternal prescriptions.
Contraction stress test and oxytocin challenge test
- Used to induce uterine contractions to correlate fetal movement to the contractions.
Alpha-fetoprotein levels
- Screens for neural tube defects.
- Abnormal findings lead to ultrasound, quad marker screening, genetic counseling, and amniocentesis referrals.
- Elevated indicates neural tube defects such as spina bifida and hydrocephalus.
- Decreased indicates Down’s syndrome.
- Completed at 16 to 18 weeks.
Nursing Considerations
Breast engorgement
- Breastfeeding
- To relieve breast engorgement, take a warm shower or apply warm compresses before breastfeeding to promote
letdown and milk flow.
- Empty each breast completely at feedings, and pump if needed. Breastfeed every 2-3 hours.
- Apply cool compresses after feedings.
- Engorgement may cause a slight rise in temperature.
- If the mother develops mastitis, the baby can still nurse on both breasts.
- Formula
- Use cold compresses for 15 minutes every hour on days 3-5 postpartum.
- Place fresh cabbage leaves in the bra for relief.
- Do NOT hand express.
- Mild analgesics can be given for discomfort.
- Avoid nipple stimulation.
Newborn care
- Avoid feeding the newborn with every cry. Overfeeding can result in abdominal discomfort and diarrhea.
- Use an approved rear-facing car seat placed in the back seat, ideally in the center.
- Keep infants rear-facing until age 2 or they reach the seat's height and weight limit.
Nutrition
Overview
1 gram of protein = 4 calories
The order of fuel use
1. Carbohydrates 2. Fat 3. Proteins
Diets
Clear liquid Gelatin, broth, apple juice, cranberry juice, tea

slides.title: Low-residue
text: Low-residue
(Low fiber)
Ordered to reduce fiber for patients with Crohn's disease, bowel rest, post-op colon surgery/bowel
surgery, esophagitis, and diarrhea.
Clear liquids, fat, eggs, white potatoes, custard
AVOID DAIRY.
High-residue
(High fiber)
Ordered to provide bulk in the stool and bring water into the colon for patients with constipation
for diverticulitis.
Those who are bedridden or inactive need small meals with high fiber to prevent constipation (older
adults).
Raw fruits and vegetables and whole grains (barley and oats), legumes (lentils and black beans), broccoli,
and cabbage.
Low-fat Increase foods high in polyunsaturated fatty acids including skim milk, egg whites,
lean meats, and fat-free soup.
AVOID containing cholesterol and saturated fatty acid.
Low-purine Recommended for patients with gout.
Avoid organ meats, shellfish, anchovies, oily fish, alcohol, sardines, beans, lentils, and anything high in
protein.
Low-oxalate Recommended for patients with kidney stones or gout to reduce the risk of stone formation, and
increase intake of fluids.
Avoid leafy greens, nuts/seeds, beets, and raspberries.
Sodium-restricted Ordered for patients with kidney or cardiovascular disease, or hypertension in order to control the
retention of water and sodium and to lower BP.
Used in patients with ascites, edema-associated advanced liver and renal disease,
congestive heart failure, essential hypertension, and patients receiving adrenocorticoids.
Processed and canned foods are high in sodium.
Fresh fruits and vegetables are low in sodium.
Avoid canned prepared foods, table salt, prepared seasoning, and processed foods.
Gluten-free Ordered for patients with malabsorption syndrome such as Celiac disease.
Bland Excludes foods that are chemically and mechanically stimulating or irritating to the GI tract.

slides.title: Small, frequent meals.
text: Small, frequent meals.
Usually for patients with ulcers and post-op patients.
Avoid fried foods, meat extracts, pepper, and chili powder.
BRAT Banana, Rice, Apple, Toast.
High-iron Must increase consumption of iron during pregnancy because of maternal RBC volume and iron
storage in the fetus.
Spinach, beef, liver, prunes, pork, broccoli, whole bread, and whole cereal.
Nursing Considerations
Cholesterol
- Levels of 200+ associated with increased risk for CAD.
- High Cholesterol: Avoid foods with cheese and eggs.
Vitamin K
- Vitamin K deficiency may affect blood coagulation (increased bleeding time).
- Green leafy vegetables are high in vitamin K and should be avoided in patients on coumadin (warfarin).
- Dark green leafy vegetables (spinach, broccoli, asparagus), carrots, eggs.
Vitamin B12
- Exclusively in animal-derived foods.
- Post-gastrectomy individuals need lifelong monthly vitamin B12 injections due to the absence of the stomach's parietal cells
producing intrinsic factor.
- Vegetarians can rely on fortified breakfast cereal as a source of vitamin B12.
- Treatment of pernicious anemia also requires B12 injections for their entire life.
Vitamin D
- Considered a nutrient of concern in elderly patients.
- Deficiency includes osteomalacia, which is weakening and softening of the bones.
- Eggs, fatty fish, fortified products (ready-to-eat cereals, milk, and OJ).
Calcium
● Green leafy vegetables are a great source of calcium.
● Patients at risk for renal calculi should adhere to a low-calcium diet.
● Pregnant mothers must maintain an adequate calcium intake to prevent losing stores of calcium.
● Cow’s milk is not suitable for infants under 1 year of age because it is high in protein and calcium which can lead to pediatric
dehydration.
Hypocalcemia nursing care:
○ Administer oral/IV calcium supplements.
○ Enhance calcium absorption with vitamin D supplements.
○ Implement fall and seizure precautions.
○ Avoid overstimulation, maintain a quiet room with limited visitors and soft lighting.
○ Keep emergency equipment ready.
○ Encourage calcium-rich foods: Dairy, canned salmon, sardines, oysters, and leafy greens.
○ Life-threatening hypocalcemia needs rapid calcium gluconate or chloride treatment.
○ Use IV infusion with diluted dextrose 5% and water, administered via pump. Administer cautiously to prevent cardiac
arrest from rapid infusion.
Cancer/Chemotherapy

slides.title: - May contribute to the development of malnutrition as a result of the effect on basal metabolism and symptoms such as n
text: - May contribute to the development of malnutrition as a result of the effect on basal metabolism and symptoms such as nausea
and decreased food intake.
- Recommendations include eggs and cottage cheese in place of meat.
Pulmonary disorders
- Encourage rest periods before meals.
Dialysis patients
- Routinely supplemented with calcium, vitamin B6, and folic acid.
- Nephrotic syndrome: Hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia.
- Chronic renal failure: Requires supplementation of water-soluble vitamins.
- Low protein, low potassium diet.
Congestive heart failure
- Offer smaller meals throughout the day due to the frequent fatigue.
- The goal is to minimize cardiac workload and reduce edema.
- Daily weights are the best indicator of fluid balance.
TPN
● D/C gradually to avoid rebound hypoglycemia.
● Can’t eternally feed → Need TPN (bypasses GI tract and goes
straight to blood).
● Administer in central line, do not give meds through the
TPN line.
● Use sterile technique, even a mask, when changing the CVL
dressing.
Nursing priority: Notify the provider of
weight gain greater than 1 kg/day.
● Effectiveness measures:
○ Daily weight: Maintain baseline or gain up
to 1 kg/day.
○ Prealbumin level rise (15-36 mg/dL reference range).
○ BUN within expected range (10-20 mg/dL).
Components of TPN
● Lipids (fats) come in 10%, 20%, and 30% concentrations.
● Formulated from soybean and/or safflower oil, plus egg phospholipids which gives lipids a milky or opaque appearance.
● IV lipids are contraindicated for clients who have severe hepatic disease, severe hyperlipidemia, or an allergy to soybean oil,
eggs, or safflower oil.
Cultural preferences
- Orthodox Judaism excludes pork from the diet.
- Kosher: Dairy and meat cannot be consumed together. If meat is consumed, 3-6 hours must pass before dairy can be
consumed.
Pediatrics
Birth
● Newborn’s weight will decrease by 10% immediately after birth, and then return to birth weight by two weeks of age.
○ Will have no purposeful movements, just primitive reflexes.
○ Will respond by blinking, crying, or quieting.
○ Have a fixed gaze, and cannot follow objects.
○ Will lift their head when placed in a prone position.
○ Hearing is preferential to a female voice.
○ Height gain of 2.3 cm per month.
○ Weight gain of 150 to 210 grams per week.
○ Sleep for only 3 to 4 hours and wake for 1 hour in between each session.

slides.title: ○ 1 month old will demonstrate head lag.
text: ○ 1 month old will demonstrate head lag.
Nursing considerations:
○ Rear-facing car seat.
○ Baby placed in the supine position while sleeping to prevent SIDS.
■ Always alone, on their back in the crib/bassinet.
○ Never allow the newborn to stay alone with another young child.
○ Maintain immunization schedule including Hepatitis B.
● Toys: Bright red colors and toys that make noise.
● Play: Solitary.
2 months old
● Posterior fontanelle closes at this time.
● In the prone position, the newborn can lift their head and neck.
○ However, there will be continued to lag on the raising of the head when pulled to a sitting position.
● Able to follow objects and consciously turn their head 180 degrees.
● They pay attention to voices and smile responsibly.
● Toys
○ Same with one month old.
Nursing considerations:
○ Rear-facing car seat, pacifier.
○ Maintain oral hygiene.
○ Raise side rails and never leave baby alone as they can now roll over.
○ Immunization schedule includes DTP, HBV, IPV, HIB.
■ DTP: Diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis
○ Post-immunization reactions can include fever, cough, or rashes.
○ Infants response to pain:
■ Irritability and reflux withdrawal to painful stimuli, facial grimacing.
4-5 months old
● Increase the weariness and interest and surroundings.
● Can make coos, squeals, and babbles.
● No head lag when pulled to a sitting position.
● Cries for many reasons including hunger, wet diaper, discomfort, and sleep.
● May repeat sounds and smile when spoken to.
● Can lift the chest when in a prone position.
● Can turn from abdomen to back by 4 months (front to back) and back to abdomen (back to front) by 6 months.
Nursing considerations:
○ Prevent aspiration and choking, burp after feeding.
■ NEVER perform a blind finger sweep. The object may be pushed further into the airway.
○ Baby-proof the home and prevent falls.
○ Introduce solid foods one at a time and in the morning.
6 months
● They will double their weight and have teeth eruption of the two lower incisors.
● Can sit without help and lean forward, they can support themselves with their arms.
● Verbalize single consonants and respond to the sounds of toys.
● They can bear weight on their legs with support and begin to exhibit stranger anxiety.

slides.title: ● Will be anxious when away from mother, indicating separation anxiety.
text: ● Will be anxious when away from mother, indicating separation anxiety.
Nursing considerations:
○ Provide finger foods and feed them with spoons and cups.
○ Monitor for teething and fever.
9 months
● Can grasp objects between thumb and forefinger (pincer grasp).
● Can pull themselves to stand and crawl.
● They turn to the sound of their name and play peek-a-boo.
● Will search for an object when it is taken away, understand that even though it can no longer be
seen (this is called object permanence).
Nursing considerations:
○ Safety concerns due to kinetic ability, and courage self-feeding, rear car seat.
● Toys: Colorful items and toys that make noise.
● Death and dying: Still do not understand death at this time.
Toddler from 12-18 months
● Their birth weight will be tripled and their height will be doubled.
● They will have 6-8 teeth.
● Head circumference and chest circumference are equal.
● They can stand alone and follow simple commands.
● They can use a cup and spoon, but they prefer their fingers.
● They can point with their index finger.
● Toys
○ Mobiles, bells, and bright-colored toys.
○ Parallel, playing side-by-side and occasionally treating toys.
■ Can also be called associative play.
○ Play therapy is one of the most effective strategies to treat this age.
Nursing considerations:
○ Talk to them and name objects to them.
○ Praise and discipline when there is a need to.
○ Provide good dental and oral care.
● Hospitalized toddler/infant
○ Will experience separation anxiety.
○ Should be the focus of the plan of care.
○ Is not uncommon to have a temper tantrum in toddlers.
○ Before procedures, give toddlers an explanation in a way they can understand.
● Toddlers' response to pain
○ Localized withdrawal in response to pain.
18 months
● Anterior fontanelle closes.
● They can walk backward and use a spoon and cup without assistance.
● They can kick and throw balls.
● They can have temper tantrums and have a vocabulary of about 15 to 20 words.
● At this age, they will attach to a security item and begin some sucking.
● Play

slides.title: ○ Parallel play is more obvious.
text: ○ Parallel play is more obvious.
■ Parallel play is when the toddler plays independently but is among other children in a group.
Nursing considerations:
○ Provide them with a variety of snacks and encourage dental hygiene.
○ Toilet training
■ Readiness will be shown by the ability to hold urine for more than 2 hours and not have a wet diaper, as well as
the child's willingness to sit on the toilet.
○ Encourage parents to go to CPR classes.
2 years old
● They can walk up and down the stairs with both legs, open doors, turn knobs.
● They can transfer objects from one hand to another.
● Development of all 20 deciduous teeth.
● Can start to learn how to tie shoes, ride a bicycle, and concentrate on activities longer.
● Bowel training will proceed bladder training.
● Voluntary control of the anal and urethral sphincters is achieved sometime after the child starts to walk.
● Hospitalized toddler
○ Ritualism is needed to maintain reliability and provide a sense of comfort.
○ Regressions and intense emotions may happen while in the hospital.
● Toys
○ Interested in the sight, smell, texture, and taste of things.
○ Objects that can be squeezed, dropped, twisted, or thrown.
○ Objects that can be stacked, open, closed, or pushed.
Preschool age
● Children use their imagination to imitate adult activity and participate in physical games.
● The foundation of writing is during this time and they enjoy drawing and painting.
● More energetic and active and spend a lot of time pretending.
● Toys and play
○ Dramatic play, the ability to cooperate with others.
○ A 3-year-old can typically ride a tricycle.
○ A 5-year-old can jump rope.
● Death and dying (ages 3-5)
○ Least anxious about death, death means sleep, the dead person is seen as alive but lacks movement, death is a punishment for
bad behavior.
● Hospitalized preschool-age child
○ Demonstrate a need for parents and fear of mutilation while hospitalized.
○ Explain procedures using simple, clear language. Promote self-independence by allowing the child to manage their own care
and express emotions/feelings.
○ Therapeutic play will establish rapport with this age child.
■ Provide toys that allow emotional expression and ensure consistency
in assigning caregivers, while giving choices when possible.
○ Allow the toddler to handle equipment, if safe.
○ Practice procedure on a toy, if appropriate.
● Preschooler’s response to pain
○ Low frustration level and strike out physically.
○ Wong Baker faces scale should be used.

slides.title: School-age
text: School-age
● Enjoy activities that lead to real products such as jewelry, clothes, and collections.
● Develop an interest in sports and enjoy having adult-like equipment.
● Children enjoy learning to make healthy snacks safely and should grasp the concept of snacking when hungry, rather than when
bored or inactive.
○ Healthy snacks such as air-popped popcorn or fruit.
● There's a better understanding of rules and playing with others.
● Play
○ Cooperative play is notoriously competitive at this age.
● Death and dying (ages 5-10)
○ Death is a cessation of life, often question what happens after death, death is now considered irreversible.
● Hospitalized child (school age and older children)
○ Fear a lack of acceptance, body disability, separation from peers.
○ Concrete experiences are the most meaningful way of learning (factual information).
■ When inserting an IV, tell the child they will feel discomfort during insertion.
○ Allow the child to express feelings.
● School-age response to pain
○ Passive resistance.
Adolescents
● Play is more verbal and have greater cognitive skills.
Fears
Infants: Stranger anxiety, the sudden appearance of unexpected and looming objects, animals, and heights.
Toddlers: Separation anxiety, the dark, loud noises, stranger anxiety.
Preschoolers: Injuries can lead to something much worse (what they think).
School-age: Fear of supernatural beings, injury, storms, staying alone, failure in school, death.
Adolescents: Fear of inept social performance, social isolation, sexuality, drugs, diverse crowds, public speaking, large accidents.
Lice (Pediculosis capitis)
- Remove using a fine-tooth comb through hair.
- Launder clothing and bedding in hot water with detergent; seal non-launderable items in a plastic bag for 14 days.
Symptoms: Intense itching. Small, red bumps on the scalp. Nits (white specks) on the hair shaft.
- Treatment: 1% permethrin shampoo
- Spinosad 0.9% topical suspension for children 4 years and older. Benzyl alcohol 5% in infants 6 months and older.
For difficult cases, use malathion 0.5%.
Pediatric Congenital Defects
Cardiovascular

slides.title: Congenital heart disease
text: Congenital heart disease
- First priority is to reduce the workload of the heart.
- Most common complaint from parents is difficulty feeding.
- Child will be tachycardic, often the first symptom the nurse can assess.
- Decrease the cardiac demands for a newborn by maintaining the temperature to 37ºC.
Patent ductus arteriosus
- Occurs when a structure that shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta that remains open.
Tetralogy of Fallot
- Mixed blood flow defects: Pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy.
- Infant exhibits cyanosis, hypoxia, and systolic murmur in pulmonic area.
- Acute cyanosis and hypoxia episodes (blue or "Tet" spells).
- In case of acute cyanosis and hyperpnea, position infant in knee-to-chest position.
- ALWAYS have a pulse oximeter on this patient.
Coarctation of the aorta
- Aortic lumen narrowing near ductus arteriosus causes ventricular blood flow obstruction.
- Bounding pulses in upper extremities.
- Elevated blood pressure in arms.
- Weak or absent femoral pulses.
- Decreased blood pressure in lower extremities.
- Cool skin of lower extremities.
- Heart failure in infants.
- Dizziness, headaches, fainting, or nosebleeds in older children.
Cystic fibrosis
- Thick mucus, foul-smelling fatty stools, salty, sweaty skin, no passage of meconium stool.
- Sweat chloride test is used to confirm.
- Pancrelipase treats pancreatic insufficiency associated with cystic fibrosis.
- Administer capsules with meals/snacks.
- Children can swallow/sprinkle capsules on food. Do not add to bottles or formula or sprinkle on hot foods.
- Postural drainage is typically given twice a day to CF patients.
- Schedule before meals, at least 1 hr after meals, or at bedtime to reduce vomiting risk. If prescribed, give
bronchodilator before postural drainage.
Hemophilia
- Drugs that contain salicylates are contraindicated for these children.
Kawasaki disease
- Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.
- Characterized by a fever over 104.5 degrees for 5 days or longer, bilateral conjunctivitis, and strawberry tongue.
- Place the child on cardiac monitoring.
Pediatric System Disorders
GI
Cleft palate/lip
- Feed the child with a soft rubber tip syringe placed on the side of the mouth.
- Ebow restraints may be used to restrain the upper extremities.
- Children are predisposed to infection because of communication between the nose and mouth.
- Burp the infant frequently.
Tracheoesophageal fistula
Symptoms: Drooling, coughing, cyanosis, and regurgitation of feedings.
- The esophagus has a connection (fistula) to the trachea that leads to the risk of aspiration.

slides.title: Pyloric stenosis
text: Pyloric stenosis
- Symptoms typically do not appear until two to three weeks of age.
- Forceful projectile vomiting after feeding.
- “Exorcism-type vomiting” or “hitting the back of the wall”
- Place the infant on their right side after feeding and feed slowly to facilitate emptying of the stomach.
Intussusception
- When a portion of the bowel telescopes into a distal portion, usually in males before the age of five.
- The child will kick and draw their legs, cry loudly, and vomiting of bilious or stomach contents.
- Hallmark sign is jelly-like stools.
Passage of normal brown stool indicates intussusception has resolved itself. Report immediately. Diagnostic and therapeutic
procedures may be altered.
Celiac disease
- Intolerance of gluten, patient will have steatorrhea (frothy, pale, bulky, foul-smelling, greasy stools).
Hirschsprung's disease
- Distention of a portion of the lower colon caused by a congenital lack of nerve cells in the wall of the colon below the
distended section.
Symptoms: Abdominal distension, constipation, bile-stained mucus and vomiting.
- There will also be a lack of meconium stool passage.
- Barium enema is a test that can be performed to see what part of the bowel is distorted.
Wilms tumor
- Encapsulated tumor of the kidney.
- Touching or palpating the abdomen may break the capsule and spread the cancer throughout the abdomen.
Musculoskeletal
Talipes equinovarus
- Most common form of clubfoot.
- Denis Browne splint - used for correction of clubfoot.
Scoliosis
- Observe for an uneven rib hump noticeable when a child bends at the waist.
- Screenings starting around ten years of age.
Hip dysplasia
- Uneven gluteal fold.
- Ortolani’s sign/Bartow’s sign is a positive diagnostic test.
Symptoms: Unequal skinfold, limitation of abduction, and unequal knee height.
Dunlop traction
- Used for treating fractures of the humerus.
Trauma
- Frank blood, or clear watery drainage that indicates CSF leakage from the ear suggests a basal skull fracture.
Neurological
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
- Autoimmune inflammatory disease affecting joints and tissues. Not typically life-threatening, may improve over time.
- Can lead to lasting joint deformities and changes in joint function.
Nursing considerations:
- Goal is to minimize damage, control pain,, and preserve joint function.
- Apply heat or warm packs to joints before exercise and encourage warm baths.

slides.title: - Encourage ROM exercises and swimming.
text: - Encourage ROM exercises and swimming.
- Encourage fluid intake and participation in school and contact with friends.
- Practice relaxation techniques (exacerbations worsen with illness).
- Schedule yearly eye exams.
- Treatment: Etanercept, Methotrexate, NSAIDS, and corticosteroids.
Spina bifida
- First priority is to prevent rupture of the external sac.
- Prone position always!
- Spina bifida occulta: Mildest, “hidden” skin that covers the opening.
- Closed neural tube defect: Spinal cord has malformations of fat, bone, and meninges, which can either cause no symptoms or
cause incomplete paralysis.
- Meningocele: Spinal fluid/meninges protrude through vertebral opening, no symptoms OR complete paralysis.
- Meningomyelocele: The most severe spinal cord is exposed through opening in the spine, partial/complete paralysis.
Retinoblastoma
- White-eye reflex nystagmus.
Hydrocephalus
Nursing considerations: Measure the head circumference and palpate the anterior fontanelle.
Infant will have a bulging fontanelle that occurs secondary to increased intracranial pressure.
*A flat fontanelle is normal. A sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration.*
*Crying with no tears suggests dehydration.*
- Support the head when lifting or turning the infant.
Bacterial meningitis
- Antibiotics will be given ASAP.
- Implement seizure precautions.
Kernig's sign and Brudzinski's sign
- Symptoms of meningitis (nuchal rigidity another symptom).
Kernig’s: Present if a lower leg cannot extend due to pain when a client is lying supine with one leg bent over the abdomen.
Brudzinski’s: Present if a client's hips and knees flex when they are lying supine with the head lifted for the chest.
A puerperal/petechial rash in a sick child could indicate meningitis and the child will need immediate care.
Respiratory
Laryngotracheobronchitis
- Respiratory distress and dyspnea. An atmosphere with high humidity will provide relief.
Bronchiolitis
Nursing considerations: Nasopharynx suctioning helps clear secretions. Humidified oxygen adds moisture to the airway.
Croup
Symptoms: Inspiratory stridor is a Hallmark find. Hoarseness, barking cough.
- Treatment
- Corticosteroids (Decadron) and nebulized epinephrine.
RSV
- Begins with cold-like symptoms and becomes more severe. More common in the winter and spring.
- Spread of infection can be prevented by proper hand-washing.
- Provider may prescribe prednisone, dexamethasone, or methylprednisolone to reduce inflammation in acute exacerbations.
- Nurse should monitor for risk of infection with steroids as well as hypervolemia (bounding pulse), hypernatremia,
hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia.

slides.title: - Dantrolene, tizanidine, baclofen, and diazepam may be given as they are antispasmodics for treatment of muscle spastic
text: - Dantrolene, tizanidine, baclofen, and diazepam may be given as they are antispasmodics for treatment of muscle spasticity.
- Nasal suction before feeding.
- Implement isolation precautions and patient-specific equipment.
Bacterial Pneumonia
- Expected signs: High fever, cough (productive/unproductive), rapid breathing, retractions, nasal flaring, chest pain, dullness
with percussion.
- Abnormal breath sounds: Rhonchi, fine crackles.
- Skin color changes: Pale or cyanotic.
- Behavioral changes: Irritability, restlessness, lethargy.
- Gastrointestinal symptoms: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting.
- Radiographic exam to detect lung infiltrates.
- Sputum culture and Gram stain (older children).
- Elevated antistreptolysin titer for streptococcal infection.
Otitis media
- Occurs because of obstruction of the eustachian tube or passage of the nasopharyngeal secretions in the middle ear.
- An infant’s eustachian tube is shorter and wider and is in a horizontal position so they are at higher risk for developing
infection.
Tonsillectomy
- Monitor their child for frequent swallowing post-procedure, which indicates bleeding.
- Milk products may coat the throat and cause the child to clear the throat and irritate the operative site, these should be
avoided.
- Coughing, clearing the throat, and blowing the nose should also all be avoided.
Epiglottitis
- Life-threatening emergency.
- Contraindication for throat cultures because swabbing the throat causes
swelling that will block the airway.
Symptoms: Muffled voice, drooling, dysphagia
Remember, dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. Dysphasia is difficulty
speaking.
- Dysphagia: Aspiration precautions - Avoid thin liquids and sticky food and provide oral care prior to eating (helps to
enhance the taste of food). Oatmeal is a good meal of choice for patients with dysphagia.
- Treatment: Ceftriaxone, Vancomycin
- Vancomycin:
- Caution needed in renal impairment due to unchanged excretion.
- Monitor for ototoxicity.
- Monitor for Red Man Syndrome due to rapid infusion.
- Monitor for rashes, flushing, increased heart rate, and low blood pressure.
Nursing considerations: Administer vancomycin over 60 minutes to prevent infusion reactions. Notify
provider for signs of acute renal injury. Monitor for hearing loss.
Communicable Diseases
Mononucleosis
- Spread by direct contact and droplet.
Symptoms: Splenomegaly, sore throat, malaise.
Pertussis
- Administer Tdap to pregnant clients at 27-36 weeks gestation to protect the fetus from pertussis.
Rubella
Symptoms: Fever, conjunctivitis, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, red rash, and cough.
- Spreads by direct contact and droplet. Incubation for 14-21 days. Can spread 7 days before to 5 days after the rash appears.

Things to remember: Administer first MMR vaccine at 12-15 months. First varicella vaccine given at a minimum age of 12 months.
Influenza: Inactivated influenza vaccine for children 6 months and older. Live vaccination should be avoided in pregnant women,
immunocompromised adults, or children who have diabetes or kidney failure, heart or lung disease, are immunocompromised, have
respiratory conditions, have a severe allergy to chicken eggs, or have a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
- Remember, immunizations are contraindicated during an infectious state and with pre-existing symptoms such as allergic
reaction.
- Hep B vaccine withheld for premature infants <2,000 g if the mother is hepatitis B-negative.
Pediatric Nursing Considerations
Newborn bathing
- Do not immerse the newborn in water for a bath until the cord has fallen off.
Eye drops
- Administering eye drops:
1. Place the child in a sitting position.
2. Ask the child to look upward.
3. Pull the lower eyelid downward.
4. Instill the drops.
5. Apply pressure to the lacrimal punctum.
Ear drops
- Ear has 3 letters → remember 3 y/o
When inserting drops
- Straighten the ear canal back and down for those younger than 3.
- Pull up and back for those older than 3.
Diaper rash
- Apply zinc oxide ointment to the irritated area.
Painful procedures
- Refrain from having the parents restrain the child, as this is seen as then making it better.
- Be honest with a child, also tell the child what behavior is appropriate.

slides.title: - “This is going to be uncomfortable.”
text: - “This is going to be uncomfortable.”
- Always refer to medicine as medicine, not as juice or candy.
- Vastus lateralis is the preferred site for an IM injection.
- Remember, the dorsogluteal has major blood vessels and nerves and is
not recommended.
Physical examination
- Leave the most distressing part to the end (least to most invasive).
- Rectal temperature should be taken last.
- Respirations will be observed by looking at the abdomen for a full minute.
- If the child is unconscious, palpate the brachial artery.
Dehydration
Mild: Dry mucous membranes, cap refill >2 seconds.
Moderate: Cap refill between 2-4 seconds. Hypotension, decreased tears, decreased skin turgor.
Severe: Tented skin, cap refill >4 seconds, hyperpnea, no tears, sunken fontanel.
Lumbar puncture
- Lay the child side-lying with their knee and neck flexed and spine in a “c” shape.
Reye's syndrome
- Associated with the presence of specific diseases and the use of Aspirin in pediatric patients.
Digoxin
- Withheld when an infant's pulse is less than 110 or when a toddler's pulse is less than 90.
- Drink a glass of water after swallowing the medication.
Rheumatic Fever
- Develops 2-6 weeks post untreated/partially treated strep throat.
Symptoms: Muffled heart sounds, tachycardia, cardiomegaly, new or changed heart murmur, pericardial friction rub, and
chest pain (indicates carditis). Pink, nonpruritic macular rash on the trunk/inner surfaces of extremities that appears/disappears
rapidly (indicates erythema marginatum).
- Will have elevated CRP and ESR due to inflammatory response.
Injection Sites in the Pediatric Patient
Intradermal
● Inject on inner forearm.
● TB syringe with 26-30-gauge needle, intradermal bevel.
● Insert at 15° angle.
● Do not aspirate.
Subcutaneous
● Administer in areas with sufficient subcutaneous tissue.
● Preferred sites include upper arm, abdomen, and front thigh.
● Inject less than 0.5 mL.
● Use a 1 mL syringe and a 26-30-gauge needle.
● Insert at 90° angle or use 45° angle for thin children.
Intramuscular
● Use a 22-25-gauge, 1⁄2-1-inch needle.
● Opt for the vastus lateralis in infants and small children.
● Position child supine, side-lying, or sitting.

slides.title: ● Administer up to 0.5 mL for infants.
text: ● Administer up to 0.5 mL for infants.
● Administer up to 2 mL for children.
Ventrogluteal
● Place the child supine, side-lying, or prone.
● Administer 0.5 to 1 mL, based on the infant's muscle size.
● Administer up to 2 mL in children.
Deltoid
● Explain the procedure to the child and guardians.
● Position the child in a sitting or standing position.
● Administer up to 1 mL of medication.
● Apply topical lidocaine and prilocaine ointment for 60 min before injection.
● Change the needle after puncturing a rubber stopper.
● Opt for the smallest needle gauge possible.
● Secure the child to minimize needle movement.
● Use distraction techniques during the injection.
● Encourage guardians to hold the child afterward and ensure gentle and comforting care.
● Provide positive reinforcement and praise.
● Incorporate play therapy for engagement.
● Offer sucrose pacifiers to infants for comfort.
Poisoning
Pediatric Poisoning Nursing Considerations
First action is to identify what was ingested and call the Poison Control Center.
Lead poisoning
Symptoms: General fatigue, difficulty concentrating, Tremors, and headache.
Chelating agents (EDTA) are used to treat, which promote the urinary excretion of lead.
Acetaminophen poisoning
Symptoms: Jaundice (liver issues), confusion, and coagulation abnormalities.
Treatment includes activated charcoal to absorb the acetaminophen, and a possible gastric lavage, and eventually Acetylcysteine
(Mucomyst).
○ Acetylcysteine is the antidote for Acetaminophen Toxicity, and should be administered as a loading dose and then followed
with a maintenance dose.
○ Gastric Lavage with aspiration is appropriate if completed within 1 hour of ingestion.
○ Syrup of ipecac is no longer recommended because it induces vomiting which is a risk for aspiration.
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Treatment is the hyperbaric oxygen chamber.

slides.title: Household chemicals
text: Household chemicals
If accidentally sprayed into a child's eyes, the first nursing action is to irrigate for 5 minutes.
Child Abuse
Neglect
- Neglect involves not meeting the following:
- Basic physical needs (feeding, clothing, shelter, medical care).
- Emotional needs (nurturing, attention, affection).
- Infants aged 1 year or younger and premature infants face higher risks due to constant attention needs.
Warning signs include indicators like:
- Lack of emotional expression/flat affect.
- Poor growth/malnutrition.
- Hygiene neglect.
- Frequent injuries and a delay in seeing healthcare.
- Absence in school and self-stimulating behaviors.
Shaken baby syndrome
Symptoms: Bradycardia, apnea, drowsiness, seizures, subdural and retinal bleeding, with no external injury signs.
- Shaking causes intracranial hemorrhage. Frustrations due to an infant’s persistent crying can lead to this.
Abuse
- Should be suspected when there is a discrepancy between the injury to a child and the
expected developmental capability of the child.
Symptoms: Bite marks, bruises to the face, neck, chest, back, and abdomen, abrasions to
the knees or elbows, and bruises suggestive of being hit in various stages of healing.
- Look for glove/stocking-like burns on hands/feet, suggestive of forced boiling
water immersion.
- Note small, round burns that could result from lit cigarettes. Document findings
in detail without opinions.
- Swiftly recognize abuse. Conduct thorough history and exam. Prioritize the child's
removal from harmful environments.
- All healthcare providers must report suspected abuse cases; mandatory reporting is
essential.
- Always report to CPS.
Failure to thrive
- Delayed development. Typically seen in infants below the 5th percentile for weight or height, or with consistent weight loss.
ADHD
- Difficult to establish and many times becomes a catch-all diagnosis for children with behavioral problems.
- Treatment includes Ritalin (Methylphenidate), the child should be monitored for weight loss.
- Administer in the morning. Ensure the last dose of the day before 4 PM.
- Avoid caffeine (coffee, soda, tea, chocolate).
- Weight loss
- Monitor height and weight, and compare to baseline.
- Discuss with the provider about medication breaks.
- Administer medicine with or after meals.
Mental Health
The ATI Comprehensive Predictor is notoriously high in mental health-related questions.

slides.title: Flight of ideas
text: Flight of ideas
● A bunch of ideas, loosely related.
Echolalia
● Repeating words spoken to them.
Clang
● Rhyming (Clang Bang Sang).
Word salad
● Meaningless jumble of words that make no sense.
Neologism
● Made-up words.
Looseness of an association
● Pattern in which ideas lack an apparent logical connection to one another.
● “Derailment.”
● Seen in schizophrenia.
Affect
● A person's mood, feelings, or tone that is observable and outward manifestation.
● May be referred to as inappropriate, flat, or blunted.
Mood
● Prolonged emotional state that is expressed by the effect.
● Typically a subjective finding.
Delusions Hallucinations
False, fixed beliefs Sensory perceptions that can be auditory, visual, tactile, or
olfactory
Can be delusions of grandeur, persecutions, erotic, jealous, and
religious.
Patient appears to be listening to someone that no one else can
hear or see.
Never refute delusional thoughts, this can increase anxiety and
reinforce delusions.
Encourage the patient who was hallucinating to engage in
activities that divert their attention away, such as watching TV
or listening to music with headphones.
Never ask the patient to elaborate on the delusion. When the patient is experiencing hallucinations, it is important to
convey an acceptance of the behavior. However, let the patient
know that we do not see the same things.
Paranoia
- Psychosis that is characterized by systematized delusions of persecution or grandeur without hallucinations.
- Never challenge these patients, as this can lead to increased anger and anxiety.
- These patients are easily threatened, avoid touching them or getting too close.
Nurse-to-Patient relationship
- Introduction/orientation, working, termination phase.
Orientation phase: Establish the responsibilities and roles.
Termination stage: Starts at admission, with awareness during orientation of the ending point.
- Preparation for ending the relationship will start at the beginning.
- Always remember that nonverbal behavior is a more precise indicator of feelings.
- Closed-ended questions are considered non-therapeutic.
- NO “Why” questions, as they require analysis of the problem and often produce anxiety.
Paralanguage
- The use of vocal effects, such as tone and tempo to convey a message.

slides.title: Proxemics
text: Proxemics
- The use of spatial relationships during interaction to communicate meaning.
Effective Communication
E�ective communication skills and techniques
● Active listening: Nurse observes and comprehends the client's message, giving feedback.
● Questions: Gather specific or additional information from the client.
● Open-ended questions: Encourage spontaneous responses and interactive discussion.
● Closed-ended questions: Useful in initial interactions for specific data.
○ Avoid repeated closed-ended questions that hinder communication.
● Projective questions: Use "what-if" scenarios for exploring feelings and solutions.
● Presupposition questions: Explore life goals without the mental health disorder.
● Clarifying techniques: Confirm message accuracy using restating, reflecting, paraphrasing, and exploring.
○ Restating, reflecting, paraphrasing, and exploring.
● Showing acceptance: Express nonjudgmental interest.
● Offering self: Demonstrate willingness to spend time and genuine concern.
● Touch: Appropriately provide comfort and convey care.
Barriers to effective communication
● Minimizing feelings.
● Giving personal opinions/advice.
● Giving false reassurance.
● Changing the subject.
● “Why” questions.
● Judgments.
● Offering approval/disapproval.
● Never be confrontational.
● Never be sympathetic.
○ Sympathetic is different than empathetic.
Group therapy
● Goal-oriented: Maintains clear direction toward a specific objective.
● Advocacy: Effective leader supports and champions the nursing unit.
● Coping strategies: Engages in proactive discussions with clients to manage challenges.
Authoritative Leadership Style Democratic Leadership Style Laissez-faire Leadership Style
Directs decisions and makes choices for
the team.
Coercion: Uses pressure to drive
motivation.
Suitable for Less Educated Staff: Effective
for employees with limited formal
education.
Involves the group in decision-making
and encourages staff accomplishments.
High-Quality Work: Achieved through
cooperation and collaboration.
Allows the group to discuss relevant
topics, with minimal decision-making.
Individual Responsibility: Motivation
mainly relies on individual staff members.
Effective with Professionals: Suitable for
skilled employees.
A nurse’s priority is to promote and provide care to a client in the least restrictive environment as possible.

slides.title: Mental Health Disorders
text: Mental Health Disorders
Depression
- Patient may require assistance to perform activities of daily living.
- Patient should not be allowed to isolate themselves and may have a diminished ability to concentrate, which suggests a decrease in
overall cognitive functioning.
- Provide structured activities for these patients, as well as small groups to provide social contacts.
Major depressive disorder
- Consists of at least five of the following every day for 2 weeks: Inability to feel pleasure, difficulty sleeping or excessive
sleeping, decreased ability to concentrate, indecisiveness, depressed mood, suicidal, increase/decrease in motor activity,
increase/decrease in weight >5% of total body weight over 1 month.
ECT (electroconvulsive therapy)
- Most effective in treating patients with severe depression over a total of 6 to 12 treatments when pharmacological treatment
(Lithium) has been unsuccessful.
- 2-3 treatments are given per week.
- Requires preoperative care including consent and NPO status.
- Short-term memory loss is the most common complication.
- Succinylcholine
- The drug given to minimize muscle movement during therapy.
- Monitor for malignant hyperthermia (fever and muscle rigidity).
- Individuals with cardiac dysrhythmias are at an increased risk for complications of ECT.
- D/C Lithium
Psychotherapy
- The therapist’s notes are never included when the patient requests a copy of his or her medical records.
www.NursingPerspective.com | The Nursing Perspective, LLC | 89
Defense Mechanisms
Adaptive use of defense mechanisms
Good, will help ease anxiety.
Maladaptive use of defense mechanisms
Bad, will disallow goals to be achieved.
Compensation: Making up for weaknesses by emphasizing strengths.
Denial: Avoiding the truth by pretending not to know, which helps deal with upsetting thoughts or feelings.
Regression
● An adult who throws temper tantrums, considered maladaptive.
● A 5-year-old who begins sucking their thumb again after their brother was born.
Adaptive: A young woman might go stay with her parents after her first fight with her husband.
Projection: When a patient blames someone or something else other than the source.
● “I got in trouble with my boss because he was having a bad day.”
Reaction formation: Acts in opposition to their feelings.
● Treating someone you strongly dislike in a kind way to hide the way you actually feel.
Sublimation: Turning anxiety into something good.
● Having a bad day at work but then going to exercise to decrease anxiety.
Intellectualization: Overuses rational explanations or abstract thinking to decrease the significance of a feeling or event.
● A woman who was raped takes self-defense classes.

slides.title: Coping Mechanism
text: Coping Mechanism
- Denial: Refusing to believe the changes even when the changes are obvious to others.
- Confabulation: Making up stories in an attempt to boost self-esteem or being aware the client is not able to recall the event.
Schizophrenia
- Marked by disturbances in affect, perception, thought content, and form.
- Disorganized, incoherent speech with loose associations and may have religious content.
- When hallucinations are occurring, ask what he/she is hearing.
- Most important nursing considerations include maintaining a consistent, predictable environment and preventing
sensory overload.
Schizophrenia Medications
“Pines”- clozapine, loxapine, olanzapine
Clozapine Usage: Not primary choice for schizophrenia
spectrum disorders due to side effects.
- Agranulocytosis Risk: Potential for serious blood
condition.
- WBC Monitoring: Baseline and ongoing white blood cell
checks required.
- Inform provider of infection signs: Fever, sore throat,
mouth sores.
Haloperidol, risperidone: Initiate fall precautions
Haloperidol
- Monitor for EPS: Look for dystonia, akathisia,
pseudoparkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia.
- Pseudoparkinsonism: Signs include bradykinesia,
rigidity, shuffling gait, drooling, and tremors.
- Nursing Care: Observe for pseudoparkinsonism in the first
month, and treat with antiparkinsonian drugs like
benztropine or trihexyphenidyl.
- Other Effects: Be aware of weight gain, high cholesterol,
orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic effects.
- Combat Anticholinergic Effects: Suggest chewing
sugarless gum.
Delirium
- Acute alcohol withdrawal
- Frequently orient to time and place.
Bipolar disorder: Manic phase
- Euphoric, expansive, or irritable mood. The patient exhibits poor judgment and is easily distracted.
- If the client becomes violent, speak in an assertive tone directly to the client.
- Diagnosis Criteria: Met if the patient shows four of the following symptoms for a week.
- Includes flight of ideas, inflated self-esteem, excessive talkativeness, heightened social, occupational, or sexual activity,
reduced sleep need, and physical restlessness.
- Nutritional needs can be met by providing finger foods.
- Carrots, peanut butter sandwiches, chicken nuggets.
Nursing considerations:
- Always stay with the patient who is manic and document the client's condition every 15 minutes.
- Ensuring safety food, and rest.
- Encourage the client to take frequent breaks.
- These patients are encouraged to perform large muscle activities, such as swimming.
- These patients are discouraged from activities that are stimulating and competitive.
- Seclusion is only appropriate when the patient is engaged in frantic, aimless physical activity, and is at risk for injury.
- If threatening harm to self or others, accompany the client away from the common area.
- Limits should be placed on settings because they have trouble distinguishing boundaries.
- Medications: Lithium, risperidone, valproic acid, clonazepam.
Restraint usage

slides.title: Prescription Considerations:
text: Prescription Considerations:
● Prescribe seclusion/restraint for the shortest necessary.
duration.
● Use only when less restrictive measures aren't enough.
● For client's and others' physical protection.
Criteria for Use:
● Try less restrictive methods first.
● Written prescription from the provider is required.
● Time limits based on client's age:
Age 18+: 4 hr
Age 9-17: 2 hr
Age 8 & under: 1 hr
Continuation and Reassessment:
● Reassess and rewrite prescription every 24 hr or per facility
policy.
● Document every 15-30 min with details such as:
○ Precipitating events and prior behavior
○ Alternatives attempted
○ Restraint start and end time
○ Behavior and vital signs
○ Medications given
Emergency Use:
● Nurse can initiate in emergency; obtain written prescription
soon after.
Borderline personality disorder
- Patients have an intense fear of abandonment, severe body image issues, and impulsivity.
- When improvement starts, the nurse will want to see an improvement in “clinginess” due to the improvement of
abandonment fear.
- Most at risk for self-mutilation.
Nursing considerations:
- Firm and consistency in rules.
- Refrain from engaging in third-party conversations.
- Rotate staff members, which will reduce the incidence of splitting.
- Set limits on unacceptable behavior.
Narcissistic personality disorder
- Lack of empathy is one of the main characteristics.
- Grandiose views of self-importance, arrogance, and the need for constant admiration.
Anxiety disorder
- Patients worry about anything and everything.
- Nursing interventions should be used when patients are experiencing mild to moderate levels of anxiety.
- Include helping the client recognize sources of anxiety and teaching a client effective coping mechanisms.
- Anxiety attack nursing care
- Stay with the patient, decrease stimuli, remain calm, and medicate as necessary.
- ALWAYS stay with the patient, no matter what!
- Offer large muscle activities that help drain off excess energy, thus reducing anxiety.
- Panic anxiety
- Patient will experience severe anxiety resulting in feelings of impending doom or death.
Nursing considerations: During a panic attack, always quietly stay with the patient.
- Reduced concentration: Difficulty learning new information.
- Anxiety management: Prevent additional stimuli that may heighten anxiety.
- Do not distract with TV, discuss relaxation techniques, or demonstrate how to change the behavior.
These are not appropriate during panic.
- Post-traumatic stress disorder

slides.title: - Treatment: Exposure therapy.
text: - Treatment: Exposure therapy.
Phobic disorder
- Constant fear of an object or situation that presents no real danger.
- Treatment: exposure therapy (desensitization through gradual exposure to the trigger).
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
- Repetitive thoughts/recurring impulses to perform certain acts.
- Patients are aware of the irrationality of their actions but are unable to stop.
- Rituals are an attempt to avoid increasing anxiety to a severe level.
Nursing considerations: Allow the patient to complete their behavior, but set time limits.
Crisis intervention
- Brief, time-limited treatment that focuses on the current situation.
- Purpose is to prevent the development of future mental health problems.
- Family violence: Considered a learned behavior and will typically lead to further violence in offspring.
- Rape survivors: May experience the hospital and policy procedures as a further violation of their privacy and integrity.
Suicide
- Those at highest risk usually have a plan, a means of carrying out the plan, and a history of previous attempts.
- Always ask the client if they have a plan to end their life.
- Establish a “no suicide contract.”
- Always place the client near to the nurses’ station.
Suicide Indicators: Depression, giving away belongings, organizing finances, leaving notes, increased energy levels.
Increased Risk During Improvement: As patients feel better, suicide risk rises due to increased energy for planning.
Factors Contributing to Suicide: Prior suicide attempts, men above 50 years, teens ages 15 to 19, weak social ties, auditory
hallucinations, or major triggers like bereavement, job loss, terminal illness
- Suspect suicide risk when patients report that life is not worth living because of unrelieved pain, depression, and poor
quality of life.
Nursing considerations:
- Continuous supervision: 24/7 one-on-one observation, maintain close proximity, higher suicide risk during staff shifts.
- Frequent documentation: Record every 15 minutes.
- Belongings and safety: Search belongings with the client present and remove harmful items, allow only plastic eating
utensils, hands always visible.
- Room and medication: No private rooms, close to nurses’ station, keep doors open, ensure medication swallowing to
prevent hoarding.
- Limit visitor access.
Eating Disorders
Anorexia
Patient teaching:
○ Consume protein-rich foods with high calories and nutrients.
○ Focus on smaller portions.
○ Eat in the morning for better appetite.
○ Steer clear of food odors.
○ Avoid low-calorie foods like liquids and broth.
○ Eat cool or room temperature foods.
● Patients typically come from families who are controlling and
overprotective.
Bulimia
Patient teaching:
● Recurrent large food intake in short time (binge eating)
followed by self-induced vomiting.
● Aim to eliminate excess calories.
● Weight usually within normal range or slightly higher
● Electrolyte imbalances and cardiac arrhythmias are
potential risks.

slides.title: ● Highest priority goal is to establish adequate daily nutritional
text: ● Highest priority goal is to establish adequate daily nutritional
intake and the establishment of a consistent eating plan and
monitoring waking.
● The patient should always be monitored before, during, and after
meals.
● The temperature of these patients is decreased because of low
metabolism, blood pressure and pulse are also lower.
Patient will believe that they are grossly obese and commonly uses manipulative ploys to resist weight gain.
Substance Abuse
Denial is typically the common defense mechanism.
Alcohol withdrawal
Chronic alcohol use effects:
● Cardiovascular damage
● Liver damage (from fatty liver to cirrhosis)
● Gastritis and gastrointestinal bleeding
● Acute pancreatitis
● Sexual dysfunction
Early withdrawal signs (8-12 hours):
● Abdominal cramping, vomiting
● Tremors, diaphoresis
● Restlessness, sleep difficulty
● Increased heart rate
● Hallucinations, anxiety
● High blood pressure, respiratory rate
Medications for alcohol withdrawal:
● Librium (anti-anxiety)
● Disulfiram (deterrent to drinking; contraindicated
post-alcohol use)
● Klonopin (prevents seizures)
Alcohol withdrawal delirium:
● Occurs 2-3 days after stopping alcohol
● Severe disorientation
● Hallucinations, high blood pressure
● Cardiac dysrhythmias, delirium
● Can progress to death
Cirrhosis
- Often due to chronic alcohol use.
Symptoms: Fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain, distention, pruritus (itching), confusion, difficulty thinking, personality
changes, emotional lability, GI bleeding, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, ascites (fluid buildup), jaundice, icterus, petechiae,
ecchymoses, nosebleeds, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, peripheral edema, asterixis, fetor hepaticus (liver breath).
- Liver enzymes elevated.
ALT: Normal 4-36 units/L
AST: Normal 0-35 units/L
ALP: Normal 30-120 units/L
- Bilirubin levels are elevated in cirrhosis due to the inability of the liver to excrete bilirubin.
- Bilirubin elevated (normal 0.3 to 1.0 mg/dL).
Opioids
- Heroin: Constricted pupils, delayed reflexes, decreased blood pressure.
- Intended effects of opioids are relief from pain and a rush of euphoria.
- Antidote: Naloxone
- Withdrawal Starts with sweating, a runny nose and progresses to tremors and weakness.
- Withdrawal is very unpleasant but not life-threatening.

slides.title: CNS Stimulants
text: CNS Stimulants
- Causes increased energy and a rush of euphoria
- Cocaine: Dizziness, hypertension, seizures, extreme fever, tachycardia, chest pain.
Naloxone (Narcan)
- Counteracts narcotic-induced breathing suppression.
- Administer IV, IM, or subcutaneously.
- Avoid oral administration.
- Rapid infusion side effects: Hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting.
- Naloxone half-life is shorter than opioids.
- Monitor respirations up to 2 hr for recurrence of breathing depression.
Amphetamines (stimulants)
- Intended effects of stimulants are increased energy or euphoria.
- Withdrawal: Fatigue, craving, depression. This is not life-threatening.
Methadone
- Opioid analgesic used to treat narcotic withdrawal syndrome.
Psych Medications
Lithium
- Used for bipolar disorder. Lithium is a mood-stabilizing medication. Blood levels will be monitored.
- Expected range is 0.6 to 1.2
- Not metabolized, excreted unchanged by the kidneys.
- Toxicity can begin at 1.4.
Symptoms: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, muscle weakness/twitching,
slurred speech, coma, convulsions/seizures, and possible cardiac arrest
(hyponatremia).
- Treatment includes gastric lavage, fluid balance correction, and Mannitol to
increase urine excretion.
- Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic. Must use a filter needle when drawing
from the vial and filter in IV tubing. This prevents administering
microscopic crystals.
- Contraindications
- Avoid diuretics and AVOID NSAIDS, use Aspirin instead. Concurrent use of NSAIDs will increase renal
reabsorption of lithium, leading to toxicity.
- Fluoxetine can increase the levels of tricyclic antidepressants and lithium.
Patient teaching:
- Take with meals to avoid GI upset.
- Encourage adequate fluid and salt intake in order to prevent toxicity.
- Patient will have blood draws every month to watch the stability of levels.
Chlorpromazine
- First-generation antipsychotic to control delusions, hallucinations, and bizarre behavior (positive manifestations).
- Side effects of antipsychotics: Dry mouth, constipation, hypotension, urinary retention, tachycardia.
Haldol/Prolixin
- Can cause extrapyramidal symptoms that affect voluntary movement.
- Shuffling gait, tremors, restlessness, pill-rolling, drooling, uncoordinated jerky movement, dry mouth, and blurred
vision.
- Most common is akathisia, a form of psychomotor restlessness that can be relieved by pacing.
Artane/Cogentin
- Anticholinergic medications that may be given to control EPS symptoms.
- Can result in dry mouth. Provide the client with hard candy and encourage increased fluid intake.

slides.title: - Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI).
text: - Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI).
- Always AVOID St. John’s Wort with SSRIs.
Anticholinergic vs. Cholinergic
Anticholinergics
Anti-Secretions
These medications dry up the body.
Remember, contraindicated in anybody who is dry.
● Can’t pee (BPH, urinary retention), can’t poop
(constipated), can’t see (glaucoma).
Cholinergic
Crazy Secretions
These medications lube up the body, help patients move.
Watch out for cholinergic crisis (lots of see, pee, spit, and
poop).
Antidote is Atropine.
● Pupil constriction, difficulty with visual
accommodation.
The big four:
Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI)
- Example: Phenelzine
- Dangerous drug-food, drug-drug interactions.
- Do not take with SSRI.
- Teach patients to avoid foods high in tyramine.
- Avoid avocados, figs, bananas, fermented and aged meats, pepperoni, salami, cheese, foods containing yeast (beer and
wine), and smoked fish.
- An example of a good snack for a patient taking Phenelzine would be low-fat yogurt or a piece of
whole-grain bread.
- Patients who are on MAOIs and consume foods high in tyramine may experience a hypertensive crisis.
- Teach patients to avoid over-the-counter drugs for cough and cold.
SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors)
- Inhibits serotonin reuptake (↑ serotonin)
Citalopram (Celexa), Sertraline (Zoloft), Fluoxetine (Prozac), Paroxetine (Paxil)
- Fluoxetine increases the levels of lithium and tricyclic antidepressants.
- Sertraline can have an insomnia effect.
- Be aware of serotonin syndrome in Sertraline: Excessive sweating, fever.
Patient teaching:
- Avoid St. John’s Wort: Increases the risk for serotonin syndrome.
- Fever, anxiety, confusion, tremors, difficulty concentrating, abdominal pain, diarrhea,
hallucinations, hyperreflexia, incoordination, sweating.
- Full effects not felt for up to a month.
- Avoid concurrent use with MAOIs or TCAs.
- D/C MAOIs for 14 days prior to starting an SSRI. If already taking fluoxetine, an SSRI, the client should
wait 5 weeks before starting an MAOI.
- Side effects: Insomnia (Paroxetine), nausea, fatigue, sexual dysfunction, weight gain.
- Watch for serotonin syndrome: Agitation, hallucinations, fever, diaphoresis, tremors.
Atypical antidepressants
- Bupropion (Wellbutrin), Trazodone.

slides.title: - Used for depression and as an aid to quit smoking.
text: - Used for depression and as an aid to quit smoking.
- Side effects: Appetite suppression, weight loss, GI distress, agitation, seizure, headache.
- Headache and dry mouth may be severe and the patient should notify the provider if this occurs.
- Contraindications: Avoid use in patients with seizure disorders.
Clozaril
- Used as an atypical antipsychotic.
- Monitor patient for agranulocytosis, white blood cell levels should be monitored weekly.
- Sore throat, fever, sudden onset of flu-like symptoms.
Disulfiram (Antabuse)
- Teach patient to avoid drinking for two weeks after the last dose.
- Alcohol is present in cough medicine, vinegar, after-shave lotion, and some mouthwashes, teach to
avoid these.
- If alcohol is consumed, acetaldehyde syndrome may occur.
- Nausea, vomiting, diuresis, weakness, palpitations, weakness. and hypotension.
- May progress to respiratory/cardiovascular collapse, seizures, and death.
Extrapyramidal symptoms
- Disabling, distressing movement disorders that are associated with antipsychotic medications.
- Teach the patient that the medications will stop the voices they are hearing.
Akathisia: Frequent movements such as pacing, rocking, shifting from one foot to the other, inability to sit still.
- Patient feels restless, nervous, and unstable.
Dystonia: Involuntary muscle spasms of the tongue, face, neck, and back.
- Patient feels a frightening sudden spasm that may be painful.
Parkinsonism: Shaking of the hands and arms while at rest, stiff posture, muscle rigidity, slow movement, shuffling gait, no
swinging of the arms while walking, an expressive face, slowed thoughts.
Tardive dyskinesia: Protrusion or twisting of the tongue, smacking, person, sucking movements of the lips, puffing of the
cheeks, chewing movements of the jaw, jerking movements, shoulder shrugging.
- Patient usually feels anxious and nervous.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
- Life-threatening EPS effect of antipsychotic medications.
- Associated with the rapid increase in temperature (hyperthermia).
- Fever, dysrhythmias, muscle rigidity.
Pharmacology
Common drug class suffixes
-dipine Ca channel blocker -phylline Bronchodilator
-afil Erectile dysfunction -arin Anticoagulant
-caine Anesthetics -dine Antiulcer
-pril ACE inhibitor -zine Antihistamine
-pam, -lam Benzodiazepine -cycline Antibiotic
-statin Antilipidemic -mycin Aminoglycoside

text: -asone, -solone Corticosteroid -floxacin Antibiotic
-olol Beta blocker -tyline Tricyclic antidepressant
-cillin Penicillin -pram, -ine SSRI

-prazole Proton pump inhibitor
