Medication Check Nursing Considerations
- Never leave medication on the patient's bedside with the assumption that they will take it, always watch the patient take it or
assist them with administration.
- Medication administration: Never crush enteric-coated tablets or long-acting tablets.
- For patients with swallowing difficulty, provide soft food that is easier to swallow than liquid (oatmeal is good).
Food-Medication Interactions
Tyramine Avoid tyramine-rich foods (avocados, figs, aged cheese, yeast extracts, beer, smoked meats, smoked
fish) with MAOIs.
Tyramine + MAOIs = hypertensive crisis.
CLIENT EDUCATION: If taking an MAOI, avoid foods high in tyramine.
Vitamin K Vitamin K reduces warfarin's effectiveness, increasing clot risk.
CLIENT EDUCATION: Maintain an intake of dietary vitamin K while taking Warfarin to avoid sudden changes
that could affect the action of warfarin.
Dairy Tetracycline can interact with milk to create an insoluble compound.
CLIENT EDUCATION: Take tetracycline at least 1 hr before or 2 hr after consuming any dairy products. Follow
provider instructions for other medications that should not be taken with dairy.
Grapefruit Grapefruit juice boosts the absorption of certain meds like nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, potentially causing
stronger effects or more severe reactions.
CLIENT EDUCATION: Do not drink grapefruit juice or consume grapefruit if taking a medication it affects.
Caffeine Theophylline and caffeine can lead to excessive CNS excitation.
CLIENT EDUCATION: Avoid caffeine if taking theophylline.
Antacids,
Vitamin C
Combining aluminum-containing antacids with citrus drinks can lead to excessive aluminum absorption.
CLIENT EDUCATION: Avoid taking vitamin C supplements or drinking citrus juices at the same time as
medications that contain aluminum.
Nursing Considerations
Nasogastric and gastrostomy tubes

slides.title: - Do not give sublingual medications through the NG tube; they should be placed under the tongue instead.
text: - Do not give sublingual medications through the NG tube; they should be placed under the tongue instead.
- Do not crush specially formulated oral medications like extended-release or enteric-coated ones.
- Do not combine medications with enteral feedings.
Administering volume-controlled infusions
- Deliver certain medications (like antibiotics) intermittently in a small solution (25-250mL) through a continuous IV fluid
system or with a saline or heparin lock.
- Administer the medications for short-term and on a set schedule.
- Utilize a secondary IV bag or bottle, volume-control administration set, or mini-infusion pump.
Nitro patches/paste
- Avoid direct contact to prevent headaches.
- Always wear gloves to administer.
Antihypertensives
- Hold medication if systolic blood pressure is less than 100.
Anti-arrhythmic
- Hold medication if the heart rate is less than 60.
Morphine
- Monitor patients for bradypnea.
Morphine is contraindicated in diverticular disease because it can increase pressure in the colon, exacerbating symptoms.
Narcotics
- Before administration, assess the patient for any respiratory depression.
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)
- Monitor PCA pump settings (dose, lockout interval, 4-hour limit).
- Reassure clients about safety precautions against excessive self-administration (cannot overdose).
- Suggest using PCA before activities that may increase pain.
- Ensure adequate PCA dosing during the transition to oral opioids.
NSAIDs
- Elderly patients receiving them on a routine basis should be monitored for congestive heart failure and hypertension as a result
of fluid retention.
Iron supplements
- Take with food or immediately after meals to reduce stomach upset.
- Give orange juice with iron for better absorption.
- Side effects: Constipation, nausea, and black stools.
- Contraindications: Do not take at the same time as antacids.
Beta-blockers (Metoprolol, Atenolol)
- Decreased heart rate and myocardial contractility.
Patient teaching: Sit or lie down if experiencing dizziness or faintness. Avoid sudden changes of position and rise slowly.
Alpha-adrenergic blockers (sympatholytics)
- Prazosin, Silodosin, Doxazosin
- Effects: Venous and arterial dilation. Smooth muscle relaxation of the prostatic capsule and
bladder neck.
Patient teaching: Rise slowly when standing.
Constipation
- If a side effect of medication, teach the patient to increase their fluid intake, exercise regularly, and increase their fiber intake.
Black cohosh
- Contraindicated with antihypertensive medication due to increasing the effect of these medications.
- Acts as an estrogen substitute (might be used during menopause).
Ginseng
- Used to improve appetite.
- Can decrease the effectiveness of Timolol.

slides.title: Saw Palmetto
text: Saw Palmetto
- Saw Palmetto can decrease prostate manifestations of benign prostatic hyperplasia.
- Saw Palmetto is category X for pregnant women.
- Interactions of Saw Palmetto include additive effects with Finasteride (a urinary retention medication that treats enlarged
prostates) and can interact with antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications.
St. John’s Wort
- Used for mild depression.
- Always AVOID St. John’s wort with SSRIs.
Medications to Know
*This is only need-to-know material, not everything about each listed med*
Alteplase
- Antidote is aminocaproic acid.
- Contraindications
- Uncontrolled HTN.
- Bleeding in the last 2-4 weeks.
- Surgery in the last 3 weeks.
- Intracranial hemorrhage or internal bleeding.
Aspirin
- Administration
- Take with meals or an 8-oz glass of milk to reduce stomach irritation.
- Stop taking for 5 days before surgery.
- Avoid giving to children who have a fever or other symptoms of a viral infection due to the risk of developing Reye's
syndrome.
- Avoid chewable aspirin for one week after a tonsillectomy or any other dental surgery.
- Adverse Reaction
- Dark stools or coffee-ground emesis indicate GI bleeding, tinnitus, and hearing loss.
- Overdose
- Hearing loss, confusion, ringing in the ears, dizziness, seizures, difficulty breathing.
- Contraindications
- Diabetic patient.
- If taking aspirin, it may cause false urine glucose test, and aspirin may increase the effect of antidiabetic medication
causing low blood glucose levels.
- Other anticoagulants due to the increased risk of bleeding.
- Allergy to aspirin
- Hypotension and shock can result if severe aspirin allergy occurs.
- Avoid ibuprofen.
Tetracycline
- Used for bacterial infections, acne, and Lyme disease.
- Side effects: Tooth discoloration in children
- AVOID use in children under 8 years old and women who are pregnant.
Isoniazid (INH)
- Used in combination with other drugs, usually Rifampin, to treat tuberculosis.
- Side effects
- Vitamin B6 deficiency and GI upset.
- Serious- abdominal pain, yellowing of the skin and eyes, and dark urine, all indicate inflammation of the liver.
- Pyridoxine
- Vitamin B6 counteracts the side effects.
Patient teaching: Avoid Swiss cheese and tuna, as these foods can cause chills, headache, tiredness, rapid and pounding
heartbeat.

slides.title: Rifampin
text: Rifampin
- Used in combination with isoniazid to treat tuberculosis.
- Side effects
- Orange-colored urine, saliva, tears, sweat, and feces.
- Negate birth control pills.
- Nausea and vomiting.
- Thrombocytopenia.
Calcium channel blockers
- Nifedipine, Amlodipine, Nicardipine, Felodipine, Verapamil, Diltiazem
- Used for hypertension and angina.
- Leads to vasodilation and decreased heart rate.
- PATIENTS CANNOT HAVE GRAPEFRUIT JUICE.
Cephalosporins (Cefaclor, Cefazolin)
- Destroy bacterial cell walls causing the destruction of microorganisms.
- Cefaclor is available only in a PO formulation.
- WBC count should be within normal limits after completing the course.
Cyclosporine
- Watch for hepatotoxicity (jaundice), nephrotoxicity, gingival hyperplasia, and hirsutism.
- Contraindicated: Recent chicken pox/herpes zoster, pregnancy, recent vaccination of live virus.
Streptomycin
- Can harm cranial nerve VIII (auditory nerve).
- Due to high toxicity, limit use to clients with MDR-TB.
- Monitor hearing and tolerance due to streptomycin's ototoxicity.
- Notify provider about notable urine output changes and renal function results.
Pregabalin
- Used for patients with fibromyalgia.
- Can cause edema, dry mouth, or weight gain.
- Suck on hard candies if experience dry mouth.
Aminophylline
- Most common side effect is hypotension.
Glucosamine
- Use with caution in clients who have a shellfish allergy.
Digoxin
- Apical pulse is essential for the accurate measurement of the heart rate before administration.
- Toxicity: Visual disturbances such as green halos.
- Antidote: Digibind.
Levodopa Carbidopa
- Effects may not occur until several weeks after administration.
Nursing considerations:
- Advise patients to moderately restrict protein intake.
- Watch for orthostatic hypotension.
Amitriptyline (Elavil)
- Teach the patient that the full effects may not occur until 2 to 4 weeks after beginning therapy.
- Side effects: Anticholinergic (everything dries up)
- Urinary retention (most serious), constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, photophobia, tachycardia, orthostatic
hypotension.
MAOI inhibitors
- Isocarboxazid: Avoid foods high in tyramine.
Gentamicin
- Antibiotic that can cause hearing loss.

slides.title: - Monitor for tinnitus.
text: - Monitor for tinnitus.
- The glomerular filtration rate of the kidneys decreases with advanced age, making this client at increased risk for
nephrotoxicity.
- Increased Creatinine and BUN levels (also occurs with Tobramycin).
Alprazolam (Xanax), Midazolam
- Antidote is Flumazenil.
Levothyroxine sodium
- Side effects include rapid heart rate and palpitations.
- Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water. Needs to be 30-60 minutes before breakfast.
Coumadin
- Patient teaching: Advise patients to shave with an electric razor, use soft toothbrushes, and Report any coffee grounds or
bloody vomit or stool.
- Antidote: Vitamin K
Heparin
- Protamine sulfate is an antidote for overdose.
- Never massage the area after injection.
Lovenox (Enoxaparin)
- During the administration, the air bubble should not be removed from the pre-filled syringe.
- Watch for bleeding signs: Elevated heart rate, lower blood pressure, bruising, petechiae, hematomas, and black tarry stools.
- AVOID Aspirin when using Enoxaparin.
- For Toxicity: Administer Protamine (Heparin antagonist).
- Rotate injection sites between abdominal walls, 2 inches away from the umbilicus.
- Inject at a 90-degree angle, full needle insertion, NO aspirating or massaging. Use the entire contents of the syringe.
Zidovudine
- Can cause bone marrow problems.
Patient teaching: Notify provider of the development of chills, fever, and sore throat.
Chemotherapeutic agents
Patient teaching: Avoid those with infections and large crowds due to immunosuppression. No fresh flowers in the room.
- If any chemotherapy drugs are spilled, the nurse must follow the facility procedure in the safe handling of hazardous material
spill (an example is doxorubicin hydrochloride).
Dilantin
Patient teaching: Maintain a comprehensive oral hygiene program due to the risk of gingival hyperplasia. Advise the patient
that this drug can also cause constipation and drowsiness and irritation to GI tissues.
Thiazide diuretics
- Promotes diuresis when renal function is not impaired.
Chlorthalidone and Chlorothiazide
- The body loses water and potassium.
- Adverse Effects: Hyperuricemia, hypomagnesemia, increased lipids, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia and hypochloremia,
dehydration and hyponatremia.
Nursing considerations:
- Watch for low magnesium signs (weakness, muscle twitching, tremors).
- Check for rising blood glucose levels.
- Eat potassium-rich foods, and be aware of hypokalemia symptoms (nausea/vomiting, weakness, fatigue, leg cramps).
- Observe for dehydration (dry mouth, thirst, low urine, weight loss).
- Monitor electrolytes, weight, and urine output (<30 mL/hr).
- Report urine output less than 30 mL/hr. Stop medication, and notify the provider.
Prednisone
- IV: Used for short-term in patients with status asthmaticus. Prevents inflammation, suppresses airway mucus production, and
promotes responsiveness of Beta 2 receptors in bronchial tree as well as reduces airway mucosa edema.
- Inhaled: Long-term prophylaxis of asthma.

slides.title: - Promotes lung maturity and decreases respiratory distress in fetuses at risk for preterm birth.
text: - Promotes lung maturity and decreases respiratory distress in fetuses at risk for preterm birth.
- Acts on the body's metabolism to increase blood glucose and decrease potassium.
- Monitor the patient for any signs of infection or delayed healing of wounds.
- Monitor patients for hyperglycemia and must taper off the drug.
- Avoid stopping the medication abruptly.
- Monitor for black, tarry stools.
Steroids
- Monitor patients for hyperglycemia.
Ibuprofen
- Take with food or antacid to reduce stomach upset.
- Supplements such as feverfew, garlic, and ginger can increase the risk of bleeding in patients who are taking NSAIDs.
- Ginkgo biloba can suppress coagulation. Use with caution in patients who are taking NSAIDs.
- Monitor for GI bleeding: Coffee-ground emesis, abdominal pain, or bloody or black, tarry stools.
Contraindications
- Do not take if allergic to aspirin.
- Do not take if the patient has impaired kidney function.
- Do not take if the patient has a history of stomach ulcers.
Strong iodine solution (Lugol’s solution)
- Non-radioactive iodine. Used in hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis and in preparation for thyroidectomy to reduce thyroid
gland size.
- Post-thyroidectomy, assess the patient for laryngeal stridor.
- Inhibits thyroid production and release due to high levels of iodide.
- Side effects: GI upset, hypersensitivity (rash, pruritus), Iodism.
- Iodism: Metallic taste, stomatitis, sore teeth and gums, frontal headache, rash.
- Stomatitis: Use a soft bristle toothbrush.
- Antidote: Sodium thiosulfate used to reverse iodine.
Patient teaching: Mix with juice to improve taste. Avoid foods high in iodine (iodized salt, seafood). Increase fluid intake.
Medications Requiring Frequent Monitoring
Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
- Contraindicated in liver disease.
- Toxicity can be shown in hepatic necrosis. Assess ALT and AST (liver tests) in patients with Acetaminophen overdose.
Aminoglycosides
- Monitor for ototoxicity (cochlear and vestibular), neurotoxicity, and nephrotoxicity
- Monitor for tinnitus or hearing loss, vertigo, rash, dizziness, or difficulty urinating.
Amitriptyline (Elavil)
Contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma and with MAOI inhibitors.
- Side effects include drowsiness, sedation, lethargy, dry mouth and eyes, blurred vision, hypotension, and tachycardia.
- Advise patients to use sunscreen.
Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
Contraindicated in bone marrow suppression.
- Toxicity can be shown in drowsiness, dizziness, and ataxia.
- Lined to Stevens-Johnson syndrome (fatal). Notify the provider if a rash occurs.
- Advise patient to use sunscreen and wear a medical alert bracelet.
- Makes oral contraceptives, Warfarin, and theophylline ineffective.
Chlordiazepoxide (Librium)
Contraindicated with comatose patients with CNS depression or narrow-angle glaucoma.
- Toxicity can be shown in drowsiness, dizziness, and delirium tremens may occur in alcohol withdrawal patients.
Disopyramide (norpace)

slides.title: Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, second or third-degree heart blocks, and sick sinus syndrome.
text: Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, second or third-degree heart blocks, and sick sinus syndrome.
- Toxicity can be shown in symptoms of congestive heart failure.
Diazepam (Valium)
- Benzodiazepine
- Along with Lorazepam, Chlordiazepoxide, Clorazepate, Oxazepam, and Clonazepam.
Contraindicated in comatose patients with CNS depression, and narrow-angle glaucoma.
- Toxicity can be shown in sedation with Ataxia, dizziness, and slurred speech.
- Avoid grapefruit juice.
Digoxin
Contraindicated in uncontrolled ventricular arrhythmias or AV blocks.
- Dysrhythmias due to digoxin toxicity may occur in a patient with hypokalemia.
- Side effects include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances, and bradycardia.
Doxepin
Contraindicated narrow-angle glaucoma.
- Toxicity can be shown in sedation, fatigue, blurred vision, hypertension, dry mouth, and constipation.
- Advise patients to always wear sunscreen.
Glucocorticoids
Contraindicated in serious infections.
- Monitor patient for adrenal insufficiency, with symptoms such as hypotension, weight loss, weakness, nausea and vomiting,
lethargy, confusion, and restlessness.
- Other serious side effects include depression or euphoria, personality changes, hypertension, decrease wound healing, patiki
eye, ecchymosis, hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, hypernatremia, fluid retention, osteoporosis, Cushing’s appearance via moon
face and buffalo hump.
Patient teaching: Monitor patient's blood sugar, BUN/creatinine levels. Medication should not be abruptly discontinued, and
taper off over the course of two to four weeks.
Lithium
Contraindicated in severe cardiovascular renal disease, as well as dehydrated or debilitated patients.
- Toxicity can be shown in vomiting, diarrhea, slurred speech, drowsiness, muscle weakness, and twitching.
- Fine hand tremors are expected, coarse hand tremors are a sign of toxicity.
Patient teaching: Effects will be seen within 1 to 3 weeks after the start of initial therapy. Maintain adequate sodium and fluid
intake to avoid toxicity.
Lidocaine (Xylocaine)
Contraindicated in advanced AV block.
- Toxicity can be shown in confusion, blurred or double vision, nausea, vomiting, ringing of the ears, tremors, convulsions,
difficulty breathing, severe dizziness, and bradycardia.
Magnesium sulfate
Contraindicated in patients with hypermagnesemia, hypocalcemia, anuria, and heart block.
- Toxicity can be seen in decreased respiratory rate, bradycardia, arrhythmia, hypotension, flushing, sweating, absence of
patellar deep tendon reflexes, urine retention (less than 30 mL/hr), decreased LOC, and hypothermia.
Nursing considerations: Measure the client’s urine output hourly.
- If suspected toxicity occurs, stop infusion IMMEDIATELY.
- Prepare the patient for respiratory or cardiac arrest and have Calcium Gluconate available (antidote).
Patient teaching: Monitor neuro status before and throughout therapy and initiate seizure precautions.
Phenobarbital
Contraindicated in comatose patients with CNS depression.
- Toxicity can be seen in confusion, drowsiness, dyspnea, slurred speech, and staggering.
Phenytoin (Dilantin)
Nursing considerations: Ensure good oral hygiene (dental flossing). Folic acid supplements can decrease the occurrence.

Contraindicated in decompensated congestive heart failure, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, bradycardia, and heart
blocks.
- Toxicity can be seen in bradycardia, dizziness, drowsiness, dyspnea, bluish fingernails or palms, and seizures.
- Caution diabetic patients to closely monitor blood sugar levels.
Quinidine
Contraindicated in conduction defects and digitalis glycosides toxicity.
- Toxicity can be seen in tinnitus, hearing loss, visual disturbance, headache, nausea, and vomiting.
- Cardiotoxicity includes QRS widening and asystole, as well as ventricular ectopic beats, paradoxical tachycardia, and arterial
embolism.
Salicylate
Contraindicated in hypersensitivity to aspirin or other salicylates, bleeding disorders, or thrombocytopenia.
- Toxicity can be seen in tinnitus, headache, hyperventilation, mental confusion, lethargy, diarrhea, and sweating.
Theophylline
- Main action is to relax bronchial smooth muscles.
- Give with food to prevent GI upset.
- Toxicity: Dizziness, vomiting, agitation, apical pulse above 200.
Contraindicated in uncontrolled arrhythmias and hyperthyroidism.
- Toxicity can be seen in anorexia, nausea and vomiting, stomach cramps, diarrhea, confusion, headache, flushing of the skin,
increased urination, insomnia, and tacky arrhythmias.
- First signs of toxicity include tachycardia, ventricular arrhythmias, and seizures.
Valproic acid (depakene)
Contraindicated in hepatic impairment.
- Toxicity can be seen in anorexia, nausea and vomiting, yellowing of the skin and eyes, fever, sore throat, weakness, facial
edema, lethargy, unusual bleeding or bruising, and seizures.
- The main side effect is hepatotoxicity.

Test-Taking Strategies
Use priority-setting guidelines to answer questions.
Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs
● Indicates that physiological needs come first, followed by safety and security; love and belonging; self-esteem; and
self-actualization.
ABC
● Airway, breathing, and circulation needs will frequently take priority.
● NEVER perform ABC checks blindly without considering whether ABC issues are acute vs. chronic or stable vs. unstable.
● For example: A client who is quadriplegic and receiving ventilation has chronic airway/breathing problems. However, if there
is not an acute consideration such as pneumonia, the client should be considered chronic and stable. This client would not be
the nurse’s first priority.
● Airway is always the first priority.
○ Note that an exception occurs when cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is performed; in this situation, the nurse
follows CAB (compressions, airway, breathing) guidelines.
Always go with the least invasive action before the most invasive!
NEVER leave the client. Always choose the answer that keeps the nurse with the client.
Rule out an option if you know it is associated with something else.
● For example: You may not know about the lab value for Warfarin therapy, but you do know the lab values for heparin and
aspirin. Those values can be eliminated because you are using what you know.
Early vs. Late Signs/Symptoms
● Early manifestations are generalized and nonspecific whereas late signs are specific and serious. Eliminate incorrect answer
choices by using this strategy.
Prevent Harm

slides.title: ● When in doubt, always choose a nursing action that could prevent harm to the client. Even if you don’t know whether it
text: ● When in doubt, always choose a nursing action that could prevent harm to the client. Even if you don’t know whether it is
related to the stem, it is still a life-saving maneuver that, in all likelihood, is correct.
Safe and Effective Delegation
● RNs perform all initial client teaching. The Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) may reinforce teaching performed by the RN.
● RNs should perform all admission assessments and vital signs so that an accurate baseline is established.
● Client care assignments are made by the RN, not the support staff.
